lessons.title: Vectors, matrices and gradients
lessons.goal: Models work with numbers arranged in lists and tables. A vector is an ordered list of features, such as a flower's length and width. A matrix holds several such lists or the weights that combine them. Calculus tells us how changing one weight would change a prediction or its error.
section_titles: Vectors: numbers with a shared meaning
The matrix derivative you will actually use
topics: Gradient: how the weight affects error
The matrix derivative you will actually use

lessons.title: Probability, uncertainty and statistics
lessons.goal: Probability describes how likely different outcomes are. Statistics uses a finite set of observations to estimate quantities such as a model's accuracy. These are related but different: a model's confidence in one prediction is not the same as our uncertainty about an accuracy measured on a small test set.
section_titles: Probability is a distribution over possibilities

lessons.title: Training, validation and generalization
lessons.goal: A model learns from training examples, but we want it to work on new examples. That is generalization. To check it honestly, separate data used to learn weights, data used to choose settings, and data reserved for the final evaluation.
topics: Fit candidate models on training data
Evaluate on the reserved test set
A transfer experiment that separates style from definition

lessons.title: How models learn: loss and optimization
lessons.goal: Training adjusts a model's learned numbers so its predictions better match examples. The usual loop is: calculate a prediction, measure its error with a loss function, compute how each weight affects the loss, and use an optimizer to update the weights. A neural network repeats this idea across many connected layers.
section_titles: From a linear score to a network

lessons.title: Evaluation metrics
lessons.goal: A metric turns predictions and known answers into a number that summarizes one aspect of performance. Different metrics answer different questions: accuracy counts correct decisions, recall counts recovered positives, and a numerical error measures distance from a target value. Choose a metric to match the task and the consequences of mistakes, not because it gives the largest-looking score.
section_titles: Choose the quantity before comparing models
topics: Accuracy: fraction of all cases correct

lessons.title: Machine learning tasks and baselines
lessons.goal: Machine learning fits a rule from examples rather than writing every decision by hand. In supervised learning, each training example has input features and a target: classification predicts a category, while regression predicts a number. Unsupervised learning instead looks for patterns without these target labels.
topics: Why high accuracy can be misleading
Compare models on the same problem

lessons.title: Features and preprocessing
lessons.goal: Most models need inputs in a consistent numerical form. Preprocessing handles missing values, represents categories and puts numerical measurements on suitable scales. Some transformations learn statistics from data, so they must be fitted on training data and reused unchanged on new cases.
section_titles: Example: test the effect of scaling
topics: Example: test the effect of scaling
Settings: Numeric scaling, Missing-value handling, Feature encoding

lessons.title: Linear regression
lessons.goal: Linear regression predicts a number by adding weighted feature contributions and, usually, a constant intercept. Fitting chooses weights that reduce prediction errors on training examples. Ridge regression adds a cost for large weights, which can make the fit less sensitive to limited or correlated data.
section_titles: Example: choose the task for an ordered rating
From the loss to a stable solver
topics: Example: choose the task for an ordered rating
From the loss to a stable solver
Settings: Fit intercept, Solver tolerance, Solver iteration limit

lessons.title: Logistic regression and classification
lessons.goal: Classification predicts a category rather than a numerical measurement. Binary logistic regression first calculates a weighted score, then maps it to a probability for one of two classes. A separate decision threshold turns that probability into a yes/no prediction.
section_titles: Why cross-entropy gives a useful update
topics: Choose a class using a threshold
Training loss for a known label
Why cross-entropy gives a useful update
Settings: Inverse regularization C, Class weighting

lessons.title: Regularization and model selection
lessons.goal: A model can fit its training examples closely but perform poorly on new data. Regularization discourages some kinds of overly flexible fit, for example by penalizing large coefficients. Model selection uses validation data to choose how much regularization or complexity to allow.
section_titles: Example: tune inside the training folds
Why choosing the best result is itself learning
topics: Example: tune inside the training folds
Why choosing the best result is itself learning
Settings: Penalty strength, L1 share, Polynomial feature degree

lessons.title: Nearest neighbours, kernels and SVMs
lessons.goal: Nearest-neighbour prediction compares a new example with stored training examples and uses the answers of the closest ones. It is a local rule: the prediction depends on nearby cases rather than one fitted line. A support vector machine, or SVM, is a different method that learns a separating boundary with a margin.
section_titles: Example: compare nearest neighbours and SVMs
Margin, kernel and regularization work together
topics: A different method: SVM and kernels
Example: compare nearest neighbours and SVMs
Margin, kernel and regularization work together
Settings: Number of neighbours, Neighbour weighting, Minkowski distance power

lessons.title: Naive Bayes classification
lessons.goal: Naive Bayes predicts a class by combining how common the class is with how likely the observed features are within that class. For example, a word can be more common in spam than ordinary email. With several features, the model simplifies the calculation by treating them as independent once the class is known; that is the 'naive' assumption.
section_titles: Bayesian updating: keep a distribution over a probability
Probabilistic graphical models: factor a joint distribution
topics: Multiply each prior by its likelihood
Bayesian updating: keep a distribution over a probability
Probabilistic graphical models: factor a joint distribution

lessons.title: Decision trees and random forests
lessons.goal: A decision tree predicts by asking feature questions, such as whether a measurement is below a cutoff. Each answer sends an example down one branch until a leaf returns a prediction. A random forest trains many varied trees and combines their predictions, making the result less dependent on one particular tree.
section_titles: How trees differ from random forests
Tree depth, leaf size and forest size
Example: feature importance is not causality

Tree depth, leaf size and forest size
Example: feature importance is not causality

lessons.title: Gradient boosting
lessons.goal: Gradient boosting builds a predictor in stages. Each new small model tries to correct errors made by the current combined model. For squared-error regression, the correction can be trained on the remaining differences between targets and predictions. This differs from a random forest, whose trees are trained without sequentially correcting a running prediction.
section_titles: A boosting update, not just a collection of trees
topics: A boosting update, not just a collection of trees
Settings: Boosting learning rate, Boosting rounds, Boosting row fraction
Settings: Maximum boosting leaves, Development-based stopping

lessons.title: Probability calibration and decision costs
lessons.goal: Two models can make the same yes/no decisions but assign different probabilities. Calibration asks whether those probabilities agree with observed frequencies: among predictions made with about 80% confidence, roughly 80% should be correct in an appropriate evaluation population. Decision costs ask a separate question: how harmful are false alarms and missed cases?
section_titles: Example: separate confidence from test uncertainty
topics: Choose a cutoff from error costs
Example: separate confidence from test uncertainty

lessons.title: Clustering and K-means
lessons.goal: Clustering groups examples without using target class labels. K-means describes each group by a center, assigns training points to their nearest center, then moves each center to the mean of its assigned points. Repeating these two steps seeks compact groups; it does not establish that the groups are meaningful real-world categories.
section_titles: Example: inspect clusters without using labels to fit
How a Gaussian mixture learns soft assignments
topics: Example: inspect clusters without using labels to fit
How a Gaussian mixture learns soft assignments
Settings: Number of clusters, Cluster restarts, Density radius
Settings: Density minimum population, Mixture covariance structure

lessons.title: PCA, dimensionality reduction and anomalies
lessons.goal: Dimensionality reduction replaces many input features with fewer coordinates. Principal component analysis, or PCA, chooses directions that preserve as much training-data variance as possible. Reconstructing an input from those fewer coordinates shows information that was lost. A large reconstruction error can be an anomaly signal, but does not prove that an example is invalid.
section_titles: PCA versus feature selection and anomaly methods
Example: separate compression from prediction quality
topics: PCA versus feature selection and anomaly methods
Example: separate compression from prediction quality
Settings: PCA components, PCA whitening, Assumed anomaly fraction

lessons.title: Time-series forecasting
lessons.goal: Forecasting predicts a future value using information available when the prediction is made. A time series is a sequence of observations ordered in time, such as daily demand. A forecast origin is the prediction time; the horizon is how far ahead we predict. These boundaries determine which inputs are legitimate.
topics: Mark when the forecast is made
Settings: Forecast history lags, Forecast horizon, Temporal evaluation gap

lessons.goal: A recommender ranks items, such as films or products, for a user. A simple model scores how well learned user and item vectors match. When today's choice also affects future outcomes, we need a sequential-decision view rather than treating each recommendation as an isolated ranking problem.

lessons.title: Generalization and distribution shift
lessons.goal: Generalization means performing well on new examples, not only examples used for fitting. A score may change because the new population contains a different mixture of easy and difficult cases. Distribution shift is the broader name for a change between the data used to develop a model and the data where it is evaluated or used.

lessons.title: Neural networks and multilayer perceptrons
lessons.goal: A neural network combines learned weighted sums with nonlinear functions. A multilayer perceptron, or MLP, uses dense layers: each output feature reads all features in the preceding layer. Hidden layers create intermediate representations that can support a more flexible prediction rule than one linear transformation.
section_titles: Example: when deeper is not better
topics: Example: when deeper is not better
Settings: Hidden width, Hidden layers, Activation function

lessons.title: Backpropagation and automatic differentiation
lessons.goal: Backpropagation calculates how each trainable weight affects a loss by following the model's operations backwards. It applies the chain rule and adds contributions when a weight affects the loss through several paths. Automatic differentiation records these operations for you; the optimizer, not backpropagation itself, changes the weights.
section_titles: Autograd, manual derivatives and graph retention
topics: Gradient buffers and the optimizer step
Autograd, manual derivatives and graph retention

lessons.title: Optimizers, initialization and training stability
lessons.goal: An optimizer turns gradients into parameter updates. Plain stochastic gradient descent, or SGD, subtracts a learning-rate-scaled gradient. Adam keeps moving averages of gradients and squared gradients to adapt update sizes. Initialization chooses the starting weights; a schedule changes learning rate over time. These are related choices, not interchangeable methods.
section_titles: Starting weights, normalization and update size
Adam, weight decay, clipping and schedules
topics: Starting weights, normalization and update size
Adam, weight decay, clipping and schedules
Settings: Optimizer learning rate, Gradient norm limit, Optimizer
Settings: SGD momentum, Adam first-moment decay, Adam second-moment decay

Settings: Decoupled weight decay, Learning-rate schedule

lessons.title: Regularization, dropout and training diagnostics
lessons.goal: Regularization changes training to discourage a model from relying too strongly on limited or accidental patterns. Dropout is one method: during training it randomly masks activation values, encouraging the network to cope without any particular selected feature. It does not permanently delete weights, and it is not a guaranteed improvement.
section_titles: Choosing a response to training failures
Example: compare dropout with the same split
topics: Choosing a response to training failures
Example: compare dropout with the same split
Settings: Dropout probability, Early-stopping patience, Label smoothing

lessons.title: Convolutional neural networks
lessons.goal: A convolutional neural network, or CNN, learns local pattern detectors and reuses their weights across image positions. Each filter produces a feature map. Stacking convolutions and nonlinearities lets later features combine earlier patterns; pooling can reduce spatial resolution, and a final head maps the remaining features to task outputs.
section_titles: Local filters, channels and receptive fields
Shapes through the actual local CNN
Vision Transformers: turn image patches into a sequence

lessons.title: Residual networks and transfer learning
lessons.goal: A residual block adds its input to a transformed version of that input: output = input + correction. This shortcut lets information and gradients use a direct path around the transformation. Transfer learning is a separate choice: reuse a pretrained model and decide which parameters to freeze or adapt. Residual architectures can be trained from scratch or transferred.
section_titles: Contrastive image–text learning and multimodal transfer
topics: Contrastive image–text learning and multimodal transfer

lessons.title: Recurrent networks, GRUs and LSTMs
lessons.goal: A recurrent neural network (RNN) processes an ordered sequence by updating a state at each position. The same cell weights are reused over time, so the current output can depend on earlier inputs. A vanilla RNN has one hidden-state update; a gated recurrent unit (GRU) controls how new and old states are mixed, and long short-term memory (LSTM) additionally maintains a separate cell-memory state.
section_titles: State, gates and allowed sequence history
GRU gate convention and gradient history
topics: State, gates and allowed sequence history
GRU gate convention and gradient history
Settings: Sequence window, Recurrent hidden width, Bidirectional context

lessons.title: Attention and Transformer building blocks
lessons.goal: Attention updates a representation by taking a weighted combination of value vectors. A query is compared with keys to calculate matching scores; after masking forbidden positions, softmax turns those scores into mixing weights. The values supply the content being combined. Attention weights are not automatically explanations of truth or model correctness.
topics: Settings: Attention hidden width, Attention query heads

lessons.title: Autoencoders and self-supervised representations
lessons.goal: An autoencoder learns to encode an input into a representation and decode it back into a reconstruction. A bottleneck can limit how much information passes through, but accurate copying alone does not prove the representation is useful for another task. Self-supervised learning is broader: its training targets are derived from the data rather than supplied as separate human labels.

lessons.title: Generative models: VAEs, GANs and diffusion
lessons.goal: A generative model learns a way to produce new samples with patterns resembling its training data. The main families use different mechanisms: a variational autoencoder, or VAE, encodes a distribution over latent codes and decodes samples; a generative adversarial network (GAN) trains a generator against a real/fake discriminator; diffusion learns to remove controlled noise. Their objectives are not interchangeable quality scores.

lessons.title: Graph neural networks
lessons.goal: A graph represents objects as nodes and relationships as edges. A graph neural network, or GNN, updates node features by collecting messages from connected neighbours. Its calculation therefore depends on both the feature values and which connections are present; merely listing nodes in a table would omit important information.

lessons.title: Prediction heads, targets and losses
lessons.goal: A prediction head maps learned features to the outputs a task needs. One class for a whole example, one label for each token, a numerical value and a segmentation map need different shapes and objectives. The head, target alignment, loss reduction and evaluation metric must agree with one another.

lessons.title: The neural training loop and its system state
lessons.goal: Training is a repeated procedure: fetch a batch, calculate predictions and loss, compute gradients and update trainable parameters. The data loader, device, optimizer state and checkpoint rules are part of that procedure, not extra neural-network layers. Validation checks a model without fitting on those cases; saving state makes selected results or later resumption possible.

lessons.title: Compare neural and classical models
lessons.goal: A useful neural-model experiment asks whether it improves a real outcome over a strong classical alternative. Both candidates need the same target definition and held-out evaluation cases. Their preprocessing and fitting procedures may differ, but each must use legitimate training information and a declared selection budget.

lessons.title: Language, tokens and model inputs
lessons.goal: Natural language processing, or NLP, builds systems that analyze or produce human language. A model first needs a numerical input: tokenization splits text into chosen units, and a vocabulary assigns each unit an integer ID. These units are not necessarily words, and the IDs do not represent meaning by their numerical size.

Learning BPE rules and comparing tokenizer families

lessons.title: Embeddings, similarity and retrieval
lessons.goal: An embedding represents an object, such as a token, sentence or document, as a numerical vector. A retrieval system compares a query with candidate documents and returns a ranked list. Vector similarity can help find related text, but it does not establish that the text answers the question or supports a claim.
topics: Use compatible query and document vectors

lessons.title: NLP tasks and annotation guidelines
lessons.goal: An NLP task specifies what a system must predict from language: a document label, a token tag, an answer span, a relation or a generated sequence. Annotation guidelines explain what each label means and which context may be used. A task name such as sentiment or argument identification is not enough to define the correct answer.

Record the policy and independent sources

lessons.title: Text processing, morphology and source offsets
lessons.goal: Text processing changes how language is represented before a model uses it. Normalization, stemming, lemmatization and subword tokenization perform different jobs and may discard different information. Extraction tasks also need a reliable map back to the original text so that a predicted name or answer can be located exactly.
topics: Keep original text and offset conventions
Check whether a transformation changes meaning
Distinguish lemmas, stems and subword pieces
Align word labels and model pieces

lessons.title: Word counts, TF-IDF and lexical retrieval
lessons.goal: A bag-of-words representation gives each vocabulary term a feature column and counts its occurrences in a document. TF-IDF weights those counts using term frequency and inverse document frequency, reducing the relative influence of terms that occur across many documents. This supplies sparse features for classification or lexical search without learning contextual word meaning.

Fitting text features without test leakage

lessons.title: Naive Bayes and linear text classifiers
lessons.goal: A text classifier turns a feature representation into a task label. Multinomial Naive Bayes combines class-specific word probabilities; logistic regression combines learned feature weights into a conditional class score. Both can use simple lexical features, but they estimate different quantities and should be evaluated rather than ranked by their complexity.
section_titles: Class probabilities, linear weights and margins
topics: Class probabilities, linear weights and margins

lessons.title: N-gram language models and smoothing
lessons.goal: A language model assigns probabilities to text sequences, often by predicting each token from an earlier history. An n-gram model restricts that history to the previous n−1 tokens. Smoothing adjusts count estimates so that unseen continuations can receive probability rather than making an entire held-out sequence impossible.
topics: Fix the history and next-token vocabulary

lessons.title: Static word vectors: Word2vec, GloVe and fastText
lessons.goal: A static word embedding assigns a reusable numerical vector to a word or lexical unit. Word2vec, GloVe and fastText learn these vectors from different forms of corpus evidence. Nearby vectors can capture useful regularities, but the same static lookup does not change meaning according to the sentence in which a word appears.
section_titles: Averaging, vocabulary coverage and vector bias

Score the positive and negative pairs
Averaging, vocabulary coverage and vector bias

lessons.title: Convolutional networks for text
lessons.goal: A text convolutional neural network applies shared filters to nearby positions in a sequence. A filter can detect local patterns across token embeddings or characters, and pooling summarizes responses for a larger unit such as a sentence. Local feature extraction and sentence-level aggregation are separate operations with different information losses.
section_titles: Text convolution, channels and local windows
topics: Arrange token features in sequence order
Reuse one filter across local windows
Text convolution, channels and local windows

lessons.title: Recurrent and bidirectional recurrent networks
lessons.goal: A recurrent neural network, or RNN, processes a sequence by updating a hidden state at each position. The state combines the current token with information carried from earlier positions. A bidirectional RNN adds a separate right-to-left pass, allowing each aligned token representation to use both sides of an already available input.
section_titles: Padding, terminal states and gradient paths
topics: Set sequence order and directional parameters
Choose token outputs or terminal summaries
Padding, terminal states and gradient paths

lessons.title: LSTMs and bidirectional LSTMs
lessons.goal: A long short-term memory network, or LSTM, is a recurrent model with a cell state for carried memory and a hidden state exposed to other layers. Gates determine how much old memory to retain, new information to write and memory to expose. A bidirectional LSTM uses two independent such recurrences when both input directions are available.
section_titles: Cell state, gates and hidden output
topics: Read the token and both previous states
Align directions for the downstream task
Cell state, gates and hidden output

lessons.title: GRUs and recurrent training
lessons.goal: A gated recurrent unit, or GRU, controls a recurrent hidden state without a separate LSTM memory cell. The reset gate controls old-state information used in the candidate; the update gate mixes the candidate with the old state. The exact gate convention and reset placement must be read from the equation, because implementations can differ.
section_titles: Gradient history, parameter counts and packed batches
topics: Read the token and previous hidden state
Mix the candidate and old state
Gradient history, parameter counts and packed batches

lessons.title: Encoder–decoder models, attention and beam search
lessons.goal: An encoder–decoder model represents an input sequence and generates a separate output sequence. Attention lets a decoder read different source positions while producing each target token. Beam search is a decoding procedure that keeps several candidate target prefixes; it changes the search, not the learned model weights or the definition of attention.

lessons.title: Sequence labelling with HMMs, CRFs and Viterbi
lessons.goal: Sequence labelling assigns a tag to each position while allowing neighboring tags to influence one another. A hidden Markov model, or HMM, uses probabilities for hidden transitions and observed emissions; a conditional random field, or CRF, uses scores to model tag sequences given an input. Viterbi finds a best path, while summing paths supplies a different normalization calculation.
section_titles: From tag sequences to exact entities
topics: Keep the best prefix for each ending tag
Sum paths to obtain a normalizer

From tag sequences to exact entities

lessons.title: Syntax: dependency and constituency parsing
lessons.goal: Syntactic parsing predicts how words form a grammatical structure. A dependency parse connects words through head–dependent links; a constituency parse groups spans into nested phrases. These are alternative representations of a sentence, not successive processing stages or the same object as a list of word-class tags.

lessons.title: Contextual token encoders: ELMo and BERT
lessons.goal: A contextual encoder gives a token a representation that depends on its occurrence, not just its word identity. ELMo combines directional recurrent language-model features; BERT uses bidirectional Transformer context and masked-token pretraining. These methods produce token-level features that still need an appropriate head or pooling rule for a downstream task.
section_titles: Token outputs, pooling and task heads
topics: Produce one contextual vector per position
Choose a downstream representation and head
Token outputs, pooling and task heads

lessons.title: Sentence encoders and query–document interaction
lessons.goal: A sentence encoder represents a larger text unit for comparison rather than assigning one static vector to each word. A bi-encoder computes query and document representations separately; a cross-encoder reads the pair jointly; late interaction keeps token vectors and compares them later. Where the texts first interact determines caching, computation and what information can be compared.
topics: Choose separate query and document encoding
Pool valid query states and normalize
Compare vectors and calculate a training loss

lessons.title: Text classification and paired-input inference
lessons.goal: Text classification maps a document, token sequence or input pair to a defined label structure. Single-label classification chooses one mutually exclusive class; multilabel classification can assign several labels at once. The target structure determines the loss and decoding rule, not merely how many label names appear in a dataset.
topics: Decode labels with a declared decision rule
Match the head to the input and output unit

lessons.title: Information extraction: entities, relations and events
lessons.goal: Information extraction converts text into structured records about mentions, entities, relations and events. A mention is a source span; coreference links mentions intended to refer to the same entity. Relation and event extraction add typed connections or roles. A valid output format does not by itself make these records supported by the text.
topics: Group mentions that share a referent
Extract typed relations and event roles

lessons.title: Machine translation and BLEU evaluation
lessons.goal: Machine translation produces a target-language sequence intended to preserve a source's meaning. Automatic reference-based metrics compare a candidate with permitted reference translations, but they test different kinds of agreement. BLEU combines clipped n-gram precision with a brevity penalty; the simple example here isolates unigram BLEU-1 rather than implementing standard corpus BLEU.
topics: Fix the candidate, reference and token units
Audit meaning and report scorer settings

lessons.title: Question answering, answer spans and abstention
lessons.goal: Question answering predicts an answer to a question under a defined information-access setting. An extractive reader chooses a span in supplied context; a generative system may produce new wording. Answer correctness, source support and deciding when no answer is available are separate requirements, with different evaluation rules.
section_titles: Answer spans, generated answers and missing answers
Exact match, token overlap and source support

Compare exact match and answer-token F1
Decide when to abstain and localize failures

lessons.title: Summarization, dialogue and source faithfulness
lessons.goal: Summarization selects and compresses source content, either by extracting passages or generating new wording. Source faithfulness asks whether the output preserves what the source supports; external truth asks a different question. Dialogue adds an interaction goal: helping a user may require clarification, correction or abstention rather than simply producing agreeable text.
topics: Identify the source claim and its scope
Check whether the candidate changes meaning
Interpret lexical overlap as limited evidence
Evaluate useful interaction, not automatic agreement

lessons.title: Inference, discourse and argument mining
lessons.goal: Language understanding involves more than classifying a sentence in isolation. Natural-language inference compares a premise with a hypothesis; discourse analysis relates text units; argument mining identifies claims, reasons and support or attack relations under a specified scheme. These tasks share language evidence but do not define the same output or universal argument label.
topics: Separate text, context and argumentative role
Test intermediate representations and their scope

lessons.title: Cross-lingual and cross-domain transfer
lessons.goal: Transfer evaluation tests whether a system developed under one condition works under another. Cross-lingual transfer changes language; cross-domain transfer changes the source or content distribution; annotation-policy changes can alter the label meaning itself. These shifts can coexist, so a score drop alone does not explain its own cause.
section_titles: Transfer protocols and types of shift
topics: Name the source and target conditions
Transfer protocols and types of shift

lessons.title: Long-document encoding and evidence coverage
lessons.goal: A long-document system must specify how distant text can influence a prediction. Chunking encodes local windows and combines their representations; a hierarchical encoder adds a second level; sparse attention changes token-to-token connections within a sequence. These are different information paths, not interchangeable ways of increasing a context-length setting.
topics: Locate the evidence the task requires
Build windows and count repeated exposure
Compare local and global attention paths
Combine representations for the required output

lessons.title: NLP evaluation and a complete study
lessons.goal: An NLP evaluation counts matches between predicted and reference objects under a declared task rule. Token tags, complete entity spans, answer tokens and generated sequences are different objects, even when some metrics share a familiar name. A complete study also records preprocessing, model selection, source groups and failures so the result can be interpreted and reproduced.

Keep token accuracy and answer matching distinct

lessons.title: The language-model training loop
lessons.goal: Training changes a language model's parameters using examples. A batch supplies input tokens and known targets; the model predicts, a loss measures mistakes, backpropagation computes gradients and an optimizer updates the parameters. Validation and generation use the model differently: they do not apply these training updates.
topics: Apply one optimizer update and repeat
Save state for selection, resumption or use

lessons.title: Language-model training objectives
lessons.goal: A training objective defines what the model predicts, which information it may use and how mistakes are scored. Causal language modelling predicts successors from prefixes; masked modelling reconstructs selected tokens from permitted surrounding text; encoder–decoder learning predicts a target sequence conditioned on a source. These are different prediction problems, not interchangeable names for pretraining.
topics: Why one forward pass can learn many next tokens

lessons.title: LLM training data, tokenization and packing
lessons.goal: A language-model data pipeline converts permitted source material into the exact token inputs and prediction targets seen during training. It includes extraction, duplicate grouping, splits, tokenization, packing and masks. Corpus descriptions alone are insufficient: the resulting batches must preserve the intended information and evaluation boundaries.
topics: Encode text with a compatible tokenizer

lessons.title: Decoder Transformer architecture
lessons.goal: A decoder Transformer predicts a token from a permitted prefix by repeatedly transforming one vector per input position. Attention mixes information between allowed positions, while feed-forward layers transform features within each position. Residual connections preserve direct paths around these transformations. Training compares predictions with known targets; generation instead chooses and appends tokens with fixed parameters.
topics: Input token IDs and tensor axes
Input of the selected decoder block
Training loss for a known successor
Read the actual local grouped-query model

lessons.title: Language-model architecture families
lessons.goal: An architecture defines which representations interact and what state is carried through a model. Encoders, causal decoders and encoder–decoders differ in information access and output interface; expert layers and state-space operations change other parts of the computation. These categories can overlap within one model, so architecture names are not an ordered quality ranking.
section_titles: MHA, MQA, GQA and latent attention
State spaces and alternative sequence models

MHA, MQA, GQA and latent attention
State spaces and alternative sequence models

lessons.title: Gradient accumulation and stable LLM training
lessons.goal: Gradient accumulation combines several small forward/backward calculations before one optimizer update. The loss weighting must match the intended objective, especially when microbatches contain different numbers of valid targets. Numerical stability, clipping, scheduling and diagnostics are additional training choices, not substitutes for correctly aligned data and targets.
topics: Count the scored targets in this update
Recover loss sums from the means
A two-microbatch update, with the denominator made explicit

lessons.title: LLM parameter counts, memory and compute
lessons.goal: A model's parameter count, raw weight storage, training-state memory and compute budget measure different things. Training can require gradients, optimizer history, activations and temporary workspaces beyond the weights. Resource estimates are conditional accounting tools; measured peak memory and throughput must establish whether a real configuration fits and runs usefully.
topics: Account for gradients and optimizer history
Measure peaks and budget the full experiment

lessons.title: Distributed LLM training and gradient reduction
lessons.goal: Distributed training divides data, arithmetic or stored state across cooperating processes. Data parallelism uses model replicas on different examples and combines gradients; tensor, pipeline and state-sharding schemes divide other objects. Correct loss normalization and communication are required before more devices can be treated as a performance improvement.
topics: Define replica ownership and local evidence
Scale local losses for the reducer

lessons.title: LLM evaluation and interpretability evidence
lessons.goal: LLM evaluation tests a specified claim, such as better token prediction, task accuracy, source support, robustness or efficiency. Interpretability asks different questions about computation and mechanism. A score gain, an attention picture and a controlled intervention provide different evidence; none alone establishes every claim about useful or reliable behavior.
topics: Define the comparison before interpreting a gain

lessons.title: Supervised fine-tuning and LoRA
lessons.goal: Supervised fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model using demonstrations of desired outputs. Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, changes selected projections through small trainable matrix factors while keeping their base weights frozen. These choices concern the training signal and trainable parameters; they do not remove the base model or guarantee better behavior.
topics: Send the same features to both branches
Define what training updates and saves
Why zero initial adapter output does not stop learning

lessons.title: Preference learning: DPO, PPO and GRPO
lessons.goal: Preference and reward methods adapt which responses a language model favors. Direct preference optimization, or DPO, fits labelled response pairs relative to a reference model. Proximal policy optimization, or PPO, uses sampled behavior and an advantage-based surrogate. Group relative policy optimization, or GRPO, derives a comparison signal from responses sampled for the same prompt. Their signals and complete objectives differ.

PPO: careful updates from sampled behaviour
DPO: learn directly from preference pairs
GRPO: compare a group of responses

lessons.title: Prompting, reasoning and output decoding
lessons.goal: Prompting changes the input on which a model conditions; decoding changes how its token scores become outputs. Neither ordinarily updates learned weights. Intermediate reasoning, tool use and structured outputs add distinct procedures or constraints that must be evaluated for usefulness, source support and cost rather than assumed to make answers reliable.

lessons.title: Retrieval-augmented generation and vector indexes
lessons.goal: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, supplies external evidence to a model at use time. Ingestion builds a versioned, permission-aware source index; a query-time pipeline retrieves candidates, assembles context and generates an answer. Finding similar text and checking support are different tasks, and retrieval does not ordinarily update the generator's weights.
topics: Check source support and decide whether to answer

lessons.title: Tool-using agents and MCP boundaries
lessons.goal: A tool-using system turns a model's proposed action into a request that application code must validate, authorize and execute under limits. An agent can choose some next actions from observations; a workflow fixes more of the sequence. Model Context Protocol, or MCP, standardizes an integration boundary but does not supply planning, correctness or universal permission.
topics: Propose an action for the user's task
Follow a consequential tool request without confusing intent and execution

lessons.title: LLM inference, KV caching and serving
lessons.goal: Inference uses a model's parameters to calculate outputs, while serving adds request admission, scheduling, state management and delivery. Prefill processes the known prompt; autoregressive decoding processes successive chosen tokens. A key/value cache can reuse earlier attention projections, but its memory, compatibility and privacy constraints remain separate from model-weight storage.
topics: Prefill the prompt and build cache state
Calculate KV value storage as a side estimate
Decode successive tokens with fixed weights
Measure latency and throughput under load

lessons.title: LLM quantization, compression and deployment
lessons.goal: Compression changes a model or its representation to reduce selected storage or execution costs. Quantization approximates numerical values using a declared code range and scale; pruning and distillation use different mechanisms. Smaller values or files do not automatically produce a faster, fitting or equally capable deployed model.
topics: Round and clip to integer codes
Reconstruct values and calculate numerical error
Verify actual savings and task quality

lessons.title: LLM system evaluation, security and operations
lessons.goal: A deployed LLM system must satisfy task-quality, access, reliability and resource requirements across its components, not just produce fluent model outputs. Release evaluation, authorization, budget enforcement, monitoring and recovery address different failure paths. They are coordinated controls rather than one model-forward chain or a certificate of complete safety.
topics: Define task success and critical failure cases
Check projected cost before another action

lessons.title: LLM research methods and activation steering
lessons.goal: Research methods can change data, parameters, activations, decoding or system operations, and those interventions support different claims. Activation steering changes selected runtime representations while keeping model weights fixed. A local output change demonstrates sensitivity under that intervention, not that a named concept has been isolated or reliable behavior achieved everywhere.

What are self-consistency decoding, verifier models, and reasoning-model distillation?
What is the difference between reasoning capability, reasoning-token expenditure, and task accuracy?
You fine-tune a model to provide better explanations, but its factual accuracy drops. How would you test whether alignment, training data, or decoding caused the regression?
What is the difference between full fine-tuning, LoRA, QLoRA, and prompt tuning?
How does LoRA work mathematically? Why represent a weight update as a low-rank product?
What is the relationship between LoRA rank, scaling factor, trainable parameters, and adaptation capacity?
What is QLoRA, and how can a quantized base model support adapter training?
What are NF4 quantization and double quantization?
Does QLoRA mean that every parameter of a 4-bit model is trained in 4-bit precision?
Why might LoRA underperform full fine-tuning?
What is the difference between applying LoRA to attention projections versus feed-forward layers?
What are the differences between instruction tuning, classification fine-tuning, and continued pretraining?
What is loss masking? Why might you exclude user and system tokens from the SFT loss?
What are sequence packing and dynamic padding, and why can they influence training efficiency or correctness?
How can incorrectly configured chat templates, EOS tokens, or padding cause a fine-tuned model to behave badly?
How would you select hyperparameters for a LoRA experiment under a fixed GPU budget?
A fine-tuned 7B model performs worse than the original instruction model on your test set. How would you debug the result?
You have one 24 GB GPU and 50,000 labeled text examples. How would you build a competitive domain classifier, and which alternatives to LLM fine-tuning would you benchmark?
What is the difference between greedy decoding, beam search, top-k sampling, and nucleus (top-p) sampling?
How do temperature and sampling parameters affect output diversity and reproducibility?
Does setting temperature to zero guarantee identical outputs across all runs and serving systems?
What are repetition penalties and length penalties?
What is a KV cache, and why does autoregressive generation benefit from it?
What is the difference between prefill and decode phases in LLM inference?
What is the difference between time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency, throughput, and end-to-end latency?
What is quantization? Compare PTQ, QAT, INT8, 4-bit quantization, and FP8.
Why doesn't 4-bit quantization necessarily reduce total GPU memory usage by exactly 75%?
What is speculative decoding, and under what conditions can it improve performance?
What are FlashAttention and PagedAttention? Which different bottlenecks do they address?
What is continuous batching, and how does it differ from static batching?
What are tensor, pipeline, data, and expert parallelism?
A model fits comfortably in GPU memory but runs out of memory under concurrent requests. Why could that happen?
Your model serves 10 requests per second, but the business requires 100 with acceptable latency. What would you measure and optimize first?
What is RAG, and how does it differ from fine-tuning?
What is the difference between sparse retrieval, dense retrieval, and hybrid retrieval?
What is BM25, and why does it remain competitive for retrieval?
What is document chunking? Compare fixed-size, recursive, semantic, and structure-aware chunking.
How do chunk size and overlap affect retrieval precision, context coverage, and token costs?
What is the difference between a retriever and a reranker?
What is query rewriting, query expansion, and multi-query retrieval?
What are metadata filtering, parent-document retrieval, and hierarchical retrieval?
How do you measure retrieval quality using recall@k, MRR, MAP, and NDCG?
How can increasing retrieval recall make final answer quality worse?
What are context precision, context recall, groundedness, and faithfulness?
How do you detect and mitigate conflicting information in retrieved documents?
What is the difference between RAG, long-context prompting, and a model with domain-specific continued pretraining?
Your RAG system retrieves the correct document but gives the wrong answer. How would you separate retrieval, context construction, and generation failures?
Design a RAG system for 500,000 technical PDFs that supports document updates, citations, access permissions, and low-latency queries.
What is the difference between a chatbot, an LLM-powered workflow, and an autonomous agent?
What is function calling, and how is it different from generating ordinary natural-language output?
What is the ReAct pattern, and how does it combine reasoning and tool use?
What is the difference between planning, execution, and reflection in an agent architecture?
What are structured outputs, JSON schema validation, and constrained decoding?
Why can a syntactically valid tool call still be semantically incorrect or unsafe?
What is the difference between short-term conversational state, external memory, and parametric knowledge?
How would you handle tool failures, retries, timeouts, and idempotency?
How do you prevent an agent from repeatedly calling the same tool without making progress?
What are single-agent and multi-agent architectures, and when does multi-agent design add unnecessary complexity?
Does adding more agent reasoning steps necessarily improve performance?
How would you measure agent success, tool-call correctness, and completion cost?
What are the differences between deterministic workflow orchestration and open-ended agent planning?
Your agent keeps modifying the wrong database records despite producing valid SQL. How would you make the workflow safer?
Design an agent that reads research papers, extracts methodology and results, validates citations, and creates structured literature-review records.
What is hallucination in an LLM, and why does it occur?
What is the difference between factual accuracy, faithfulness, relevance, and helpfulness?
How would you evaluate an LLM when there is no single correct reference answer?
What is LLM-as-a-judge, and when is it reliable or unreliable?
What are position bias, verbosity bias, and self-preference bias in LLM evaluation?
What is the difference between exact-match evaluation, semantic evaluation, and human evaluation?
How would you build an evaluation dataset for a domain-specific assistant?
What is benchmark contamination, and how does it distort model comparisons?
What is the difference between model calibration, uncertainty estimation, and selective prediction?
Why can a model confidently produce an incorrect answer even when its next-token probabilities are well estimated?
What are adversarial examples, jailbreaks, and prompt injection attacks?
What is the difference between a system instruction and untrusted retrieved content?
How do you evaluate toxicity, harmfulness, fairness, and privacy risks?
What is the difference between memorization, verbatim extraction, and generalization?
How do you evaluate an LLM's robustness to paraphrasing, formatting changes, and misleading context?
Why can leaderboard improvements fail to translate into real-world usefulness?
What is the difference between pairwise evaluation, rubric-based evaluation, and absolute scoring?
How do you evaluate a refusal mechanism without rewarding excessive refusal?
An LLM's human preference score increases while its factual correctness decreases. How would you interpret this?
You need to compare five open-weight LLMs for a sensitive document-analysis application. Design a rigorous evaluation protocol.
What is the difference between deploying a machine learning model and deploying a conventional software application?
What is the difference between batch inference, online inference, and streaming inference?
What are model registries, experiment tracking, and artifact versioning?
What is the difference between data drift, concept drift, model degradation, and infrastructure failure?
How would you detect distribution drift without immediate access to ground-truth labels?
What is training–serving skew, and how can you prevent it?
What is the difference between a model's offline accuracy and its online business performance?
What are canary deployments, shadow deployments, and blue–green deployments?
How would you implement rollback for a failing ML service?
What are SLAs, SLOs, latency percentiles, and error budgets?
Why might average latency look acceptable while users still complain about slow responses?
How would you monitor an ML system when labels arrive weeks after predictions?
How can feedback loops cause a deployed model to reinforce its own errors?
What is the difference between a reproducible experiment and a reproducible deployed system?
What are deterministic operations, random seeds, and sources of nondeterminism in GPU training?
How would you optimize model quality subject to constraints on latency, throughput, cost, and memory?
What are data parallelism and distributed training strategies such as DDP, FSDP, and ZeRO?
Why might distributed training with more GPUs fail to produce proportional speedups?
A classification API suddenly becomes slower after a model update. How would you isolate the root cause?
You must deploy a domain-specific LLM serving thousands of requests daily under a limited cloud budget. Describe your architecture, scaling strategy, monitoring, and fallback behavior.
What is the difference between in-domain and out-of-domain generalization?
What is the difference between domain adaptation, domain generalization, and transfer learning?
How can you distinguish a domain-shift problem from a change in annotation guidelines?
What is dataset bias, and how can models exploit superficial correlations instead of learning the intended task?
Why might a model trained on several datasets perform worse on one dataset than a specialist trained only on that dataset?
How would you harmonize inconsistent label definitions across multiple corpora?
What is the difference between label noise, ambiguous examples, and annotator disagreement?
Is majority voting always appropriate when annotations are subjective?
What are hard-negative mining and adversarial data augmentation, and when can they introduce unwanted bias?
How can data augmentation or text simplification change the original labels or meaning?
What is an ablation study, and how does it differ from a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis?
How should you report performance across multiple seeds, datasets, and metrics?
Why might the model with the highest average score not be the most robust model?
What are worst-group risk, minimax optimization, and distributionally robust optimization?
How do you avoid selecting a model indirectly using test-set information?
What is the difference between a static ensemble, stacking, and a learned mixture-of-experts router?
Why can a learned ensemble or router perform worse than a simple average of model predictions?
How would you establish that a new modeling technique actually causes an improvement rather than merely correlating with one?
Your proposed research method improves performance on 3 out of 10 datasets but loses on the other 7. How would you analyze the result?
A reviewer says your NLP paper lacks evidence of generalization and relies on a weak baseline. What experiments would you add?
The 99% accuracy trap. You train a fraud detector achieving 99% accuracy, but it misses almost all fraudulent transactions. Diagnose the problem and propose a new training and evaluation strategy.

The impressive benchmark. Your new model beats the published state of the art by 5 F1 points. How do you rule out leakage, duplication, preprocessing differences, test-set tuning, and invalid baselines?

The 7B vs. 70B decision. Your company wants a customer-support assistant. A 70B model is more accurate but costly and slow. A 7B model is cheaper but makes more mistakes. How would you decide, including possible RAG, routing, and escalation strategies?

The limited-data problem. You have only 500 labeled examples for a specialized NLP task. Compare the expected merits of traditional ML, encoder fine-tuning, prompting, weak supervision, synthetic data, and active learning.
The dataset shift. A model trained on news articles is deployed on Reddit discussions and performance collapses. How would you diagnose linguistic, semantic, labeling, and distributional differences?

The hallucinating legal assistant. Your RAG assistant invents legal citations. How would you modify retrieval, generation, citation verification, abstention, and evaluation to reduce unsupported answers?
The GPU bottleneck. You must fine-tune an 8B model, but the available GPU cannot hold the model, gradients, and optimizer states. Explain your practical memory-saving options and their trade-offs.

The apparently successful fine-tuning. Training loss declines substantially, but validation performance deteriorates. Design a systematic troubleshooting plan covering data, labels, regularization, learning rates, evaluation, and catastrophic forgetting.

The multilingual deployment. You must build a classifier for English, German, Urdu, and Arabic with heavily imbalanced amounts of labeled data. How would you choose the base model, handle tokenization and language imbalance, and evaluate each language?

The latency incident. An LLM API has acceptable average latency but severe slowdowns at peak traffic. How would you investigate queuing, prefill, decode, batching, KV-cache memory, and request scheduling?

The conflicting annotators. Three annotators disagree over whether a sentence contains an argument. How would you determine whether the problem is annotation quality, ambiguity, or incompatible guidelines?
The cheaper retrieval system. BM25 outperforms your expensive dense retriever on internal documents. What hypotheses would you test before replacing it?
The unstable experiment. Five random seeds give substantially different F1 scores. How would you investigate instability, quantify uncertainty, and choose a fair model-selection protocol?

The ensemble failure. You combine five independently strong NLP classifiers, but their ensemble performs worse than the best individual classifier. Explain possible causes and methods for diagnosing them.

The impossible threshold. The business simultaneously demands 99% precision and 99% recall. Your best model cannot meet either requirement at the same threshold. How would you explain the trade-off and propose alternatives?
The model that says no. A safety-trained assistant refuses many harmless questions. How would you evaluate and improve the balance between helpfulness and appropriate refusals?

The million-document search engine. Build a semantic search system for one million research papers. Explain indexing, embeddings, hybrid retrieval, reranking, freshness, metadata, evaluation, and computational cost.

The adversarial document. An attacker inserts instructions into a retrieved PDF that tell your assistant to reveal confidential information. How should the system architecture prevent the document from overriding authorized instructions?

The negative research result. You spend three months developing a new model, but a simple RoBERTa baseline performs better. How would you analyze the result, communicate it, and determine whether the work is publishable?

The full system-design interview. Design an end-to-end multilingual document-analysis service that performs classification, information extraction, grounded question answering, and confidence-based escalation. Explain your architecture, datasets, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, and expected failure modes.
Implement precision, recall, and F1-score from raw predicted and true labels without using scikit-learn.
Implement gradient descent for linear regression using NumPy.
Implement a numerically stable softmax function.
Implement binary cross-entropy loss and explain why naive implementations can suffer numerical instability.
Implement a simple multilayer perceptron and training loop in PyTorch.
Implement scaled dot-product attention using tensor operations.
Implement causal masking and explain the required tensor dimensions.
Implement multi-head attention and verify that the tensor reshaping is correct.
Implement a basic LoRA-enabled linear layer and calculate its number of trainable parameters.
Write a PyTorch training and validation loop with gradient accumulation, mixed precision, and gradient clipping.
Implement macro-F1 and micro-F1 for a multiclass classifier, including appropriate zero-division handling.
Implement a simple cosine-similarity search function for document embeddings.
Write code to detect exact train–test duplicates and propose an approach for near-duplicate detection.
Build an evaluation pipeline that runs several random seeds and reports mean performance, dispersion, and confidence intervals.
Implement a small RAG pipeline using a document corpus, embeddings, retrieval, and generation, then describe how you would test each component independently.

glossary.meaning: A piece of text represented by an ID. Depending on the tokenizer it can be part of a word, a whole word, a symbol or a byte.
Numbers learned during training. They are different from the settings you choose, such as learning rate or batch size.
A choice made before or during an experiment, such as model size, learning rate or number of updates.
Repeatedly predict a target, measure the mistake and update learned numbers.
The documents used to fit the tokenizer/model. Evaluation documents must stay outside fitting.
Practice-check documents used to choose configurations or checkpoints. They are not the final independent check.
Held-out documents intended for a final check. Repeatedly choosing experiments from their scores makes them part of development.
How much the model is penalized for giving too little probability to the correct next piece. Lower is better for a matched task/tokenizer; it is not an answer-trustworthiness score.
The exponential of average next-token loss. Its units depend on tokenization, so do not compare different tokenizers blindly.
Total prediction cost measured per raw text byte. It can help compare tokenizers on identical text, with context/boundary/budget caveats.
How a small change in a learned number would locally change the loss. The optimizer uses this signal to choose an update.
How large an adjustment the optimizer attempts. Larger can learn faster, overshoot, or become unstable.
The rule that turns gradients into weight updates. This lab offers AdamW and plain SGD.
Windows of text processed together in one forward/backward calculation.
Combine several microbatch gradients before changing the weights once.
One optimizer update. It can include several microbatches and many next-token targets.
One pass over a dataset. This lab samples windows and reports updates/exposures rather than pretending they are exact dataset passes.
One valid target practised during training. Repeating the same target counts again; this is not unique data.
The maximum number of preceding input tokens available in one model window.
A learned numerical vector looked up for a token or position.
A calculation that mixes information from allowed token positions. Its weights are not automatically an explanation of correctness.
A rule blocking future positions so the model cannot read the next answer during prediction.
Saved model state. Resumable training also needs optimizer, sampling and random states—not just weights.
Getting better at the training material while performance on unseen practice-check text stops improving or worsens.
A simpler comparison system. Here a bigram predicts using only the previous token.
One recorded training experiment with its own configuration, results and files.
A group of related runs, such as three learning-rate choices, plus your prediction and reflection.
A starting value for random generators. It helps repeat a setup, but does not guarantee identical results across hardware/software.
Using learned weights to produce predictions. Sampling settings change outputs without retraining weights.
A sampling control that sharpens or flattens next-token probabilities. Zero chooses the highest-scoring token directly.
Continue training on demonstrations to teach behaviour. This lab implements local LoRA response training; that does not imply full LLM preference/RL training is implemented.
Retrieve evidence and include it in the model input. Retrieval does not by itself update the model's weights.

learning_rate.label: Learning rate
learning_rate.explanation: How large an adjustment the optimizer attempts. Smaller is not automatically safer or better within a fixed training budget.
learning_rate.equation: w_next = w - η × update; w = weights, η = learning rate. AdamW rescales the gradient before this update.
effects: Too small: loss may fall slowly.
Too large: updates may overshoot or become unstable.
The best value depends on the model and data; predict, then measure.
interactions: Batch size and accumulation change gradient noise.
Clipping limits the gradient, not the learning rate itself.
Warmup and the schedule change the rate over time.

steps.label: Optimizer updates
steps.explanation: How many weight updates to perform. More updates reuse this small corpus; they do not create new information.
steps.equation: token exposures ≈ updates × microbatch × accumulation × context; padding/short windows reduce the actual count.
effects: More updates may improve fitting first and overfit later.
The best-dev checkpoint can be earlier than the last update.
interactions: Changing context, batch or accumulation also changes tokens seen per update.
At a fixed schedule horizon, extra updates can continue at the minimum rate.

def train(name, preset="tiny", steps=None, seed=17, device="auto", resume=False,
          corpus=None, runs_root=RUNS, overrides=None, learning=None):
    if preset not in PRESETS:
        raise ValueError("Choose smoke or tiny.")
    settings = {**DEFAULTS, **PRESETS[preset]}
    settings["seed"], settings["device"] = seed, device
    if overrides is not None:
        settings = validate(overrides)
        seed, device = settings["seed"], settings["device"]
    steps = settings["steps"] if steps is None else steps
    if not isinstance(steps, int) or not 1 <= steps <= 2000:
        raise ValueError("This local lab allows 1–2000 optimizer steps per run.")
    if not isinstance(seed, int) or not 0 <= seed <= 2**31 - 1:
        raise ValueError("Seed must be an integer in [0, 2^31-1].")
    corpus = Path(corpus or ROOT / "data" / "corpus.jsonl")
    rows = load_corpus(corpus)
    rows = select_training_data(rows, settings["train_fraction"])
    device = choose_device(device)
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    random.seed(seed)
    tokenizer = ByteBPE.fit([r["text"] for r in rows if r["split"] == "train"], settings["merges"])
    config = {"preset": preset, "seed": seed, "learning_rate": settings["learning_rate"],
              "batch_size": settings["batch_size"], "accumulation": settings["accumulation"],
              "optimizer":settings["optimizer"], "weight_decay":settings["weight_decay"],
              "clip_norm":settings["clip_norm"], "schedule":settings["schedule"],
              "warmup_steps":settings["warmup_steps"], "schedule_steps":settings["schedule_steps"],
              "train_fraction":settings["train_fraction"],
              "corpus_sha256": sha256(corpus), "tokenizer": tokenizer.to_dict(),
              "model": asdict(ModelConfig(tokenizer.vocab_size, settings["block_size"], settings["width"],
                                          settings["layers"], settings["heads"], settings["dropout"],
                                          settings["positions"],settings["residuals"],settings["normalization"]))}
    directory = run_path(name, runs_root)
    if resume:
        verify(directory)
        previous = read_json(directory / "manifest.json")
        if previous["config"] != config or previous["hardware"]["device"] != device:
            raise ValueError("Resume requires identical config, data, seed and device.")
        if previous["source_hashes"] != source_hashes():
            raise ValueError("Source changed since checkpoint; start a new run instead of silently resuming.")
    else:
        directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)
    model = TinyDecoder(ModelConfig(**config["model"])).to(device)
    optimizer = make_optimizer(model, config)
    sampler = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed + 1)
    start_step, exposures, best_dev, metrics = 0, 0, float("inf"), []
    if resume:
        state = torch.load(directory / "last.pt", map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)
        model.load_state_dict(state["model"])
        optimizer.load_state_dict(state["optimizer"])
        sampler.set_state(state["sampler_rng"])
        torch.set_rng_state(state["torch_rng"])
        if device == "mps":
            torch.mps.set_rng_state(state["mps_rng"])
        if device == "cuda":
            torch.cuda.set_rng_state(state["cuda_rng"])
        start_step, exposures, best_dev = state["step"], state["tokens_processed"], state["best_dev"]
        if steps <= start_step:
            raise ValueError("Resume steps is the TOTAL target, and must exceed the saved step.")
        metrics = read_json(directory / "metrics.json")
    split_items = {s: examples(rows, tokenizer, s, settings["block_size"]) for s in ("train", "dev", "test")}
    baseline = Bigram(tokenizer.vocab_size).fit(rows, tokenizer)
    manifest = {"schema_version": 2, "id": name, "status": "RUNNING", "purpose": "educational_pretraining",
                "started_at": previous["started_at"] if resume else now(), "updated_at": now(),
                "resumed": resume, "requested_steps": steps, "completed_steps": start_step,
                "config": config, "model": model.description(), "source_hashes": source_hashes(),
                "settings":{**settings,"steps":steps,"seed":seed,"device":device}, "learning":learning or {},
                "evaluation_protocol":"document_chunks_v1", "metric_definition":"next-token NLL including EOS; excludes PAD/BOS",
                "hardware": {"device": device, "machine": platform.machine(), "python": platform.python_version(),
                             "torch": str(torch.__version__), "threads": 1},
                "limits": ["Authored miniature corpus, not general language competence.",
                           "Development loss selects checkpoint; test is evaluated only at run completion.",
                           "Same-tokenizer bigram baseline; training compute and model capacity differ.",
                           "Fixed synthetic splits share templates; exact dedup is not semantic dedup.",
                           "CPU restart equivalence tested; accelerator bitwise determinism not promised."]}
    write_json(directory / "manifest.json", manifest)
    write_json(directory / "tokenizer.json", tokenizer.to_dict())
    write_json(directory / "data.json", {"license": "CC0-1.0 authored synthetic learning fixture",
                                        "documents": rows, "counts": dict(Counter(r["split"] for r in rows)),
                                        "duplicates": 0, "audit": "NFKC + casefold + whitespace exact dedup only"})
    write_json(directory / "metrics.json", metrics)
    elapsed_before = previous.get("training_seconds", 0) if resume else 0
    started = time.perf_counter()
    telemetry=Telemetry(directory)
    try:
        for step in range(start_step + 1, steps + 1):
            model.train()
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            current_lr = learning_rate_at(step, config)
            for group in optimizer.param_groups:
                group["lr"] = current_lr
            microbatches = []
            for _ in range(config["accumulation"]):
                indices = torch.randint(len(split_items["train"]), (config["batch_size"],), generator=sampler)
                microbatches.append(batch([split_items["train"][i] for i in indices.tolist()], device))
            # Divide by ALL valid tokens, not an average of unequal microbatch means.
            valid_total = sum(int((y != -100).sum()) for _, y in microbatches)
            summed_loss = 0.0
            for x, y in microbatches:
                loss, count = loss_sum(model(x), y)
                if not torch.isfinite(loss):
                    raise FloatingPointError("Non-finite loss; run stopped.")
                (loss / valid_total).backward()
                summed_loss += loss.item()
            grad_norm = clip_gradients(model, config["clip_norm"])
            if not math.isfinite(grad_norm):
                raise FloatingPointError("Non-finite gradients; run stopped.")
            optimizer.step()
            exposures += valid_total
            row={"step":step,"sampled_train_nll":summed_loss/valid_total,
                 "gradient_norm_pre_clip":grad_norm,"learning_rate":current_lr,"tokens_processed":exposures,
                 "elapsed_seconds":elapsed_before+time.perf_counter()-started,
                 "tokens_per_second":(exposures-state["tokens_processed"] if resume else exposures)/max(time.perf_counter()-started,1e-6)}

batch_size.label: Examples per microbatch
batch_size.explanation: How many sampled windows are processed together in one forward/backward pass.
batch_size.equation: effective batch (windows) = microbatch size × accumulation; valid-token count can differ between windows.
effects: Larger batches usually need more activation memory.
They can reduce gradient noise, but may not improve held-out performance.
interactions: At fixed steps, a larger batch sees more tokens: this is not a compute-matched comparison.
Accumulation can increase effective batch without holding all activations at once.

    steps = settings["steps"] if steps is None else steps

        raise ValueError("This local lab allows 1–2000 optimizer steps per run.")
    if not isinstance(seed, int) or not 0 <= seed <= 2**31 - 1:

              "clip_norm":settings["clip_norm"], "schedule":settings["schedule"],

              "train_fraction":settings["train_fraction"],

              "model": asdict(ModelConfig(tokenizer.vocab_size, settings["block_size"], settings["width"],
                                          settings["layers"], settings["heads"], settings["dropout"],
                                          settings["positions"],settings["residuals"],settings["normalization"]))}
    directory = run_path(name, runs_root)
    if resume:
        verify(directory)
        previous = read_json(directory / "manifest.json")

            raise ValueError("Resume requires identical config, data, seed and device.")
        if previous["source_hashes"] != source_hashes():
            raise ValueError("Source changed since checkpoint; start a new run instead of silently resuming.")
    else:
        directory.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)
    model = TinyDecoder(ModelConfig(**config["model"])).to(device)
    optimizer = make_optimizer(model, config)
    sampler = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed + 1)
    start_step, exposures, best_dev, metrics = 0, 0, float("inf"), []
    if resume:
        state = torch.load(directory / "last.pt", map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)
        model.load_state_dict(state["model"])
        optimizer.load_state_dict(state["optimizer"])
        sampler.set_state(state["sampler_rng"])
        torch.set_rng_state(state["torch_rng"])
        if device == "mps":
            torch.mps.set_rng_state(state["mps_rng"])
        if device == "cuda":
            torch.cuda.set_rng_state(state["cuda_rng"])
        start_step, exposures, best_dev = state["step"], state["tokens_processed"], state["best_dev"]
        if steps <= start_step:
            raise ValueError("Resume steps is the TOTAL target, and must exceed the saved step.")
        metrics = read_json(directory / "metrics.json")
    split_items = {s: examples(rows, tokenizer, s, settings["block_size"]) for s in ("train", "dev", "test")}
    baseline = Bigram(tokenizer.vocab_size).fit(rows, tokenizer)
    manifest = {"schema_version": 2, "id": name, "status": "RUNNING", "purpose": "educational_pretraining",
                "started_at": previous["started_at"] if resume else now(), "updated_at": now(),
                "resumed": resume, "requested_steps": steps, "completed_steps": start_step,
                "config": config, "model": model.description(), "source_hashes": source_hashes(),
                "settings":{**settings,"steps":steps,"seed":seed,"device":device}, "learning":learning or {},
                "evaluation_protocol":"document_chunks_v1", "metric_definition":"next-token NLL including EOS; excludes PAD/BOS",
                "hardware": {"device": device, "machine": platform.machine(), "python": platform.python_version(),
                             "torch": str(torch.__version__), "threads": 1},
                "limits": ["Authored miniature corpus, not general language competence.",
                           "Development loss selects checkpoint; test is evaluated only at run completion.",
                           "Same-tokenizer bigram baseline; training compute and model capacity differ.",
                           "Fixed synthetic splits share templates; exact dedup is not semantic dedup.",
                           "CPU restart equivalence tested; accelerator bitwise determinism not promised."]}
    write_json(directory / "manifest.json", manifest)
    write_json(directory / "tokenizer.json", tokenizer.to_dict())
    write_json(directory / "data.json", {"license": "CC0-1.0 authored synthetic learning fixture",
                                        "documents": rows, "counts": dict(Counter(r["split"] for r in rows)),
                                        "duplicates": 0, "audit": "NFKC + casefold + whitespace exact dedup only"})
    write_json(directory / "metrics.json", metrics)
    elapsed_before = previous.get("training_seconds", 0) if resume else 0
    started = time.perf_counter()
    telemetry=Telemetry(directory)
    try:
        for step in range(start_step + 1, steps + 1):
            model.train()
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            current_lr = learning_rate_at(step, config)
            for group in optimizer.param_groups:
                group["lr"] = current_lr
            microbatches = []
            for _ in range(config["accumulation"]):
                indices = torch.randint(len(split_items["train"]), (config["batch_size"],), generator=sampler)

            if step == 1 or step % 20 == 0 or step == steps:
                dev = evaluate(model, split_items["dev"], device)
                train_eval = evaluate(model, split_items["train"], device)
                row.update(train_nll=train_eval["nll"],dev_nll=dev["nll"])
                if dev["nll"] < best_dev:
                    best_dev = dev["nll"]
                    save_checkpoint(directory / "best.pt", model, optimizer, sampler, step, exposures, best_dev, config)
            metrics.append(row);telemetry.log(row)
            # A resumable last checkpoint is recorded for EVERY completed optimizer step.
            save_checkpoint(directory / "last.pt", model, optimizer, sampler, step, exposures, best_dev, config)
            manifest.update(completed_steps=step, tokens_processed=exposures, updated_at=now(),
                            elapsed_seconds=elapsed_before+time.perf_counter()-started,phase="Training the decoder",
                            tokens_per_second=row["tokens_per_second"],
                            eta_seconds=(time.perf_counter()-started)/(step-start_step)*(steps-step))
            write_json(directory / "metrics.json", metrics)
            write_json(directory / "manifest.json", manifest)
        synchronize(device)
        manifest["training_seconds"] = elapsed_before + time.perf_counter() - started
        state = torch.load(directory / "best.pt", map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)
        model.load_state_dict(state["model"])
        evaluations = {s: evaluate(model, split_items[s], device) for s in ("train", "dev", "test")}
        for split, result in evaluations.items():
            byte_count = sum(len(r["text"].encode("utf-8")) for r in rows if r["split"] == split)
            result["utf8_bytes"] = byte_count
            result["bits_per_byte"] = result["nll"] * result["tokens"] / (byte_count * math.log(2))
        baselines = {s: baseline.evaluate(rows, tokenizer, s) for s in ("dev", "test")}
        write_json(directory / "evaluation.json", {"checkpoint_step": state["step"], "transformer": evaluations,
                   "bigram": baselines, "selection": "lowest dev NLL; never selected on test",
                   "units": "nats per shared BPE next-token target; lower is better"})
