reading.title: Optimizers, initialization and training stability
reading.definition: An optimizer turns gradients into parameter updates. Plain stochastic gradient descent, or SGD, subtracts a learning-rate-scaled gradient. Adam keeps moving averages of gradients and squared gradients to adapt update sizes. Initialization chooses the starting weights; a schedule changes learning rate over time. These are related choices, not interchangeable methods.
reading.example: We compare one SGD step with the first Adam step from weight 1 and gradient 2 at learning rate 0.1. The Adam-state sections explain Adam even when SGD is selected; the final update uses the selected rule. No weight decay is included in this arithmetic.
reading.connection: Backpropagation supplies gradients. This lesson explains how optimizer rules use them, then the deeper notes cover initialization, clipping, normalization, schedules and failure diagnosis.

steps.title: The same starting gradient
steps.prose: Use the same weight, gradient and learning rate to isolate the update rule. SGD uses the current gradient directly. Adam's result also depends on its stored averages, which start at zero for this first-step example.
steps.terms: The learning rate scales the attempted update; it does not have an identical numerical effect under every optimizer.
steps.next: The next two sections explain the state used by Adam, not additional stages of plain SGD.

steps.title: Adam's moving averages
steps.prose: Adam retains a smoothed history of gradients and squared gradients. Beta values determine how strongly old history is retained. With zero starting state and this gradient, its first stored values are 0.2 and 0.004.
steps.terms: The first moment is a moving average of gradients; the second moment averages squared gradients. Plain SGD has neither state in this comparison.
steps.next: Adam corrects the initial shrinkage caused by starting those averages at zero.

steps.title: Adam's bias correction
steps.prose: Early moving averages are pulled towards their zero initialization. Dividing by the appropriate factors corrects that effect under the optimizer's definition. On this first step, corrected values are 2 and 4, producing a normalized direction close to 1.
steps.terms: This bias correction concerns optimizer-state initialization, not statistical fairness or an intercept term. Epsilon prevents a zero denominator.
steps.next: The chosen optimizer's direction is multiplied by the learning rate to update the parameter.

steps.title: Compare the actual parameter change
steps.prose: SGD subtracts 0.1 × 2. First-step Adam subtracts approximately 0.1 × 1 under these assumptions. Neither this one-step difference nor a common learning rate establishes which method will learn better on a real task.
steps.terms: AdamW additionally applies decoupled weight decay. That operation is intentionally absent here; later Adam steps depend on history.
steps.next: Use the initialization and stability notes to interpret real learning curves, rather than treating this first step as an optimizer ranking.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Once gradients exist, an optimizer decides how to change parameters. SGD uses the current estimated gradient; momentum carries a running direction; Adam tracks moving averages of gradients and squared gradients to adapt update scales by coordinate. These history variables are optimizer state, not extra predictions.

For a first scalar gradient 2 with Adam beta values 0.9 and 0.999, the uncorrected moments are 0.2 and 0.004. Bias correction divides by $1-0.9$ and $1-0.999$, giving 2 and 4. Ignoring epsilon, their ratio is $2/\sqrt4=1$, so a learning rate of 0.01 produces an approximately 0.01 update, not SGD's 0.02. Later updates depend on accumulated history. Epsilon stabilises a small denominator.

Initialisation sets the starting signal scale and breaks symmetry between hidden units. Identically initialised hidden units can receive identical updates and fail to learn diverse features. This is different from a simple convex linear model where zero initialisation may be fine. Normalisation controls activation statistics; clipping limits a gradient norm; a schedule changes learning rate over time. These are distinct interventions.

Check non-finite values, data scale, loss reduction, and gradient norms before blaming the optimizer. AdamW's decoupled weight decay is not generally identical to putting an L2 penalty inside Adam's gradient calculation.

Sources: [D2L: Adam](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/adam.html), [D2L: numerical stability and initialisation](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/numerical-stability-and-init.html), [AdamW paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101).

/api/learning/document/DL04.title: Regularization, dropout and training diagnostics
/api/learning/document/DL04.goal: Regularization changes training to discourage a model from relying too strongly on limited or accidental patterns. Dropout is one method: during training it randomly masks activation values, encouraging the network to cope without any particular selected feature. It does not permanently delete weights, and it is not a guaranteed improvement.

parameters.label: Dropout probability
parameters.definition: Probability an eligible activation is removed during training.
parameters.mathematical_meaning: Inverted dropout: a×Bernoulli(1−q)/(1−q).
parameters.expected_effect: Adds stochastic regularization; too much removes useful signal.
failure_modes: Disabled during normal evaluation; reject q=1 for this rule.
parameters.api_mapping: Confirm estimator/version/objective semantics in stage 2; no executable mapping exists yet.

parameters.label: Microbatch examples
parameters.definition: Examples processed by one forward/backward calculation.
parameters.mathematical_meaning: Tensor leading dimension B; final batch may be smaller.
parameters.expected_effect: Changes memory, throughput and gradient noise.
failure_modes: Epoch counts are not update counts when batch size changes.
parameters.api_mapping: Confirm estimator/version/objective semantics in stage 2; no executable mapping exists yet.

parameters.label: Training epochs
parameters.definition: Planned full passes through the declared fitting dataset.
parameters.mathematical_meaning: Without dropping: batches per epoch=ceil(n/B).
parameters.expected_effect: More exposure can help or overfit and costs work.
failure_modes: Sampled-window training may not correspond to exact passes; report actual exposures.
parameters.api_mapping: Confirm estimator/version/objective semantics in stage 2; no executable mapping exists yet.

parameters.label: Development-based stopping
parameters.definition: Stop or select training duration using a declared development metric.
parameters.mathematical_meaning: Record minimum improvement, evaluation cadence and retained checkpoint.
parameters.expected_effect: Can avoid wasted work or overfitting but adds selection decisions.
failure_modes: A backend's hidden internal random split can violate a temporal/group protocol.
parameters.api_mapping: Confirm estimator/version/objective semantics in stage 2; no executable mapping exists yet.

parameters.label: Early-stopping patience
parameters.definition: Number of declared evaluation checks without sufficient improvement before stopping.
parameters.mathematical_meaning: Counts evaluation events, not necessarily epochs.
parameters.expected_effect: Longer patience tolerates noise but adds training/selection work.
failure_modes: The selected checkpoint and final state are not necessarily the same.
parameters.api_mapping: Confirm estimator/version/objective semantics in stage 2; no executable mapping exists yet.

parameters.label: Label smoothing
parameters.definition: Mixes one-hot targets with a stated distribution.
parameters.mathematical_meaning: Uniform convention: y_smooth=(1−epsilon)y+epsilon/K.
parameters.expected_effect: Changes the objective and can affect confidence and class separation.
failure_modes: It does not correct wrong labels or certify calibrated probabilities.

# DL04. Regularization, dropout and training diagnostics

Regularization changes training to discourage a model from relying too strongly on limited or accidental patterns. Dropout is one method: during training it randomly masks activation values, encouraging the network to cope without any particular selected feature. It does not permanently delete weights, and it is not a guaranteed improvement.

The features are [2,4]. Choose the probability of keeping a feature, q. A declared mask shows the arithmetic: retained values are divided by q. This fixed demonstration mask is not a randomly sampled training run.

Regularization was introduced in ML. Here we distinguish a particular dropout sample, its expectation over many masks and evaluation-mode behaviour; those are three related explanations, not a serial architecture.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: DL03, ML10.

## 1. Different ways to control overfitting

**Key terms.** **Overfitting** improves fitting data while worsening new data; **dropout** randomly removes activations during training; **augmentation** changes examples under an assumed label-preserving transformation; **early stopping** selects a training duration using development data.

**Process.** Establish a small learning sanity check, train with a declared regularization recipe, inspect train/development behaviour and stop/select only under the declared rule. Evaluate the selected checkpoint separately from the final training state.

A failure to overfit a tiny clean batch can expose bugs, but is not proof that generalization is impossible. Once the mechanics work, compare learning curves, class errors and probability quality. High loss on both splits suggests different first checks from low train/high development loss. NaNs and out-of-memory errors are execution/numerical failures, not ordinary underfitting.

Dropout changes the training function stochastically. Weight decay changes parameter updates. Augmentation changes observed inputs. Label smoothing replaces a completely one-hot target with a distribution that leaves some probability on other classes. Early stopping changes the selected training duration. These are not equivalent controls even if all can limit brittle fitting. For a batch-size change, record whether epochs, updates, examples and scheduler timing remain matched.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** p_drop is the probability of dropping a feature and q_keep=1−p_drop is its keep probability. Inverted dropout divides a retained activation by q_keep during training so its expectation matches the original. PyTorch's p argument specifies p_drop; the walkthrough control specifies q_keep. Evaluation disables this masking and scaling.

For activation a=2 and p_drop=0.5 (q_keep=0.5), the training output is either 0 or 4, each with probability 0.5, so its expected value is 2. It is not 2 on every forward pass. Under K-class label smoothing convention, target distribution is (1−epsilon)one_hot+epsilon/K: for K=4 and epsilon=0.1, target class is 0.925 and each other class 0.025.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Choosing a response to training failures

Try a smaller model, more representative data, justified augmentation or a changed regularizer based on observed failure. A drop probability of 0.9 (keep probability 0.1) can remove useful signal; no smooth monotonic improvement is promised. Loss reduction and class weighting affect gradient scale, so record their interaction with learning rate.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: compare dropout with the same split

Train a small image MLP under identical splits with dropout off/on. Save the best development checkpoint including an unchanged baseline where appropriate. Keep transformations used for training out of deterministic evaluation unless a separate test-time augmentation protocol is declared.

**Check.** Development loss is noisy. May you choose whichever checkpoint gives the prettiest test samples?

**Answer.** That uses test evidence for selection. Use a declared development criterion and reserve test prompts/scores for the final check.

## Sources

- [CS231n practical neural-network training notes](https://cs231n.github.io/neural-networks-3/).
- [PyTorch 2.9 CrossEntropyLoss](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss.html).
- [Deep Learning, author site](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/).

notes.title: Settings: Dropout probability, Early-stopping patience, Label smoothing
notes.markdown:
### Dropout probability

Probability an eligible activation is removed during training.

Inverted dropout: a×Bernoulli(1−q)/(1−q).

Adds stochastic regularization; too much removes useful signal.

Interactions: model capacity; train/eval mode.

Disabled during normal evaluation; reject q=1 for this rule.

### Early-stopping patience

Number of declared evaluation checks without sufficient improvement before stopping.

Counts evaluation events, not necessarily epochs.

Longer patience tolerates noise but adds training/selection work.

Interactions: evaluation cadence; minimum improvement; schedule.

The selected checkpoint and final state are not necessarily the same.

### Label smoothing

Mixes one-hot targets with a stated distribution.

Uniform convention: y_smooth=(1−epsilon)y+epsilon/K.

Changes the objective and can affect confidence and class separation.

Interactions: class_weight; calibration; class count.

It does not correct wrong labels or certify calibrated probabilities.

steps.title: Activations before dropout
steps.prose: Start with the computed feature values [2,4]. These are outputs of a layer, not the saved weights. Dropout will perturb these values during a training forward pass while leaving the model's parameter dimensions unchanged.
steps.terms: An activation is a computed feature value. Keep probability q is the chance a feature survives the random mask.
steps.next: Apply the mask and scaling rule to these activations.

steps.title: Training mask and scaling
steps.prose: For each feature, a sampled mask would choose keep or drop. Multiply by that mask, then divide retained values by q under inverted dropout. Here the mask is explicitly selected so the calculation can be inspected; changing q does not generate repeated random samples.
steps.terms: The drop probability is 1−q. PyTorch Dropout's p argument is the drop probability, not this control's keep probability.
steps.next: The expectation section explains the average over possible masks, not another operation applied to this particular output.

steps.title: Expected values across random masks
steps.prose: Under independent Bernoulli sampling with keep probability q, the mask's mean is q. Dividing surviving activations by q therefore preserves each activation's expected value over masks. A single masked vector can be very different from the original vector.
steps.terms: Expectation is an average over possible random outcomes. Mean preservation does not preserve every downstream nonlinear prediction.
steps.next: Evaluation uses the original activations without this dropout sampling or rescaling.

steps.title: Evaluation mode versus gradient tracking
steps.prose: With inverted dropout, evaluation returns [2,4] unchanged at this layer. model.eval() switches dropout and other mode-sensitive modules to evaluation behaviour. A no_grad context separately disables gradient recording; one does not replace the other.
steps.terms: Evaluation mode controls module behaviour. Gradient tracking controls whether operations are recorded for differentiation.
steps.next: The deeper notes connect these distinctions to train/validation curves, early stopping and small-data diagnostics.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A network can learn patterns specific to its training sample. Regularisation changes fitting so those patterns have less influence. Dropout randomly removes selected activations during training; weight decay discourages large weights; early stopping chooses a checkpoint before further fitting damages validation performance. These techniques address different mechanisms and are not substitutes for correct data splits.

With **inverted dropout**, let q be the probability of keeping an activation. A kept value is divided by q, while a dropped value becomes zero. For activation 4 and q=0.5, the output is either 8 or 0, each with probability 0.5. Its expectation is 4. This preserves the individual activation's mean, not every nonlinear downstream output. At evaluation, ordinary dropout is disabled and no such random rescaling is applied.

Keep “drop probability” and “keep probability” distinct: $q=1-p_{drop}$. `eval()` selects evaluation behaviour; it does not prevent gradients. Conversely, `no_grad()` does not automatically disable dropout.

Interpret curves alongside the objective and data. Rising validation error while training error falls can suggest overfitting; high error on both may indicate underfitting or a bug. Adding dropout to an already struggling fit can make it worse. Verify masks, targets, and learning rate before adding constraints.

Sources: [D2L: dropout](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/dropout.html), [PyTorch: Dropout](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.Dropout.html).

# DL05. Convolutional neural networks

A convolutional neural network, or CNN, learns local pattern detectors and reuses their weights across image positions. Each filter produces a feature map. Stacking convolutions and nonlinearities lets later features combine earlier patterns; pooling can reduce spatial resolution, and a final head maps the remaining features to task outputs.

The walkthrough uses one 8×8 grayscale image, two convolution blocks with ReLU (zeroing negative values) and max pooling (keeping local maxima), and three illustrative classes. Kernel size sets filter width; stride sets its movement; padding supplies boundary zeros here. All weights are fixed teaching values, so the example explains computation rather than measuring image-recognition accuracy.

A dense layer combines all input features at once; a convolution first combines local patches with shared weights. The final dense head still uses the weighted-sum and classification ideas introduced earlier.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: DL01.

## 1. Local filters, channels and receptive fields

**Key terms.** A **convolution kernel** is a shared local filter; **channels** are feature maps; **stride** controls movement; **padding** extends boundaries; **dilation** spaces kernel samples. A **receptive field** is the input region that can influence an output.

**Process.** An image tensor enters local shared filtering, activation and optional spatial downsampling. Later layers combine larger regions, then a task head converts features to class or structured outputs. Track spatial sizes and channels at each transition.

A dense layer connects every flattened pixel to each output, while a convolution reuses a local weight pattern at different positions. This encodes locality and sharing assumptions, not perfect invariance. Pooling/downsampling changes spatial resolution; padding and stride affect boundary and alignment behaviour. Standard deep-learning Conv2d commonly performs cross-correlation rather than reversing the kernel as a mathematical convolution would.

Convolution arithmetic is worth a static patch/filter diagram. A decorative image of a robot is not. Visualize one patch, shared weights and the corresponding output cell, then show how layers expand receptive fields.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** For one spatial dimension, output length is floor((H+2p−d(k−1)−1)/s+1). Here H is input size, k kernel size, p padding, d dilation and s stride. groups divides channel connectivity.

For H=28,k=3,p=1,d=1,s=1, output size is 28. With stride 2 it is floor(27/2+1)=14. A biased Conv2d with 1 input channel, 16 output channels and a 3×3 kernel has 16×1×3×3+16=160 parameters. Two stride-1, dilation-1 3×3 layers have a theoretical 5×5 receptive field, not 6×6.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Kernel, stride and pooling choices

Larger filters, more channels, more depth and dilation enlarge different aspects of capacity/context with different costs. A 1×1 convolution mixes channels without enlarging spatial neighbourhood. Groups/depthwise convolution change connectivity and weight count; they are not merely fewer output channels.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: compare image architectures

Compare a linear classifier, MLP and small CNN on Fashion-MNIST with the official test reserved and a separate training-derived development split. Start with a bounded subset for a pilot, but label subset results distinctly from full-data results.

**Check.** Why must the classifier head change if spatial pooling changes the flattened feature size?

**Answer.** Its input dimension must match the new tensor shape. Global average pooling is an alternative design, not a reason to silently reshape incompatible arrays.

## 5. Shapes through the actual local CNN

**Key terms.** Channels are learned feature maps. Padding preserves boundary access; stride controls movement. Pooling reduces spatial resolution. Flattening concatenates spatial positions before the classification head.

**Process.** The lab's CNN applies a padded 3×3 convolution, normalization/activation and 2×2 pooling twice. It then flattens the retained map, applies dropout and a linear head. The residual variant inserts same-shape shortcut blocks.

For a 28×28 input, first width 32 and ten classes without normalization: Conv 1→32 has 32×1×9+32=320 parameters. The second Conv 32→64 has 64×32×9+64=18,496. Pooling twice gives 7×7; the linear head uses 64×7×7×10+10=31,370. Total: 50,186. On 8×8 digits, the final map is 2×2, so the same channel choices produce 21,386 parameters. The interface records the actual count.

### Do not confuse this with global pooling

Global average pooling would average each final channel into one number and use a smaller head. That is an alternative architecture, not the current local implementation. A fixed 3×3 filter is shared at every location; this reduces free parameters relative to an equally wide dense spatial map but does not make the model fully translation invariant.

## 6. Vision Transformers: turn image patches into a sequence

**Read after DL08 attention.** A Vision Transformer (ViT) represents an image as a sequence of patch vectors and mixes them with Transformer blocks. It is an alternative to the CNN's built-in local filtering pattern, not a promise that attention is always a better image model.

Begin with an image of height H, width W and C channels. Divide it into non-overlapping P×P patches, assuming both dimensions are divisible by P. Flatten each patch into P²C values and multiply by a learned projection to hidden width D. Add the architecture's position information so identical patch content at different locations is distinguishable. The original ViT adds a learned class token; other designs pool or use dense prediction heads differently.

\[
N=HW/P^2,\qquad X_{patch}\in\mathbb R^{B\times N\times(P^2C)},\qquad E=X_{patch}W_E.
\]

N counts patches and B counts images. A 224×224 RGB image with 16×16 patches has 196 patches, each containing 768 raw values. With D=192, the projected patch tensor is [B,196,192]; adding a class token gives [B,197,192]. Projection weights alone number 768×192=147,456, or 147,648 with a 192-value bias. Raw patch width 768 does not force hidden width to be 768.

Image → patch vectors → learned embedding/positions → attention/MLP blocks → task head is the computation. With global attention, each head forms a 197×197 score map in this example. Halving patch width to eight quadruples patch count to 784; the pairwise score count grows approximately sixteen-fold, before considering special tokens. Windowed/hierarchical attention restricts connectivity or changes resolution to control this cost. Patch size also changes spatial detail and learned inductive assumptions.

A CNN already shares local filters; a ViT learns interactions over its permitted patches. Compare data exposure, pretraining, augmentation, resolution, compute and adaptation, not just architecture labels. The original ViT's strong transfer results depended on substantial pretraining. A small scratch ViT is not guaranteed to outperform a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST.

**Practice.** Does a class token represent a ground-truth category supplied at the input? **Answer.** No. It is a learned input vector whose final representation can feed a classifier. It must not encode the correct test label. Continue to DL12 for changing an image representation into boxes or pixel maps; keep the original CNN walkthrough as the local-filter reference.

[Original Vision Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929) · [Swin Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14030).

## Sources

- [PyTorch 2.9 Conv2d](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.Conv2d.html).
- [Computing Receptive Fields of CNNs](https://distill.pub/2019/computing-receptive-fields/).
- [Stanford CS231n, Spring 2026](https://cs231n.stanford.edu/).

N=HW/P^2,\qquad X_{patch}\in\mathbb R^{B\times N\times(P^2C)},\qquad E=X_{patch}W_E.
\]

Windowed/hierarchical attention restricts connectivity or changes resolution to control this cost. Patch size also changes spatial detail and learned inductive assumptions.

A CNN already shares local filters; a ViT learns interactions over its permitted patches. notes.title: Kernel, stride and pooling choices
notes.markdown: Larger filters, more channels, more depth and dilation enlarge different aspects of capacity/context with different costs. A 1×1 convolution mixes channels without enlarging spatial neighbourhood. Groups/depthwise convolution change connectivity and weight count; they are not merely fewer output channels.

notes.title: Example: compare image architectures
notes.markdown: Compare a linear classifier, MLP and small CNN on Fashion-MNIST with the official test reserved and a separate training-derived development split. Start with a bounded subset for a pilot, but label subset results distinctly from full-data results.

notes.title: Shapes through the actual local CNN
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** Channels are learned feature maps. Padding preserves boundary access; stride controls movement. Pooling reduces spatial resolution. Flattening concatenates spatial positions before the classification head.

For a 28×28 input, first width 32 and ten classes without normalization: Conv 1→32 has 32×1×9+32=320 parameters. The second Conv 32→64 has 64×32×9+64=18,496. Pooling twice gives 7×7; the linear head uses 64×7×7×10+10=31,370. Total: 50,186. On 8×8 digits, the final map is 2×2, so the same channel choices produce 21,386 parameters. The interface records the actual count.

### Do not confuse this with global pooling

Global average pooling would average each final channel into one number and use a smaller head. That is an alternative architecture, not the current local implementation. A fixed 3×3 filter is shared at every location; this reduces free parameters relative to an equally wide dense spatial map but does not make the model fully translation invariant.

The original ViT adds a learned class token; other designs pool or use dense prediction heads differently.

notes.title: Settings: Convolution output channels, Convolution kernel size, Convolution stride
notes.markdown:
### Convolution output channels

Learned feature maps produced by a convolution.

Weights=C_out×(C_in/groups)×kernel_area, plus biases if used.

More channels increase feature capacity and activation cost.

Interactions: kernel; groups; next layer shape.

Channel count is not spatial resolution.

### Convolution kernel size

Size of each local filter in each spatial dimension.

Effective extent=dilation×(kernel−1)+1.

Larger filters enlarge local context and weight/work requirements.

Interactions: padding; stride; dilation.

A 1×1 kernel mixes channels, not neighbouring pixels.

### Convolution stride

Distance between adjacent output sampling locations.

Appears in the output-size divisor.

Higher stride often reduces spatial resolution and cost, losing detail.

Interactions: padding; kernel; task head shape.

Do not keep an incompatible flattened-head size after changing stride.

notes.title: Settings: Convolution padding, Convolution dilation, Convolution groups
notes.markdown:
### Convolution padding

Boundary extension under a declared padding mode.

Output size includes 2×padding per dimension for symmetric padding.

Preserves or changes spatial extent and boundary effects.

Interactions: kernel; stride; padding mode.

A numeric value is not universally same-padding for every kernel/dilation.

### Convolution dilation

Spacing between filter samples.

Effective kernel=dilation×(kernel−1)+1.

Expands receptive extent without adding kernel entries.

Interactions: padding; stride; coverage pattern.

Larger dilation can skip fine local patterns; it is not equivalent to a dense larger kernel.

### Convolution groups

Partitions input/output channel connectivity.

C_in and C_out must satisfy the group's divisibility contract.

Can reduce weights/work while changing cross-channel mixing.

Interactions: channels; pointwise layers.

Depthwise needs a precise groups=C_in/channel-multiplier convention.

notes.title: Settings: Spatial pooling
notes.markdown:
### Spatial pooling

Aggregates spatial values, often reducing resolution.

A 2×2 stride-2 pool downsamples under a stated boundary rule.

Changes invariance, detail and downstream shape.

Interactions: stride; task head; image size.

Pooling does not guarantee invariance to arbitrary transformations.

reading.title: Convolutional neural networks
reading.definition: A convolutional neural network, or CNN, learns local pattern detectors and reuses their weights across image positions. Each filter produces a feature map. Stacking convolutions and nonlinearities lets later features combine earlier patterns; pooling can reduce spatial resolution, and a final head maps the remaining features to task outputs.
reading.example: The walkthrough uses one 8×8 grayscale image, two convolution blocks with ReLU (zeroing negative values) and max pooling (keeping local maxima), and three illustrative classes. Kernel size sets filter width; stride sets its movement; padding supplies boundary zeros here. All weights are fixed teaching values, so the example explains computation rather than measuring image-recognition accuracy.
reading.connection: A dense layer combines all input features at once; a convolution first combines local patches with shared weights. The final dense head still uses the weighted-sum and classification ideas introduced earlier.

steps.title: Image tensor and channels
steps.prose: The image is arranged by example, channel, row and column. One grayscale image has one channel; an RGB image usually has three. A channel is a plane of features, not another independent training example.
steps.terms: B is batch size, C is channels, H is height and W is width. This input has shape [1,1,8,8].
steps.next: The first convolution reads local patches of this image.

steps.title: First convolution: shared local filters
steps.prose: Place a small filter over an image patch, multiply matching entries, add the products and the filter's bias. Reuse that same filter at other positions. Inspecting another output cell changes the patch, not the shared weights.
steps.terms: Kernel size is patch width/height. Stride is movement between positions; padding adds specified boundary values. PyTorch uses cross-correlation without reversing the kernel.
steps.next: ReLU transforms the signed filter responses before pooling.

steps.title: ReLU: keep positive responses
steps.prose: A filter can produce positive or negative values. ReLU replaces a negative response with zero and keeps a positive response unchanged. Applying it between learned layers makes the overall network nonlinear.
steps.terms: ReLU means rectified linear unit. It changes values without changing their dimensions or adding learned parameters.
steps.next: Pooling summarizes small regions within each activated feature map.

steps.title: First pooling: reduce spatial size
steps.prose: For each channel separately, keep the maximum value in each non-overlapping 2×2 window. This reduces the number of spatial positions while retaining strong local responses. It can also discard small patterns or precise location information.
steps.terms: Pooling has no learned weights in this example. It changes spatial resolution, not the number of channels.
steps.next: The second convolution combines patterns across both pooled channels.

steps.title: Second convolution: combine channels
steps.prose: Each new output filter has a spatial kernel for every input channel. Add contributions across those channels and then add one output bias. This produces four new feature maps here; input-channel contributions are summed, not returned as separate predictions.
steps.terms: Input channels describe available feature planes; output channels count new filter banks. Shared weights still apply at all valid positions.
steps.next: A second ReLU transforms these new combinations.

steps.title: Second ReLU
steps.prose: Apply the same nonnegative activation rule to every entry in the four new maps. The feature values change but the four-channel structure remains. Later features depend on a wider region of the original image because earlier operations have already combined nearby inputs.
steps.terms: A receptive field is the part of the original input that can affect a particular computed feature.
steps.next: The second pooling layer reduces these maps before the final head.

steps.title: Second pooling
steps.prose: Keep a local maximum from each 2×2 region of each later feature map. All channels are retained while their height and width decrease. A different pooling scheme would change the retained representation and may change the required classifier dimensions.
steps.terms: Local max pooling differs from global average pooling, which averages a whole channel.
steps.next: Flatten arranges the retained values into the vector expected by the head.

steps.title: Flatten into a feature vector
steps.prose: List the channel and spatial values in a defined order. Flattening changes the arrangement, not the values or their count. If stride or pooling changes the retained map size, the head's input width must match that new feature count.
steps.terms: Flattening is a reshape, not feature selection, averaging or a learned layer.
steps.next: A dense classifier now combines this vector into three class scores.

steps.title: Class logits from the dense head
steps.prose: Calculate a weighted sum of the retained features for each class, then add its bias. The three logits can be any real values. Their ordering gives a score preference before normalization.
steps.terms: A logit is a raw class score. The head's weights and biases are learned parameters in a real trained CNN.
steps.next: Softmax converts these three scores into a class-probability vector.
steps.node: Class logits from the dense head

steps.title: Softmax over classes
steps.prose: Normalize the class logits into three probabilities that sum to one for this image. The largest probability gives the default predicted class. This normalization is across classes, not image positions or feature channels.
steps.terms: A predicted probability is the model's assigned probability, not automatically a calibrated confidence guarantee.
steps.next: A labelled training example additionally supplies a target for calculating loss.

steps.title: Cross-entropy for a known target
steps.prose: The teaching target is class B. Its cross-entropy loss is minus the natural logarithm of the probability assigned to B. This is a training objective for one image, not an accuracy measurement on a dataset.
steps.terms: Nats are natural-log loss units. A real batch loss needs an explicit sum or mean reduction across examples.
steps.next: Backpropagation can calculate how changing parameters would affect this loss.

steps.title: A limited head-only update
steps.prose: The displayed SGD calculation freezes the convolutional features and updates the classifier weights and biases only. It demonstrates an exact gradient update without pretending to train the full CNN. Full training also differentiates through convolution, activation and pooling layers.
steps.terms: Backpropagation calculates sensitivities; the optimizer changes parameters. Max-pool gradients follow the winning inputs under a defined tie rule.
steps.next: Use the actual training lab for supported trained CNN runs; no checkpoint is changed by this walkthrough.

reading.legend: Solid arrows carry image features towards class predictions. The loss and dashed update path explain a separate, head-only training calculation. Selecting a component never trains or edits a checkpoint.
reading.lesson_markdown:
A convolutional layer searches for local patterns using the same filter weights at different positions. For images, nearby pixels often form meaningful edges or textures, and similar patterns can occur in different places. This **inductive bias** is useful when the input's spatial arrangement matters; it is usually inappropriate for an arbitrary ordering of unrelated table columns.

An image tensor commonly has axes `[batch, channels, height, width]`. A filter combines a spatial patch across all input channels to produce one output value. Sliding it forms a feature map. With one input channel and a 3×3 filter, the filter has nine weights plus a bias. Ten such filters produce ten channels without needing a separate filter for every image location.

Stride sets how far the filter moves; padding extends the boundary. Without dilation, output size per axis is $\lfloor(H+2P-K)/S\rfloor+1$. For H=8, K=3, P=1, S=2, the result is 4. ReLU changes values without learning additional weights. Pooling summarises local regions; flattening changes representation shape before a dense classifier.

The diagram follows two convolutions and a class head, showing actual small arithmetic. Its gradient example updates the head only. A real CNN fit in Model Lab also differentiates through trainable convolutional layers. Do not mistake a worked forward trace for a measured trained classifier.

Sources: [D2L: convolutions for images](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-neural-networks/conv-layer.html), [D2L: padding and stride](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-neural-networks/padding-and-strides.html).

failure_modes: Not every layer/model supports interchangeable normalization without a structural change.

# DL06. Residual networks and transfer learning

A residual block adds its input to a transformed version of that input: output = input + correction. This shortcut lets information and gradients use a direct path around the transformation. Transfer learning is a separate choice: reuse a pretrained model and decide which parameters to freeze or adapt. Residual architectures can be trained from scratch or transferred.

The input is 2 and the transformed branch multiplies it by a chosen scale. We calculate the addition and its derivative. A separate section then compares a frozen 1,000-parameter backbone with a trainable 20-parameter head; it is not another operation on the scalar output.

The CNN lesson stacks transformations. A residual connection changes how those transformations are connected; freezing changes which weights an optimizer may update. Keep these two decisions separate.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: DL05, DL03.

## 1. Shortcut structure versus adaptation policy

**Key terms.** A **residual block** adds a learned change to a skip path; a **projection shortcut** aligns incompatible shapes. A **backbone** supplies features; a **head** maps them to a task. **Transfer learning** reuses pretrained representations.

**Process.** Choose scratch weights or a compatible pretrained backbone, replace the task head if needed and declare which layers are trainable. Forward through the residual network, fit the allowed parameters and compare against the unchanged starting representation.

Writing a block as x+F(x) supplies a direct additive path. It is not concatenation and does not guarantee stable learning at arbitrary depth. If channel or spatial shapes change, use a justified projection or another specified shortcut. The normalization/order must match the actual architecture.

A frozen feature extractor still needs forward computation, memory and a trained new head. Full fine-tuning adds optimizer/gradient requirements and may damage useful prior behaviour. Training/evaluation modes of BatchNorm require particular care when freezing a backbone. Pretrained weights can contain evaluation-related exposure; source and revision are part of the comparison.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** x is the block input and F(x) its learned branch. y=x+F(x) requires equal shapes; otherwise use y=P(x)+F(x) with a declared projection P.

For x=[1,2] and F(x)=[0.1,−0.2], residual output is [1.1,1.8]. Adding [1,2] to a three-feature vector is undefined under the intended residual contract. A [batch,64] feature extractor with a ten-class linear head adds 64×10+10=650 trainable parameters if only that head is trained.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Scratch, frozen and fine-tuned comparisons

Compare scratch training, frozen features and full fine-tuning in separate rows. Their starting information differs; a pretrained gain is not solely an architecture effect. Use smaller rates or staged unfreezing only when development evidence and controlled budgets justify them.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: avoid training-data reuse

The first local lab should use a small scratch residual model or an explicitly supplied compatible feature extractor. Do not silently resize grayscale clothing images into a pretrained RGB pipeline and call the result a fair scratch-vs-transfer study.

**Check.** Why is requiring_grad=False not always enough to freeze every behavioural aspect of a backbone?

**Answer.** Non-parameter running state and mode-dependent layers can still change. Specify BatchNorm/dropout behaviour and verify the saved state as well as parameter gradients.

## 5. Residual derivatives and frozen-module state

**Key terms.** A residual block returns x+F(x). An identity shortcut requires equal shapes. A projection shortcut learns a shape-changing map. Freezing a parameter disables its gradient update, not necessarily all state changes.

**Process.** Send the input through a learned correction branch and a shortcut, add the equal-shaped outputs and continue. During backward propagation both paths contribute.

For y=x+F(x), dy/dx=I+∂F/∂x. The identity term supplies a direct path even if the learned branch initially contributes little. It does not guarantee that every gradient stays well-scaled or that an arbitrarily deep network will optimize.

### Transfer learning needs an access and state policy

A frozen backbone can still change BatchNorm running means if left in training mode. A proper frozen-feature comparison fixes both learned weights and relevant state; dropout also changes behaviour between training and evaluation. A pretrained encoder may already have seen evaluation data, so a new task split does not prove an untouched representation.

The local residual CNN starts from random weights and uses same-channel identity blocks. It is not pretrained transfer learning. Comparing it to the plain CNN changes depth, parameter count and compute; the saved settings make those differences visible. External-backbone transfer remains a course topic rather than a hidden automatic download.

## 6. Contrastive image–text learning and multimodal transfer

**Read after DL08 attention and the embedding/retrieval foundations.** A multimodal model connects information from different kinds of input, such as images and text. In a CLIP-style contrastive system, separate encoders map an image and its paired text into a shared comparison space. This is representation learning, not by itself an image generator or a chatbot that can inspect arbitrary images.

A training batch contains B matched image–text pairs. Normalize their embeddings, form all B×B similarities, and train the matching pair to score above the other batch entries. A common row loss is:

\[
L_i=-\log\frac{\exp(s_{ii}/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{B}\exp(s_{ij}/\tau)}.
\]

s is a similarity and tau a positive temperature. The symmetric objective also predicts the matching image from each text. A real batch may contain near-duplicate or equally valid descriptions: treating every off-diagonal pair as negative is an assumption, not ground truth about meaning.

For one image with two text similarities 1 and 0, temperature 1 assigns its matched text probability e/(e+1)=0.7311 and row loss 0.3133 nats. Temperature 0.5 gives probability 0.8808 and loss 0.1269 for these fixed scores. This sharper distribution does not establish improved recognition or calibration; changing temperature in training also changes gradients.

For zero-shot classification, encode descriptions of candidate classes and compare each with the image embedding. “Zero-shot” here means no supervised adaptation to that target task under the stated protocol, not that the pretrained model saw no relevant data. Prompt wording, class-set choice, source exposure and image preprocessing affect the result. A frozen encoder can also support retrieval or a fitted downstream head.

**Practice.** An image–text model finds a matching caption. Has it generated an image or learned the target task online? **Answer.** Neither follows. Similarity retrieval, supervised adaptation and conditional generation are different operations. This distinction leads naturally to conditioning in DL10 without duplicating the Transformer internals owned by T3.

[CLIP primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020).

## Sources

- [Deep Residual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385).
- [PyTorch transfer-learning tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/transfer_learning_tutorial.html).

notes.title: Scratch, frozen and fine-tuned comparisons
notes.markdown: Compare scratch training, frozen features and full fine-tuning in separate rows. Their starting information differs; a pretrained gain is not solely an architecture effect. Use smaller rates or staged unfreezing only when development evidence and controlled budgets justify them.

notes.title: Example: avoid training-data reuse
notes.markdown: The first local lab should use a small scratch residual model or an explicitly supplied compatible feature extractor. Do not silently resize grayscale clothing images into a pretrained RGB pipeline and call the result a fair scratch-vs-transfer study.

notes.title: Residual derivatives and frozen-module state
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** A residual block returns x+F(x). An identity shortcut requires equal shapes. A projection shortcut learns a shape-changing map. Freezing a parameter disables its gradient update, not necessarily all state changes.

For y=x+F(x), dy/dx=I+∂F/∂x. The identity term supplies a direct path even if the learned branch initially contributes little. It does not guarantee that every gradient stays well-scaled or that an arbitrarily deep network will optimize.

### Transfer learning needs an access and state policy

A frozen backbone can still change BatchNorm running means if left in training mode. A proper frozen-feature comparison fixes both learned weights and relevant state; dropout also changes behaviour between training and evaluation. A pretrained encoder may already have seen evaluation data, so a new task split does not prove an untouched representation.

The local residual CNN starts from random weights and uses same-channel identity blocks. It is not pretrained transfer learning. Comparing it to the plain CNN changes depth, parameter count and compute; the saved settings make those differences visible. External-backbone transfer remains a course topic rather than a hidden automatic download.

notes.title: Contrastive image–text learning and multimodal transfer
notes.markdown:
**Read after DL08 attention and the embedding/retrieval foundations.** A multimodal model connects information from different kinds of input, such as images and text. In a CLIP-style contrastive system, separate encoders map an image and its paired text into a shared comparison space. This is representation learning, not by itself an image generator or a chatbot that can inspect arbitrary images.

A training batch contains B matched image–text pairs. Normalize their embeddings, form all B×B similarities, and train the matching pair to score above the other batch entries. A common row loss is:

\[
L_i=-\log\frac{\exp(s_{ii}/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{B}\exp(s_{ij}/\tau)}.
\]

s is a similarity and tau a positive temperature. The symmetric objective also predicts the matching image from each text. A real batch may contain near-duplicate or equally valid descriptions: treating every off-diagonal pair as negative is an assumption, not ground truth about meaning.

For one image with two text similarities 1 and 0, temperature 1 assigns its matched text probability e/(e+1)=0.7311 and row loss 0.3133 nats. Temperature 0.5 gives probability 0.8808 and loss 0.1269 for these fixed scores. This sharper distribution does not establish improved recognition or calibration; changing temperature in training also changes gradients.

For zero-shot classification, encode descriptions of candidate classes and compare each with the image embedding. “Zero-shot” here means no supervised adaptation to that target task under the stated protocol, not that the pretrained model saw no relevant data. Prompt wording, class-set choice, source exposure and image preprocessing affect the result. A frozen encoder can also support retrieval or a fitted downstream head.

**Practice.** An image–text model finds a matching caption. Has it generated an image or learned the target task online? **Answer.** Neither follows. Similarity retrieval, supervised adaptation and conditional generation are different operations. This distinction leads naturally to conditioning in DL10 without duplicating the Transformer internals owned by T3.

[CLIP primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020).

reading.title: Residual networks and transfer learning
reading.definition: A residual block adds its input to a transformed version of that input: output = input + correction. This shortcut lets information and gradients use a direct path around the transformation. Transfer learning is a separate choice: reuse a pretrained model and decide which parameters to freeze or adapt. Residual architectures can be trained from scratch or transferred.
reading.example: The input is 2 and the transformed branch multiplies it by a chosen scale. We calculate the addition and its derivative. A separate section then compares a frozen 1,000-parameter backbone with a trainable 20-parameter head; it is not another operation on the scalar output.
reading.connection: The CNN lesson stacks transformations. A residual connection changes how those transformations are connected; freezing changes which weights an optimizer may update. Keep these two decisions separate.

steps.title: Keep an unchanged shortcut
steps.prose: Carry the original input directly to the later addition. This is a forward path, not a repetition or a backwards training loop. Its values must have a compatible shape with the transformed branch when they meet.
steps.terms: An identity shortcut copies values without changing them. A projection shortcut can adjust dimensions when an identity is insufficient.
steps.next: In parallel, the transformation branch calculates a change to add to this input.

steps.title: Calculate the transformation branch
steps.prose: The branch applies a transformation to the same input. Our scalar example multiplies by a chosen scale; a real residual CNN branch can include convolutions, normalization and activations. A branch scale of zero leaves only the shortcut contribution.
steps.terms: F(x) names the branch's transformation. It need not be a complete replacement for the incoming representation.
steps.next: Add its output to the unchanged shortcut at the matching dimensions.

steps.title: Add the two paths
steps.prose: Add corresponding values from the shortcut and the transformed branch. This is elementwise addition, not concatenation. The structure lets a block produce a small change when that is useful, but does not guarantee every network will train well.
steps.terms: Concatenation joins feature lists; addition combines matching entries and keeps their compatible shape.
steps.next: The next section analyzes the derivative of this addition, not another forward layer.

steps.title: Why the shortcut helps gradients
steps.prose: For y = x + sx, the derivative with respect to x is 1+s. The identity term contributes a direct gradient route alongside the transformed branch. This can help optimization in deep networks, but gradients can still behave poorly elsewhere.
steps.terms: Different paths contribute terms that are added by the chain rule. A gradient route is not a separate stored copy of the model.
steps.next: Transfer learning is a distinct policy about parameters, explained next rather than connected as a forward operation.

steps.title: Separate choice: freeze or fine-tune
steps.prose: A pretrained backbone produces features; a task head maps them to the new target. Freezing the backbone prevents its parameter updates while the head can learn. Unfreezing selected layers permits adaptation but changes data and compute requirements.
steps.terms: A backbone is the main feature-producing network. A frozen module can still have mode-sensitive running statistics that need deliberate handling.
steps.next: The deeper notes compare freezing, partial fine-tuning and scratch training without assuming every residual network is pretrained.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A residual block learns a correction to an existing representation: $y=x+F(x)$. The bypass carries x unchanged; F is a learned branch. If both have shape `[batch, features]`, they can be added element by element. If dimensions differ, a projection must make them compatible. A bypass is not a backwards pass or a generation loop.

For x=2 and a branch output of −0.3, the result is 1.7. During differentiation, the input affects the output through both paths: locally, $dy/dx=1+F'(x)$. The direct contribution helps gradients reach earlier layers, but does not guarantee perfect optimisation or permit incompatible shapes. Deep residual networks use many such blocks.

Transfer learning starts with parameters learned on another task or dataset. A frozen encoder supplies features for a new head; fine-tuning allows some or all encoder weights to change. Freezing saves gradient and optimizer-state work for those weights, but the forward computation and activations needed by later trainable layers still have costs.

Compare a pretrained frozen baseline, selective fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning only when the data and budget justify them. Similarity between source and target tasks influences usefulness. A pretrained model can carry source biases, and a good source score does not establish target-domain reliability.

Sources: [D2L: residual networks](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-modern/resnet.html), [D2L: fine-tuning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_computer-vision/fine-tuning.html).

# DL07. Recurrent networks, GRUs and LSTMs

A recurrent neural network (RNN) processes an ordered sequence by updating a state at each position. The same cell weights are reused over time, so the current output can depend on earlier inputs. A vanilla RNN has one hidden-state update; a gated recurrent unit (GRU) controls how new and old states are mixed, and long short-term memory (LSTM) additionally maintains a separate cell-memory state.

The inputs are [1,0,1]. We calculate three state updates with fixed teaching weights. The GRU and LSTM gates are held constant to expose the arithmetic; real gates are computed from learned transformations of inputs and previous states.

This is the DL overview of shared weights and sequence history. The NLP course provides the detailed RNN/BiRNN, GRU/BiGRU and LSTM/BiLSTM gate/state walkthroughs, so their full architecture explanations are not duplicated here.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: DL02, ML13.

## 1. State, gates and allowed sequence history

**Key terms.** A **recurrent state h_t** carries sequence information; **BPTT** backpropagates through time; **gates** modulate information flow. **LSTM** adds a cell state and gates; **GRU** uses a different gated update; **bidirectional** models also read later input.

**Process.** Read an input step, update hidden state and produce an output or continue to the next step. During training, propagate error backwards through a declared sequence length; at prediction, preserve only state allowed by the actual task.

A simple RNN shares its transition weights over time. Repeated derivatives can shrink or grow, complicating long-range fitting. LSTM/GRU introduce controlled paths, but do not guarantee unlimited memory. Truncated BPTT bounds derivative history and memory; carrying state and carrying gradients are separate decisions.

For a complete document classification task, bidirectional context may be available. For causal forecasting or streaming generation, future observations are not. Variable-length batches need padding/length handling, and document boundaries must not accidentally share hidden state. Masked losses and allowed information should be audited just as in the LLM course.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** A simple recurrence is h_t=tanh(x_t W_x+h_(t−1)W_h+b). In an LSTM cell-path illustration, c_t=f_t c_(t−1)+i_t g_t, where f/i are forget/input gates and g is proposed content; other gates determine the output.

Holding illustrative gates fixed at f=0.9,i=0.2 with previous cell c=2 and candidate g=0.5 gives new cell 1.9. The direct cell-path derivative is 0.9 under that fixed-gate calculation, not the entire network derivative. Repeated simple-path multipliers 0.5 over 10 steps give 0.0009766; multipliers 2 give 1,024.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Recurrence versus other sequence models

Lagged linear/boosted models, temporal convolutions, gated recurrence and attention represent history differently. More recurrent width increases capacity/cost; longer derivative windows increase training memory. Use a causal baseline before claiming a recurrent forecast gain.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: valid forecasting inputs

Compare a lagged demand predictor with a small GRU on the same bike forecast origins. Calendar/feature availability and forecast horizon must match; bidirectional access to the future is not a legitimate advantage.

**Check.** May you keep hidden state from the final training row when starting an unrelated shuffled test document?

**Answer.** Not under an independent-document protocol. Reset or initialize state according to the task and record any legitimate streaming carry-over explicitly.

## 5. GRU gate convention and gradient history

**Key terms.** A hidden state summarizes earlier positions. A GRU reset gate controls use of the previous state in the candidate; an update gate mixes old and candidate state. Gate conventions differ between formulations.

**Process.** At each position, combine the new input with the previous hidden state, calculate gates, form a candidate and mix it into the state. The next position receives the updated state; the task head reads a declared state or sequence.

This course uses the PyTorch-style update convention h_t=(1−z_t)h̃_t+z_t h_(t−1), so z weights the old state. With old state 0.8, candidate 0.2 and z=0.25, the result is 0.75×0.2+0.25×0.8=0.35. A larger z preserves more of the old state under this convention. Some references instead place z on the candidate; their numerical gate value has the opposite interpretation. The live DL and NLP examples use the same old-state convention.

### Backpropagation through time

Unrolling makes repeated applications of shared weights visible to autograd. Their gradient contributions add across time. A state Jacobian describes how one state changes with the previous state's entries. Multiplying many such local derivatives can shrink or amplify the gradient over a long sequence. Truncated backpropagation detaches the carried state at boundaries: it preserves a forward summary but cuts gradient paths across those boundaries.

A bidirectional encoder can read future positions, which is useful for complete-input tagging but invalid for a causal next-token task. Sequence architecture is taught here; this release does not include an executable recurrent trainer.

## Sources

- [PyTorch 2.9 GRU equations and implementation convention](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html).

- [Deep Learning, author site](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/).
- [Stanford CS230, Fall 2026 syllabus](https://cs230.stanford.edu/syllabus/).
- [Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/).

reading.definition: A recurrent neural network (RNN) processes an ordered sequence by updating a state at each position. The same cell weights are reused over time, so the current output can depend on earlier inputs. A vanilla RNN has one hidden-state update; a gated recurrent unit (GRU) controls how new and old states are mixed, and long short-term memory (LSTM) additionally maintains a separate cell-memory state.

steps.title: Initial state and sequence boundary
steps.prose: Define the state before reading the first input. This example starts hidden state at zero and, for LSTM, cell memory at zero. Separate sequences need a deliberate reset or carry policy so one example's history does not leak into another.
steps.terms: A hidden state is a computed summary of earlier inputs. An LSTM cell state is a separate memory quantity.
steps.next: The chosen cell combines its initial state with the first input.

steps.title: First input and cell update
steps.prose: Use input 1 and the initial state in the selected recurrent equation. A vanilla RNN applies tanh to an input/state weighted sum. A GRU mixes a candidate with the old hidden state; an LSTM updates cell memory before exposing a hidden output.
steps.terms: Here GRU reset r=0.5 and update z=0.25; z weights the old state. LSTM input/forget/output gates are 0.5/0.8/0.7. These are fixed illustrative coefficients.
steps.next: Carry the resulting state, not newly fitted weights, into the next position.

steps.title: Second input with retained history
steps.prose: The next input is zero, but the previous state may be nonzero. Reusing the cell therefore still produces a history-dependent result. The picture's repeated cells are copies of the operation, not separate parameter sets.
steps.terms: Unrolling draws time positions separately while keeping their weights shared. Time index is different from network-layer depth.
steps.next: The third update uses this newly calculated state.

steps.title: Third input and sequence output
steps.prose: Process the final input 1 with the state from the second position. A final-state head could summarize the sequence, while a per-position head could use every hidden state. Neither choice turns the state into a loss without a target and objective.
steps.terms: A recurrent state is a finite representation and can lose information about long sequences. LSTM cell and hidden state remain different values.
steps.next: The separate training section explains gradient contributions through these reused operations.

steps.title: Training: backpropagation through time
steps.prose: Attach a loss to the appropriate sequence outputs, then differentiate through the unrolled operations. Because the same parameters were used repeatedly, their gradient contributions are added. Truncated backpropagation deliberately cuts how far that gradient history extends.
steps.terms: Forward state carry and backward gradient history are separate choices. This demo calculates forward states, not a complete recurrent training loss or gradient.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A recurrent network processes a sequence by updating a hidden state. At each position it combines the new input with the previous state using the same learned weights. The state summarises earlier inputs for a later prediction. Sequence length changes how many times the update runs, not how many copies of its parameters are learned.

A basic update is $h_t=\tanh(W_xx_t+W_hh_{t-1}+b)$. Repeated multiplication through time can shrink or amplify gradients. A GRU adds gates that control how much old state to retain and how a candidate is constructed. Under the convention used here, $h_t=z_th_{t-1}+(1-z_t)\tilde h_t$: an update gate near one mostly retains the previous state. Other presentations reverse the naming, so follow the equation.

An LSTM maintains a cell state as well as a hidden output. Forget and input gates scale old cell memory and a candidate update; an output gate controls how much cell content is exposed. Gates are learned continuous values, not hard-coded decisions about which word matters.

The worked trace compares recurrent cells on a fixed small sequence. It does not train them. A bidirectional variant also reads from the right, which is legal for complete-sequence classification but would leak future tokens in ordinary causal next-token prediction.

Sources: [D2L: RNNs](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/rnn.html), [D2L: GRUs](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/gru.html), [D2L: LSTMs](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/lstm.html).

# DL08. Attention and Transformer building blocks

Attention updates a representation by taking a weighted combination of value vectors. A query is compared with keys to calculate matching scores; after masking forbidden positions, softmax turns those scores into mixing weights. The values supply the content being combined. Attention weights are not automatically explanations of truth or model correctness.

We update one query using two candidate key/value pairs. Allow both positions or block the later one with a causal mask, then see how the allowed scores, weights and output change. The model weights and vectors are authored examples, not trained measurements.

Recurrent cells carry information through a sequence state. Attention provides another way to combine information across positions. The LLM Transformer lesson shows how heads, projections, residuals and feed-forward layers surround this operation.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: DL07, P2.

## 1. Matching and mixing across positions

**Key terms.** A **query Q** asks for a match; a **key K** supplies matching features; a **value V** carries mixed content; **attention weights** normalize allowed matches. A **causal mask** excludes future input; **position information** represents order.

**Process.** Project token/sequence features into Q/K/V, compare queries with permitted keys, normalize scores and mix values. Multi-head outputs return to hidden width, pass through residual/feed-forward structure and reach the task head.

Attention permits content-dependent interactions across positions without a recurrent state transition for every input step. This can parallelize training positions, but exact dense attention can involve quadratic pair interactions. Efficient kernels change memory traffic without necessarily changing the function. A causal mask still matters when every training token is stored in the same batch.

Transformers add position design, feed-forward layers, residuals and normalization. They are not attention alone. Encoder, decoder and encoder–decoder forms permit different information flow. The existing T3 lesson supplies the complete modern decoder and real GQA shapes; this lesson is the bridge from general DL, not a duplicate full LLM textbook.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** For one head, S=QK^T/sqrt(d_k)+M; row-wise softmax gives A; output O=AV. d_k is key width and M is 0 on allowed scores and negative infinity on blocked ones.

With query [1,0], allowed keys [1,0]/[0,1], key width 2 and values [2,0]/[0,4], scores are [0.7071,0]. Softmax weights are approximately [0.6698,0.3302], producing [1.3395,1.3210]. Blocking the second key before softmax instead gives output [2,0]. A large weight is a mixing coefficient, not truth confidence.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Attention and architecture alternatives

Compare recurrence's compact evolving state with attention's position-specific interactions/cache. A small Transformer can be worse than a simpler model when data, compute or task structure differ. Head count at fixed hidden width changes per-head width; it does not automatically increase total representation width.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: compare allowed information

Use a tiny authored sequence task to verify future-token invariance, then continue into T3 and T0. No new language-model training backend is required to write this bridge.

**Check.** Does masking only the loss on a future token stop earlier positions attending to it?

**Answer.** No. The attention mask controls information flow; the loss mask controls scoring. They must be constructed and tested separately.

## 5. Attention dimensions, masking and memory

**Key terms.** Queries ask which keys to read. Keys determine match scores; values carry the content mixed by those scores. A mask excludes unavailable positions before normalization.

**Process.** Project input vectors into Q, K and V, score permitted position pairs, scale by the square root of key width, normalize each query row and combine value vectors. Concatenate head outputs and project them onward.

In these equations, T is the number of query positions, S the number of key/value positions and d_k the width used to compare a query with a key. Each row of A describes one query's weights over S possible sources. Multiplying A by V combines source content into output features.

\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}+M),\qquad O=AV.
\]

With Q shaped B×T×d_k and K shaped B×S×d_k, the score matrix is B×T×S. Each row sums to one after softmax over S permitted keys. Masked scores behave like negative infinity, yielding zero weight. An entirely masked row needs special handling rather than an undefined softmax.

### A training-system consequence

Standard attention materializes a quadratic position matrix when T=S. Memory-efficient kernels change the computation order to avoid storing that full matrix; they are not a different semantic license to read future tokens. Positional information remains necessary because content-only self-attention cannot distinguish arbitrary input order by itself.

The existing LLM course supplies the full Transformer walkthrough and the scratch trainer. The image lab's CNN does not become a Transformer simply because both architectures use matrices and backpropagation.

## Sources

- [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).
- [Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/).

steps.title: Query, keys and values
steps.prose: Use one query vector and two key/value pairs. Comparing the query with a key determines how strongly the corresponding value contributes. In a real model these vectors usually come from learned projections; queries and keys are not text strings being searched literally.
steps.terms: Q contains queries, K keys and V values. Their matching-vector widths must agree; output width follows the value vectors.
steps.next: Compare the query with each key and apply the visibility mask.

steps.title: Matching scores and visibility
steps.prose: Take a dot product with each key and scale by the square root of key width. A causal mask blocks future positions before normalization. Its blocked entry receives zero mixing weight after softmax, rather than merely being ignored by the training metric.
steps.terms: The attention mask controls information access. A loss mask instead controls which target positions count in the objective.
steps.next: Normalize the allowed scores across keys for this query.

steps.title: Softmax over allowed positions
steps.prose: Exponentiate and normalize the score row so its weights sum to one across permitted keys. These numbers tell us how to mix input content for this query. They are not probabilities over output vocabulary words.
steps.terms: The normalization axis is key positions. With only one allowed key, its weight becomes one.
steps.next: Multiply each value vector by its mixing weight and add them.

steps.title: Weighted sum of the values
steps.prose: Use the weights to combine the two value vectors. The result keeps the value-feature width; it is usually a mixture, not a hard choice of one source. Changing visibility changes which information can contribute.
steps.terms: Multi-head attention repeats this calculation with separate projected features, then combines the head outputs.
steps.next: The full Transformer architecture is linked as further reading rather than repeated on this page.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Attention lets one position retrieve a weighted mixture of information from other permitted positions. Instead of compressing the whole past into one recurrent state, it constructs a query for the current position, keys used for comparison, and values carrying information to mix. All three are learned projections, not separate natural-language questions and answers.

For a query q and key $k_j$, a scaled dot product gives score $q^Tk_j/\sqrt{d_k}$. A mask removes disallowed positions before softmax normalises the scores over keys. With two allowed scores 0 and $\ln3$, the weights are 0.25 and 0.75. Values 2 and 6 then produce $0.25(2)+0.75(6)=5$. The weights describe this mixture; they do not alone prove an explanation of the final prediction.

Self-attention takes queries, keys, and values from the same sequence. Cross-attention takes queries from one stream and keys/values from another. Causal masking permits only the prefix. Multiple heads learn different projections and combine their outputs; they do not simply vote on labels.

A Transformer block adds position information, normalization, residual paths, and a position-wise feed-forward network. The attention mixture communicates across positions; the feed-forward branch transforms each position's features. The decoder lesson follows the complete block and distinguishes forward inference, repeated generation, and weight updates.

Sources: [D2L: self-attention and positions](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/self-attention-and-positional-encoding.html), [Vaswani et al.: Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).
