/api/learning/document/N24.markdown:
# N24. NLP evaluation and a complete study

An NLP evaluation counts matches between predicted and reference objects under a declared task rule. Token tags, complete entity spans, answer tokens and generated sequences are different objects, even when some metrics share a familiar name. A complete study also records preprocessing, model selection, source groups and failures so the result can be interpreted and reproduced.

Two gold entities and two predicted entities have one exact span-and-type match, giving one correct match, one false positive and one false negative. A separate six-token example has five correct tags. The scores differ because the evaluated objects differ.

The task lessons introduced distinct outputs and error sources. This final lesson connects them to the shared metric formulas and an executable research workflow without inventing one universal NLP accuracy.

## 1. Task-specific matching and metric units

For exact NER evaluation, both the entity span and type must match under a declared scheme/scorer. A wrong boundary can produce one false positive and one false negative even if most token labels are correct. POS token accuracy, NER entity F1 and QA answer-token F1 evaluate different objects.

The authored example has two gold entities and two predictions, only one of which exactly matches: precision=recall=F1=0.5. A separately defined six-token labelling example has five correct tags, or 0.8333 token accuracy. These are not alternative calculations of the same metric. Use the right record-level matcher before invoking a shared count formula.

For generation, BLEU/chrF/ROUGE, semantic similarity and human/learned factuality checks add different evidence. Their scores must not be mixed into one unexplained universal accuracy.

## 2. Reproducible NLP studies and practice routes

Build one source-grouped text-classification study: lexical baseline, masked sentence-vector classifier and an optional fine-tuned encoder, keeping splits and selection budgets explicit. Then build a separate token/span study so pooling and sequence decoding are not confused. Record data/model licenses, revision IDs, seeds, preprocessing, label policies and per-case outputs.

Use scikit-learn for sparse pipelines; PyTorch for sequence tensors/packing; spaCy or NLTK for linguistic processing; Transformers/Tokenizers/Datasets for pinned encoders and data alignment; Sentence Transformers for pooling and retrieval; seqeval and SacreBLEU for task-specific scoring. These links describe an implementation route, not libraries automatically installed or new web trainers. Verify dataset access/licences and dependencies before downloading anything.

Inspect important slices and valid counterfactuals, report conditional uncertainty with appropriate groups, and distinguish development exploration from final checking. Dataset/model cards document intended use and limitations; they are not safety certificates.

### Data routes for progressively harder exercises

| Task | First-party route | What to preserve or inspect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sparse text classification | [20 Newsgroups in scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/datasets/real_world.html#the-20-newsgroups-text-dataset) | Original split, headers/quotes/footers as possible shortcuts, corpus provenance |
| POS and dependency parsing | [UD English EWT](https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/en_ewt/index.html) | CoNLL-U tokenization, sentence/document metadata, scheme and original licence |
| Reading and no-answer decisions | [SQuAD official data and scoring](https://rajpurkar.github.io/SQuAD-explorer/) | Context groups, character anchors, answerability and evaluation normalization |

These links were checked during course preparation. Nothing is automatically downloaded. Review the original data/source terms, version and permitted use before obtaining or redistributing a corpus. Dataset availability does not mean identical permissions or an absence of sensitive content.

### A local first coding exercise

Use a tiny authored fixture only to check the pipeline wiring:

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

train_text = [
    "the service was helpful", "a useful and clear answer",
    "excellent support today", "a pleasant experience",
    "the service was awful", "a confusing and wrong answer",
    "poor support today", "an unpleasant experience",
]
train_y = [1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
pipeline = make_pipeline(
    TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)),
    LogisticRegression(C=1, max_iter=200, random_state=0),
)
pipeline.fit(train_text, train_y)
probe = ["helpful support", "not helpful support", "unseen jargon"]
print(pipeline.predict(probe))
print(pipeline.classes_, pipeline.predict_proba(probe))
```

First inspect the vocabulary and the difference between the two negation probes. Do not call these three outputs a measured generalization result: there is no independent benchmark here, and eight training sentences are deliberately insufficient for a useful sentiment system. Next obtain one approved real corpus, preserve source groups/splits, fit preprocessing only on training and perform the capstone's controlled comparisons.

## Sources

### A local first coding exercise

Use a tiny authored fixture only to check the pipeline wiring:

```python

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

train_text = [
    "the service was helpful", "a useful and clear answer",
    "excellent support today", "a pleasant experience",
    "the service was awful", "a confusing and wrong answer",
    "poor support today", "an unpleasant experience",
]

pipeline = make_pipeline(
    TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)),
    LogisticRegression(C=1, max_iter=200, random_state=0),
)
pipeline.fit(train_text, train_y)

print(pipeline.predict(probe))
print(pipeline.classes_, pipeline.predict_proba(probe))
```

reading.definition: An NLP evaluation counts matches between predicted and reference objects under a declared task rule. Token tags, complete entity spans, answer tokens and generated sequences are different objects, even when some metrics share a familiar name. A complete study also records preprocessing, model selection, source groups and failures so the result can be interpreted and reproduced.
reading.example: Two gold entities and two predicted entities have one exact span-and-type match, giving one correct match, one false positive and one false negative. A separate six-token example has five correct tags. The scores differ because the evaluated objects differ.
reading.connection: The task lessons introduced distinct outputs and error sources. This final lesson connects them to the shared metric formulas and an executable research workflow without inventing one universal NLP accuracy.

steps.title: Define what counts as one match
steps.prose: For exact named-entity evaluation, both the source boundary and type must agree. Matching only part of a name can leave one missed gold entity and one incorrect predicted entity. Start with the objects and matcher before choosing an aggregation formula.
steps.terms: A true positive is a matched prediction; a false positive is an unmatched prediction; a false negative is an unmatched reference object.
steps.next: Apply the shared precision, recall and F1 definitions to these entity-level counts.

steps.title: Calculate exact entity precision, recall and F1
steps.prose: One of two predictions matches one of two references, so precision and recall are both one half and their F1 is one half. Report entity types, strict or permissive boundary-tag handling and scorer version with a real result.
steps.terms: The count formula can be reused across tasks, but the matching objects determine its interpretation. Entity F1 is not automatically macro classification F1.
steps.next: Compare this with a separate token-level example without treating it as a replacement score.
steps.node: Calculate exact entity precision, recall and F1

reading.lesson_markdown:
An NLP study should connect its annotation policy, representation, training objective, and reported output metric. Token accuracy, exact entity F1, retrieval recall, and summary faithfulness count different things. A complete report names the unit, the split, and the model-selection process before interpreting the score.

For two gold entities, predicting one exact typed span and one wrong span gives one True Positive, one False Positive, and one False Negative: precision and recall are both 0.5. A token-level metric can give a different impression because many non-entity tokens are easy. Show a concrete error, not only a leaderboard.

Behavioural testing complements a representative held-out sample. CheckList-style tests ask whether capabilities such as negation handling or name invariance behave as intended. They are test suites, but do not automatically estimate performance on a naturally sampled deployment population. A successful template test also does not prove the broader capability is solved.

Keep a baseline, meaningful ablations, uncertainty with the right independent unit, and evidence for generated intermediate records. Save prompts, preprocessing, data versions, and evaluation scripts. When a result fails to transfer, narrow the conclusion rather than hiding the target. That is a scientific outcome, not a reason to replace the metric after seeing the answer.

Sources: [Ribeiro et al.: CheckList](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.442/), [scikit-learn: evaluation metrics](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/model_evaluation.html).

# T0. The language-model training loop

Training changes a language model's parameters using examples. A batch supplies input tokens and known targets; the model predicts, a loss measures mistakes, backpropagation computes gradients and an optimizer updates the parameters. Validation and generation use the model differently: they do not apply these training updates.

A sequence [3,7,2,9] supplies inputs [3,7,2] and next-token targets [7,2,9]. One supplied target probability illustrates loss, while a separate scalar gradient illustrates an update. They explain the stages but are not one fully differentiated numerical model.

The foundations and DL course introduced loss, gradients and updates. This lesson assembles them for token sequences, keeping the repeated training path separate from periodic validation, checkpoint selection and fixed-weight use.

## 1. Training, validation and generation

**Key terms.** A **batch** is a group of training examples; **weights** are learned numbers; an **update** changes them; **validation** checks separate examples without updates.

**Process.** Preparation produces batches and starting weights. Training repeats prediction, loss, gradients and updates; periodic validation selects a saved checkpoint. Generation then uses that checkpoint without the training loop.

There are three parts: prepare once, repeat training, then check/save/use. They are connected but are not the same loop.

```text
Prepare: sources → clean and split → tokenizer → batches → initial weights

Repeat:  batch → predictions → loss → gradients → optimizer update
            ↑                                      |
            +--------------- next batch ------------+

Check:   validation text → measure without updates → choose checkpoint
Use:     chosen checkpoint → prompt → generate → inspect the output
```

A batch supplies many next-token targets. After enough batches the program checks progress, saves state and continues if the planned budget allows it. Validation is periodic, not necessarily after every update.

## 2. Text preparation

**Key terms.** A **corpus** is a collection of text; a **split** assigns independent sources to training, development or test; a **tokenizer** converts text to IDs.

**Process.** Choose permitted sources, clean and split them, then fit a tokenizer only on training text or reuse the pretrained model's tokenizer. The output is compatible token sequences for building batches.

Choose permitted text that suits the goal. A story model needs many varied stories; 24 repeated teaching paragraphs are not a substitute. Remove broken documents and obvious duplicates, then assign whole documents or related groups to training, validation and test splits.

Training supplies weight updates. Validation, also called development text, helps choose settings/checkpoints. Test is the final reserved check. If we keep changing the design after seeing test, it is no longer independent.

A tokenizer turns text into pieces and gives each piece a number. Fit a new tokenizer on training text only. A pretrained model instead needs its compatible existing tokenizer: changing IDs without changing their learned meanings breaks that compatibility.

## 3. Inputs and next-token targets

**Key terms.** A **target** is the answer to predict; a **causal mask** blocks future input; a **loss mask** excludes positions from scoring.

**Process.** Take a token sequence and align each input position with its next token. Mask forbidden attention and unscored targets, then send the aligned inputs to the model and targets to the loss.

```text
Original: <start> The cat sat <end>
Input:    <start> The cat sat
Target:   The     cat sat <end>
```

The target at each position is the next piece. That is where labels come from; someone does not label every word by hand. Some libraries shift internally, so our code must not shift twice.

Training processes many positions together. A causal attention mask still blocks future input: when predicting `cat`, the model cannot read it from a future position. A separate loss mask decides which targets count towards the grade. Padding is ignored. In our conversation adapter, the prompt provides context but only response targets contribute to loss.

## 4. Forward pass

**Key terms.** An **embedding** maps an ID to a vector; **attention** mixes allowed positions; an **MLP** transforms features; a **logit** is a raw vocabulary score.

**Process.** Token IDs become vectors, Transformer blocks transform those vectors, and the output layer produces vocabulary scores. These forward calculations precede loss and do not themselves update weights.

IDs select learned vectors, called embeddings. Position information represents order. Transformer blocks mix permitted earlier information through attention and transform it through feed-forward networks. Residual connections carry earlier information around a sublayer; normalization controls the scale of intermediate values.

The final layer produces a raw score for each vocabulary token: a logit. Softmax turns logits into probabilities summing to one. This is the forward pass. Predictions exist, but weights have not changed yet.

## 5. Cross-entropy loss

**Key terms.** **Cross-entropy loss** is the negative log probability of the correct target; a **nat** uses the natural logarithm; **N** counts scored targets; **pᵢ** is each correct-target probability.

**Process.** Combine vocabulary scores with the known targets, calculate a penalty at each included position and average those penalties. This scalar loss is the starting point for the backward calculation.

If the correct token gets probability 0.5, its penalty is about 0.693 nats. At probability 0.1, the penalty is about 2.303. Average over valid target tokens, not padding.

\[
L=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_i
\]

`N` is the included target count; `p_i` is the probability of correct target `i`. A nat is the unit from a natural logarithm. Lower loss means better prediction on that text/tokenization, not automatic truthfulness or useful conversation.

## 6. Backpropagation

**Key terms.** A **gradient** is a loss derivative; **backpropagation** applies the chain rule backwards; **sigmoid** maps a scalar score to a probability between 0 and 1.

**Process.** Start from the scalar loss and follow recorded operations backwards to each trainable parameter. The result is a set of gradients waiting for an optimizer, not a new set of weights.

Backpropagation follows the calculation backwards to find how a small change in each trainable weight would locally affect loss. These derivatives are gradients. They describe an adjustment direction; they are not updated weights yet.

As a separate numerical check, let a two-choice model use probability `sigmoid(w)` for a correct target of 1. At scalar weight zero the probability is 0.5 and the cross-entropy gradient is −0.5. Increasing that weight would locally reduce this loss. A real LLM has many interacting weights, with gradients through the complete computation.

## 7. Accumulation and optimizer updates

**Key terms.** A **microbatch** fits one forward/backward pass; **accumulation** combines gradients; **clipping** limits their overall length, called the gradient norm; **η** denotes learning rate; **g** denotes gradient.

**Process.** Accumulate correctly weighted microbatch gradients, unscale if needed, clip if configured, then apply one optimizer step. Clear gradients at the declared boundary before collecting the next update's evidence.

A microbatch is a small group that fits in memory. Gradient accumulation combines several microbatches before one optimizer update. It does not apply an update after each small batch.

With 10 valid targets in one microbatch and 90 in another, a token-average objective weights their mean losses by 0.1 and 0.9, not half each. The denominator matters. Gradient clipping can then reduce an excessively large overall gradient norm; it does not normally clip every weight separately.

The simple SGD update is:

\[
w_{\text{new}}=w-\eta g
\]

`w` is the learned number, `g` its gradient and `η` the learning rate. Weight 0, gradient −0.5 and rate 0.2 give new weight 0.1. In the two-choice example, correct-token probability becomes about 0.525 and loss falls from 0.693 to 0.644. This checked calculation is not a promise that every large-model update improves validation. AdamW also uses running statistics and weight decay rather than this bare SGD rule.

Clear gradients at the appropriate boundary so unrelated updates do not accidentally accumulate. Advance the schedule in its declared units, fetch another batch and repeat. An update is not an epoch: an epoch is a pass over a dataset, whereas our sampler can practise examples repeatedly.

### Check the complete update boundary

Before calling an experiment reproducible, trace one update with these checks:

1. Save the exact input IDs, target IDs and scoring mask of a small non-sensitive test batch. Count valid targets after shifting.
2. Compute a summed cross-entropy and divide by the intended update's target count. A response-only objective and an all-token objective are different even with the same input text.
3. Confirm that expected trainable parameters have finite gradients, frozen parameters stay frozen, and no training graph is retained accidentally in logging.
4. Apply one optimizer update and verify that the expected weights changed. Record learning rate and gradient norm, with an explicit before/after-clipping convention.
5. Restore a complete checkpoint and compare the next few CPU updates against uninterrupted training. Approximate continuation and identical replay are different acceptance criteria.

The saved-run inspector's optional scratch update is a separate diagnostic: it uses its own short text batch and SGD, not the original run's optimizer state. Do not treat it as a replay of the training trajectory. For implementation details, consult [PyTorch autograd](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/notes/autograd.html) and [checkpoint restoration](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

## 8. Validation and checkpoints

**Key terms.** **Evaluation mode** changes behaviours such as dropout; **no-grad mode** stops recording derivative history; a **checkpoint** saves model state.

**Process.** Pause training updates, measure separate validation text and choose whether to save the current state. Resume training only afterwards; validation results select checkpoints but supply no training gradient.

Periodically use separate validation text in evaluation mode, with gradient recording disabled. Dropout is off in evaluation mode. There is no backward pass or optimizer update. Validation helps choose a checkpoint, not the training gradient.

Training loss can fall while validation rises. That can indicate overfitting, although noisy checks, data changes and evaluation mistakes also matter. The lab's saved-run curves show recorded observations; the teaching process diagram is not a measured validation curve.

A checkpoint saves weights. Proper training resume also needs optimizer/schedule position, random/sampler state and compatible data/configuration. Our scratch path supports this continuation. The adapter path saves selected/final adapters but does not yet promise resumable optimizer state.

## 9. Generation with saved weights

**Key terms.** A **prompt** is starting text; **decoding** selects tokens from predicted probabilities; a **stop rule** ends generation.

**Process.** Load a chosen checkpoint, process the prompt, choose and append a token, then predict again. Generated tokens become the next inputs; no correct future targets or optimizer steps are supplied.

Process a prompt, choose a next token, append it and repeat until an end token or length limit. No weights change. Temperature and top-k affect selection, not learned knowledge. A story-completion model is not automatically an instruction-following assistant.

Training has known targets and uses gradients. Generation does not receive the true future answer and normally performs no backward pass. Inspect unedited outputs as well as loss: our adapter example became wrong about melting despite a better average loss.

## 10. Scratch training versus adaptation

**Key terms.** **Scratch training** starts from random weights; **adaptation** starts from pretrained weights; an **adapter** is a small trainable addition to a frozen base.

**Process.** Choose the learning goal before the training path. That choice determines the starting knowledge and updated parameters; evaluate success against the same starting point rather than comparing unlike training budgets.

| Path | Starting weights | Updated weights | Intended success |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scratch mechanics | Random | All weights | Correct, inspectable masking, gradients and controlled tests |
| Current language adapter | Pretrained SmolLM2 | Small LoRA matrices | Audited change against that same starting model |
| Proposed story model | Random | All weights of a roughly 14M decoder | Held-out prediction gains plus coherent completions on fixed new story beginnings |

The story model is a proposed next run, not trained already. It needs a tokenizer/corpus pipeline, throughput benchmark and approved budget. More parameters on the same tiny fixture would not supply missing language exposure.

## Quick checks

1. Does a forward pass change weights? No: it makes predictions.
2. Does backward apply the update? No: it computes gradients; the optimizer updates.
3. Does validation call the optimizer? No: that would train on the check.
4. Is lower training loss enough? No: check held-out prediction and intended behaviour.
5. Is adapting pretrained weights equivalent to learning from random weights? No: starting knowledge and compute requirements differ.

References: [PyTorch optimization](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/optimization_tutorial.html), [TinyStories paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07759), [TinyStories data/license](https://huggingface.co/datasets/roneneldan/TinyStories).

notes.title: Check the complete update boundary
notes.markdown:
Before calling an experiment reproducible, trace one update with these checks:

1. Save the exact input IDs, target IDs and scoring mask of a small non-sensitive test batch. Count valid targets after shifting.
2. Compute a summed cross-entropy and divide by the intended update's target count. A response-only objective and an all-token objective are different even with the same input text.
3. Confirm that expected trainable parameters have finite gradients, frozen parameters stay frozen, and no training graph is retained accidentally in logging.
4. Apply one optimizer update and verify that the expected weights changed. Record learning rate and gradient norm, with an explicit before/after-clipping convention.
5. Restore a complete checkpoint and compare the next few CPU updates against uninterrupted training. Approximate continuation and identical replay are different acceptance criteria.

The saved-run inspector's optional scratch update is a separate diagnostic: it uses its own short text batch and SGD, not the original run's optimizer state. Do not treat it as a replay of the training trajectory. For implementation details, consult [PyTorch autograd](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/notes/autograd.html) and [checkpoint restoration](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

notes.title: Scratch training versus adaptation
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** **Scratch training** starts from random weights; **adaptation** starts from pretrained weights; an **adapter** is a small trainable addition to a frozen base.

| Path | Starting weights | Updated weights | Intended success |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scratch mechanics | Random | All weights | Correct, inspectable masking, gradients and controlled tests |
| Current language adapter | Pretrained SmolLM2 | Small LoRA matrices | Audited change against that same starting model |
| Proposed story model | Random | All weights of a roughly 14M decoder | Held-out prediction gains plus coherent completions on fixed new story beginnings |

The story model is a proposed next run, not trained already. It needs a tokenizer/corpus pipeline, throughput benchmark and approved budget. More parameters on the same tiny fixture would not supply missing language exposure.

reading.title: The language-model training loop
reading.definition: Training changes a language model's parameters using examples. A batch supplies input tokens and known targets; the model predicts, a loss measures mistakes, backpropagation computes gradients and an optimizer updates the parameters. Validation and generation use the model differently: they do not apply these training updates.
reading.example: A sequence [3,7,2,9] supplies inputs [3,7,2] and next-token targets [7,2,9]. One supplied target probability illustrates loss, while a separate scalar gradient illustrates an update. They explain the stages but are not one fully differentiated numerical model.
reading.connection: The foundations and DL course introduced loss, gradients and updates. This lesson assembles them for token sequences, keeping the repeated training path separate from periodic validation, checkpoint selection and fixed-weight use.

steps.title: Prepare inputs, targets and masks
steps.prose: Use training-only text and a compatible tokenizer to construct a batch. Shift tokens once so each input position predicts its successor. Define visibility and target masks before the forward pass; document and conversation boundaries affect what can be learned.
steps.terms: B counts batch examples and T prediction positions. A causal mask controls access to future positions; a loss mask selects targets that contribute to the objective.
steps.next: Run the current model on these permitted inputs without changing its parameters yet.

steps.title: Calculate predictions with current parameters
steps.prose: The forward pass maps input IDs through embeddings and model layers to vocabulary logits. Softmax defines a distribution for each scored position. The supplied probability 0.5 is an illustration, not the measured output of the scalar update below.
steps.terms: A logit is an unnormalized vocabulary score. Parameters define the predictor; computing predictions is not itself an optimizer update.
steps.next: Compare the assigned target probabilities with the known labels to obtain a scalar loss.

steps.title: Calculate loss over valid targets
steps.prose: Take the negative log-probability of each included correct token, then reduce under the intended convention. Here one target with probability 0.5 gives log two. Padding and unscored prompt positions must not enter the denominator accidentally.
steps.terms: In the equation m_t selects targets, p_t(y_t) is the correct-token probability and the mask sum counts valid targets. Natural logs give nats.
steps.next: Differentiate the declared loss through the recorded computation to obtain parameter gradients.

steps.title: Compute gradients by backpropagation
steps.prose: Backpropagation follows the chain rule to measure how changing each trainable parameter would change the loss locally. It writes gradients, not new weights. The next stage's scalar gradient 2 is supplied separately to explain an optimizer.

steps.next: Pass the gradients to an optimizer under the chosen accumulation and clipping rules.

steps.title: Apply one optimizer update and repeat
steps.prose: The scalar illustration changes weight 1 using gradient 2 and the selected learning rate. A real AdamW update also uses optimizer history and decay rules. Clear gradients at the correct boundary, fetch another batch and repeat under the budget.

steps.next: Continue with the next batch; at scheduled intervals, evaluate separate validation text without updates.

steps.title: Evaluate periodically on validation text
steps.prose: Pause updates, use the intended evaluation mode and disable derivative recording. The hypothetical losses [1.2,1.0,1.1] select checkpoint two. Validation supports selection; feeding its gradients into the optimizer would change the experiment.

steps.title: Save state for selection, resumption or use

steps.terms: A checkpoint's contents determine its supported use. Selecting a checkpoint, resuming training and generating from it are different actions.
steps.next: The next lesson examines how changing prediction targets and available context changes the training objective.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Language-model training repeatedly asks the network to predict known tokens, measures their probability, and changes weights to reduce an objective. The text supplies the targets. Generating a continuation is different: the target is unknown and the model's chosen token becomes part of the next input.

### Construct the prediction problem

For a token sequence `[a,b,c,d]`, a three-position input can be `[a,b,c]` with targets `[b,c,d]`. At each position, causal attention permits only the prefix ending there. The final input c has a target d, even though d is outside the input slice. Padding masks and ignored labels remove artificial or deliberately unscored targets. Attention masks separately control what each position can read.

### Predict, score, differentiate, update

Embedding lookup maps IDs to vectors. Decoder blocks transform them. A vocabulary projection produces logits at each position. Softmax describes the next-token distribution, while a stable cross-entropy implementation can consume logits directly. If probabilities assigned to three realised targets are 0.5, 0.25, and 0.8, total negative log-likelihood is about 2.303 and mean is about 0.768 nats over three targets.

Backpropagation computes gradients of that loss through trainable operations. The optimizer applies an update using those gradients and any stored history. Clear gradient buffers at the intended update boundary, not indiscriminately between microbatches that should accumulate. Repeat with training examples. Teacher-forced training scores many positions in parallel under the causal mask; it does not sample a new sequence for every ordinary next-token update.

### Check progress without fitting the answers

Periodically evaluate development loss with frozen weights and evaluation behaviour. Use it to select a checkpoint. Test evaluates the selected model, not every trial until a pleasing score appears. Save compatible tokenizer, config, weights, and the additional optimizer/sampler state needed for continuation. A best checkpoint and the latest checkpoint answer different questions.

In this lab, scratch runs use real optimizer steps. Development loss is measured at step 1, each 20 steps, and the final step. `last.pt` is overwritten; it is not a history of model states. The standard export contains selected weights and final evidence, not a replay of all earlier token probabilities. The architecture diagram's head-only derivative is an illustration; the trainer differentiates the full trainable scratch network.

Sources: [D2L: language-model training](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/rnn-scratch.html), [PyTorch: CrossEntropyLoss](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss.html), [PyTorch: checkpointing](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

/api/learning/document/T1.markdown:
# T1. Language-model training objectives

A training objective defines what the model predicts, which information it may use and how mistakes are scored. Causal language modelling predicts successors from prefixes; masked modelling reconstructs selected tokens from permitted surrounding text; encoder–decoder learning predicts a target sequence conditioned on a source. These are different prediction problems, not interchangeable names for pretraining.

Choose an objective to compare visibility and targets. A separate fixed set of three correct-target probabilities [0.5,0.25,0.5] illustrates mean negative log-likelihood. The numbers do not establish which objective trains a better model.

The complete training loop can optimize different objectives. Define their information access before comparing losses or downstream behavior; a language-model objective alone does not establish instruction following or safe deployment.

## 1. Next-token prediction

**Key terms.** An **autoregressive objective** predicts the next token from preceding tokens; **θ** denotes learned parameters; **x₍<t₎** is the prefix before position t.

**Process.** Tokenized text supplies prefixes and known next tokens. The model assigns target probabilities; negative log likelihood turns them into the loss used to adjust θ.

For an autoregressive model:

\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}),\qquad
L(\theta)=-\frac1{N_{valid}}\sum_{b,t}m_{bt}\log p_\theta(x_{bt}\mid x_{b,<t}).
\]

`θ` is the trainable parameter collection; `m` is a 0/1 loss mask; `N_valid=Σm` counts included target positions. The loss increases when the model assigns low probability to observed targets. It does not explicitly reward truthfulness, helpfulness or obedience unless the data/objective supplies an appropriate signal.

**Where labels come from:** take token sequence `[BOS,the,cat,sat,EOS]`. Inputs are `[BOS,the,cat,sat]`; targets are `[the,cat,sat,EOS]`. At each position the correct next token is in the original text. This is self-supervision, not an absence of targets. In real code, some model APIs shift labels internally; shifting again is a bug.

Example target probabilities `[0.5,0.25,0.5,0.8]` give average loss `(0.6931+1.3863+0.6931+0.2231)/4≈0.7489` nats and perplexity about 2.115. Average across valid tokens, not padded positions.

## 2. Three major objective families

**Key terms.** An **objective** specifies the prediction problem; a **mask** hides or excludes information; **teacher forcing** supplies observed preceding tokens during training.

**Process.** Choose which text is visible and which tokens must be predicted, then construct inputs and targets accordingly. Causal, masked-token and encoder–decoder objectives therefore learn from different information patterns.

**Causal/next-token:** predict from earlier tokens. Appropriate for left-to-right generation. A causal mask prevents access to future tokens during training, even though many positions are computed in parallel.

**Masked language modelling:** hide selected input tokens and recover them from permitted surrounding text. BERT-style encoders can see both sides of unmasked context. They are useful for representations/classification but are not the same generation interface as an autoregressive decoder.

**Encoder–decoder / denoising:** encode a source, then decode a target, often reconstructing corrupted spans or performing translation. The encoder attends to source input; the decoder attends to earlier target tokens and the source representation. A prefix-LM can instead use different visibility rules within one stack.

Teacher forcing provides gold previous target tokens during training. During generation, the model receives its own earlier outputs. That mismatch is one source of compounding errors; it does not imply teacher forcing is inherently invalid.

### Why one forward pass can learn many next tokens

Suppose the text contains four input positions. The model produces vocabulary scores at all four positions, but a triangular attention mask gives each position a different permitted prefix.

1. Position 1 predicts token 2 using only position 1. Position 2 predicts token 3 using positions 1–2, and so on.
2. Gold tokens are available as later *input positions*, but the mask blocks those positions from an earlier query. Parallel computation does not imply permission to read future answers.
3. Gather the score of each correct next token, compute its negative log probability, apply the scoring mask and aggregate.
4. Backpropagate the aggregated loss once. Shared parameters receive contributions from many target positions in that pass.

At generation time there is no gold future sequence. The program must append a chosen token before computing the next output distribution. This distinction explains why training over positions can be parallel while ordinary output generation remains sequential. The statistical objective is conditional likelihood, not a direct test of whether a generated paragraph is true. Original objective examples: [Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762), [BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805) and [T5](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v21/20-074.html).

## 3. Pretraining, adaptation and inference

**Key terms.** **Pretraining** learns broad patterns; **continued pretraining** adds domain exposure; **SFT** imitates demonstrations; **inference** uses saved weights.

**Process.** First acquire general representations, then adapt them if the task requires it. Keep each stage's data and objective separate so a later behaviour change is attributed to the correct intervention.

```text
raw sources → governed corpus → tokenizer/packing → initialized architecture
→ pretraining → base checkpoint → optional continued/domain pretraining
→ supervised adaptation → optional preference/RL alignment
→ model evaluation → system integration → system evaluation → deployment
```

**Pretraining** learns broad statistical structure. **Continued pretraining** keeps a language-model objective on new data, often for a domain/language. **SFT** learns desired responses from demonstrations. **Preference optimization** changes which outputs are favoured. **Inference** computes outputs using fixed weights; an agent's memory or tool use is not automatically weight learning.

These are not mandatory steps in one universal recipe. A classifier can be adapted from an encoder without chat alignment. Retrieval can improve freshness without retraining. RL is not required to make every useful assistant.

## 4. Limits of the training objective

**Key terms.** **Fluency** is well-formed language; **factuality** concerns correctness; **alignment** concerns the desired behaviour under stated criteria.

**Process.** A training objective improves its measured prediction target. Independent behavioural tests must then establish any stronger claim about useful, truthful or safe answers.

Lower validation language-model loss demonstrates better prediction on that validation distribution. It does not alone establish factual support, robust instruction following, causality, reasoning faithfulness or successful deployment. A model may learn source style, reproduce private sequences, or inherit the corpus's stereotypes.

**Base versus instruction model:** a base model continues patterns; an instruction-tuned model is trained to respond in a particular conversational format. Comparing one as a plain completion and the other with a correct template can conflate interface and capability. Save the complete input format.

## 5. Experiment design

**Key terms.** A **factor** is the intended experimental change; a **control** fixes an alternative explanation; a **budget** specifies allowed work.

**Process.** Declare the hypothesis, data, objective and comparison budget first. Run the conditions with recorded settings, then assess held-out outcomes rather than choosing the story after seeing scores.

For a toy model, choose a small licensed/public-domain corpus, a fixed tokenizer, document-level splits, a context length, a small architecture and a compute ceiling. Record tokens processed, updates, elapsed time and validation loss. Run a trivial n-gram or unigram baseline. Inspect actual generated samples but do not choose checkpoints only because samples look entertaining.

## Exercises and answers

1. Does an unlabelled web document supply training labels? **Yes:** its next tokens become targets under a causal objective.
2. A batch has 100 valid targets and 100 padding positions. Is dividing the valid loss sum by 200 correct? **No:** it changes the scale with padding; divide by the intended valid-token count.
3. Which stage solves a request for today's weather? **An authorised current source/tool**, not merely more old-text pretraining.

Original architecture/objective context: [Transformer paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762). Full lifecycle case study: [OLMo 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00656). Read these as examples of recipes, not evidence that all models use one pipeline.

reading.definition: A training objective defines what the model predicts, which information it may use and how mistakes are scored. Causal language modelling predicts successors from prefixes; masked modelling reconstructs selected tokens from permitted surrounding text; encoder–decoder learning predicts a target sequence conditioned on a source. These are different prediction problems, not interchangeable names for pretraining.

reading.connection: The complete training loop can optimize different objectives. Define their information access before comparing losses or downstream behavior; a language-model objective alone does not establish instruction following or safe deployment.

steps.title: Define the prediction target
steps.prose: The selected objective determines whether an answer is the next token, a withheld original token or a token of a conditional target sequence. Observed text supplies these labels. Self-supervision therefore does not mean training without any targets.
steps.terms: Theta denotes learned parameters. The expectation in the loss describes averaging over examples; y is the target under the selected task.
steps.next: Specify what the model may read when predicting that target.

steps.title: Specify permitted context and visibility
steps.prose: Causal prediction uses a permitted prefix; masked prediction uses corrupted surrounding input; conditional decoding uses a source plus earlier target tokens. Attention visibility must enforce this access even when many positions are computed together.
steps.terms: An attention mask limits information flow. A loss mask chooses which positions are scored; excluding a loss does not hide its input token.
steps.next: Score only the declared targets with their correct normalization.

steps.title: Calculate mean target prediction loss
steps.prose: For the supplied probabilities [0.5,0.25,0.5], add three negative natural logarithms and divide by three. This demonstrates the scoring operation separately from the visibility examples. A different target set changes the loss's interpretation.
steps.terms: NLL is negative log-likelihood. The mean is per included target, not per padded slot or necessarily per input sentence.
steps.next: Keep the distinction between this training score and the behavior required when using the model.

reading.lesson_markdown:
An objective defines which information the model receives and what it must predict. A causal next-token objective predicts each successor from its prefix. A masked-language objective predicts selected hidden tokens using permitted surrounding text. An encoder–decoder denoising objective reconstructs target text from a corrupted source. These are related learning problems, not interchangeable prompt templates.

For causal training, the loss is the mean negative log-probability of the supplied successors over scored positions. A correct token assigned probability 0.5 contributes $-\ln0.5\approx0.693$ nats. With two valid targets and one ignored padding position, divide by two, not three. Specifying the denominator is part of specifying the objective.

In **pretraining**, a broad corpus supplies self-supervised targets. Continued pretraining adapts the same kind of objective to another distribution. **Supervised fine-tuning** typically scores desired assistant responses, sometimes masking user/prompt tokens. At **inference**, parameters are fixed and decoding chooses outputs; no optimizer step is implied by a longer answer.

The objective rewards a measurable prediction behaviour, not all qualities a user wants. Lower token loss can coexist with factual errors, poor instruction following, or unsafe actions. Evaluate the intended behaviour separately and keep context visibility matched when comparing objectives.

Sources: [SLP: Transformers and pretraining](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/7.pdf), [BERT: masked pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805), [T5: text-to-text objectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683).

# T2. LLM training data, tokenization and packing

A language-model data pipeline converts permitted source material into the exact token inputs and prediction targets seen during training. It includes extraction, duplicate grouping, splits, tokenization, packing and masks. Corpus descriptions alone are insufficient: the resulting batches must preserve the intended information and evaluation boundaries.

Four source records with one exact duplicate illustrate identity and grouping. A separate supplied token sequence [3,7,2,9] shows how window length changes the aligned input and target slices. Neither example downloads or prepares an external corpus.

An objective defines the intended prediction problem. The data pipeline must implement that problem without leaking evaluation examples, changing tokenizer meanings or introducing unintended cross-document targets.

## 1. Data provenance and permissions

**Key terms.** **Provenance** records where data came from; a **license** states permitted use; a **pipeline** converts sources into training inputs.

**Process.** Start with permitted sources and record their origins, then extract, clean and tokenize them. Audit the actual final batches: the model learns what reaches them, not the description of the source corpus.

Start with a data contract: source, rights/consent, intended use, language/domain, sensitive fields, extraction method, retention and deletion policy. Publicly accessible does not automatically mean licensed for every use. Hashing a private identifier does not necessarily anonymise it.

The pipeline is: approved sources; extraction; quality/language checks; sensitive-data handling; deduplication and grouping; tokenization/packing; versioned shards; batch audits.

Treat the pipeline as a chain of transformations that can each change the evidence. Keep rejection reasons and a sample of discarded material under appropriate access controls. Aggressive filtering can improve some benchmarks while removing dialects or lower-resource languages. “Quality” is a policy and measurement choice, not an objective universal scalar.

## 2. Extraction and deduplication

**Key terms.** **Extraction** recovers text from a source format; **deduplication** finds repeated material; a **near-duplicate** differs slightly but carries largely the same content.

**Process.** Extract text, remove corruption and identify duplicate groups before splitting. Preserve links to original sources so filtering decisions and suspicious examples can be traced later.

Web extraction removes navigation/boilerplate while retaining main text. PDFs add columns, tables, OCR errors and page breaks. Preserve headings, source order and identifiers where meaningful. A failed parser can silently train the model on menus or repeated footers.

**Exact deduplication** compares identical canonical content. **Near deduplication** compares overlapping shingles or representations. MinHash approximates Jaccard similarity between sets; locality-sensitive hashing proposes likely similar pairs without comparing everything. Semantic deduplication can remove paraphrases but may also merge genuinely distinct facts.

Canonicalization must be specified. Lowercasing, whitespace changes and punctuation deletion alter what “same” means. Keep the original alongside the normalized representation where justified.

## 3. Records, deterministic IDs and hashes

**Key terms.** A **record** is one structured data entry; a **deterministic ID** repeats for the same defined inputs; a **hash** is a content fingerprint, not a guarantee of truth.

**Process.** Normalize the intended identity fields, compute an ID and content fingerprint, then store both with provenance. Later validation can distinguish the same example, changed content and repeated pipeline output.

A **record** is one structured item plus its metadata. A deterministic ID is recreated from a stable rule: `source_id + version + span boundaries`. A content hash is a fingerprint computed from exact bytes or a documented canonical serialization. A cryptographic hash is not encryption and does not prove a record is true.

Example educational record:

```json
{
  "record_id": "paper17:v2:abstract",
  "source_id": "paper17",
  "source_version": "v2",
  "language": "en",
  "text": "A treatment reduced symptoms in a small trial.",
  "rights_status": "approved_for_this_exercise",
  "parser_version": "exercise-1"
}
```

Changing source text should change its content fingerprint. Changing only record order should not change per-record content fingerprints, though it changes a whole-file hash. Save the algorithm and serialization, not just an unexplained digest. Source links enable tracing; they do not guarantee that generated claims preserve the source.

## 4. Splits, contamination and mixing

**Key terms.** **Contamination** exposes evaluation material during fitting; a **mixture** combines data sources; **sampling weights** determine how often sources appear.

**Process.** Group related sources and reserve evaluation material before fitting or mixing. Choose training-source proportions next, then inspect exposures so a large repeated source does not silently dominate.

Split at the level that prevents leakage. Search for benchmark questions and answer-like variants in training data; exact string checks alone miss paraphrases. A clean contamination audit is evidence about the checks performed, not proof that no hidden overlap exists.

A data mixture specifies sampling weights by source/domain/language. A source with twice the weight is seen more often, not necessarily learned twice as well. Token budgets and document sampling create different exposures. Track repeated epochs and duplicated synthetic content. Continual/domain pretraining can forget earlier capabilities if the mix is too narrow.

Synthetic data can improve coverage and formatting but inherits teacher errors, biases and benchmark leakage. Verify provenance and licensing, sample outputs independently and maintain human/real-data evaluation. Model collapse is a risk under particular repeated synthetic-data conditions, not a theorem that all synthetic data is bad.

## 5. Packing and masks

**Key terms.** **Packing** combines sequences into efficient windows; an **attention mask** controls information flow; a **loss mask** controls which targets are scored.

**Process.** Token sequences enter windows with explicit boundaries and padding. Build attention and loss masks before the forward pass, then verify that neither cross-document leakage nor unintended target scoring has been introduced.

**Calculation.** With two independent documents of 12 and 8 tokens in a 32-position window, 20 positions contain document tokens and 12 are padding. Under shifted-target scoring with no cross-document transition, target counts must be computed per boundary; 20 input tokens do not automatically mean 20 valid next-token targets.

Packing concatenates short samples to use token slots efficiently. EOS boundaries indicate document endings; whether attention crosses a boundary is a design decision. A block-diagonal attention mask can isolate samples. An attention mask controls **what can be seen**; a loss mask controls **which predictions are scored**. They are different.

For SFT, packing must preserve response spans and role boundaries. For causal pretraining, verify no target sees itself/future tokens. Test padding on both short and full-length batches. One off-by-one error can make a misleadingly easy objective.

### Audit one packed sequence before scaling the corpus

Take two independent documents, A and B, packed into one token window. Decide the intended statistical task before choosing an efficient attention kernel.

1. Assign each token a document/group identity and original source offset. Keep a separate marker for padding.
2. If documents must be independent, allow a query to read only keys from its own document at the same or earlier position. A global lower-triangular mask alone lets B read A.
3. Decide whether the artificial transition from the end of A to the beginning of B is scored. If independence is intended, exclude that cross-document target rather than accidentally teaching a continuation that never existed.
4. Inspect position IDs and response-loss spans after packing. Resetting position IDs does not, by itself, prevent cross-document attention.
5. Test a counterfactual: change A while holding B fixed. Under an isolated-document policy, B's permitted predictions should not change in evaluation mode. Also verify that padding never adds targets or produces an all-masked invalid attention row.

Document isolation is a policy choice, not a universal requirement for all pretraining recipes. Some intentionally concatenate documents. The error is claiming isolation while the executed mask permits mixing. Follow the selected implementation's actual packing/attention support: [Transformers causal objectives](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/tasks/language_modeling), [TRL packing and loss masks](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/sft_trainer), and [FineWeb's data-pipeline study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557).

## 6. Storage and reproducibility

**Key terms.** A **manifest** lists exact files and versions; a **shard** is one partition of a dataset; **checksums** detect changed bytes.

**Process.** Save processed records in bounded shards with a manifest and hashes. The loader uses those artifacts to reconstruct batches; a later run can then check that it received the same data.

Use sharded files suitable for streaming; keep a manifest of source versions, row/token counts, schema, hashes and filtering configuration. A streaming loader avoids loading the whole corpus into RAM but complicates shuffling and exact resumption. Record shard order, sampler state and offsets. Checkpointing only weights is insufficient for exact continuation.

## Exercises and checks

1. A source appears as both HTML and PDF. Where should leakage checks occur? **Before treating splits as independent**, using source identity and near-duplicate checks, not file extensions alone.
2. Can a hash validate factual accuracy? **No:** it detects content identity/change under the chosen rule.
3. Design a five-record audit containing a Unicode example, duplicate, private field, malformed page and empty extraction. Specify expected outcomes.

Case study: [FineWeb](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557) documents data-pipeline decisions; [OLMo 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00656) connects data and training. Our record examples and checks are original teaching exercises, not claims about those projects' exact schemas.

steps.title: Record source provenance and identity
steps.prose: Keep source/version, permissions and content identity before deriving examples. A hash detects byte identity under its defined serialization; it does not grant rights or prove truth. Group duplicates and related records rather than treating file formats as independent sources.
steps.terms: Provenance records origin and processing. Exact duplicate detection differs from near-duplicate grouping; both require a declared comparison policy.
steps.next: Assign independent source groups to splits before learning corpus-dependent statistics.

steps.title: Reserve evaluation groups before fitting
steps.prose: Keep related documents, translations or near duplicates together under the evaluation design. Fit new tokenizer/statistical processing only on permitted training data. Reusing a pretrained tokenizer requires compatibility rather than refitting vocabulary IDs independently.
steps.terms: A group is the unit kept together in a split. Contamination includes prohibited evaluation information entering fitting or selection.
steps.next: Encode each split with the selected compatible saved tokenizer and boundary policy.

steps.title: Encode text with a compatible tokenizer
steps.prose: The example supplies token IDs [3,7,2,9]. Their values identify vocabulary entries, not semantic magnitudes. Save normalization, special tokens and tokenizer revision so new batches retain the same interpretation expected by model embeddings.
steps.terms: An end-of-sequence marker defines a boundary under a recipe; it does not alone block every cross-document attention connection.
steps.next: Build windows and score masks from these fixed IDs, checking shifts exactly once.

steps.title: Construct windows and inspect masks
steps.prose: Slice inputs and their successors under the selected prediction-window length. Real packing also decides whether documents can attend across boundaries and whether artificial boundary transitions are scored. Position resets alone do not enforce isolation.
steps.terms: T counts prediction positions in this example. Attention masks restrict reading; target masks restrict scoring, and both need independent tests.
steps.next: The Transformer walkthrough next follows the permitted input IDs through the model's actual forward calculations.

links: Use source identity and duplicate groups to reserve independent data splits.
Encode each permitted split with the compatible saved tokenizer.
Construct aligned prediction windows and the intended visibility/scoring masks.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A training corpus is a collection of examples with provenance, permissions, boundaries, and a sampling policy. More tokens do not automatically mean better evidence. Duplicate documents can overweight one source or leak near-identical answers across splits. Reserve evaluation groups before fitting the tokenizer or selecting data filters.

Tokenisation maps text to model-compatible IDs. A larger vocabulary can shorten sequences while increasing embedding and output-table size; a smaller vocabulary can increase the number of positions needed. Different tokenizers make raw token perplexity difficult to compare. Preserve exact tokenizer files and special-token conventions with the model.

**Packing** combines short sequences to reduce padding waste. It also forces a choice about cross-document attention. Resetting position IDs alone does not prevent one document reading another. Use a suitable attention boundary mask or independent windows if isolation is intended. An end-of-document token marks a boundary but does not itself enforce invisibility. Some training setups intentionally allow cross-document context; document that choice rather than assuming it.

Inspect one real batch: input IDs, shifted targets, attention visibility, padding, loss mask, and document identity. The scratch lab's examples remain within individual documents and use shifted targets. Changing window length changes available context and computational work; it does not alter what a target label means.

Sources: [Hugging Face: tokenizer algorithms](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/5), [D2L: language-model datasets](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/language-model.html), [PyTorch: causal attention masks](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html).

# T3. Decoder Transformer architecture

A decoder Transformer predicts a token from a permitted prefix by repeatedly transforming one vector per input position. Attention mixes information between allowed positions, while feed-forward layers transform features within each position. Residual connections preserve direct paths around these transformations. Training compares predictions with known targets; generation instead chooses and appends tokens with fixed parameters.

The walkthrough uses a small supplied vocabulary and fixed weights: hidden width four, additive positions, LayerNorm and a 4→8→4 GELU feed-forward branch. Select a head, position or block to inspect the actual arithmetic. This is not the architecture or learned competence of the locally prepared pretrained model.

The data lesson produced aligned token inputs. This walkthrough follows their full computation while keeping tensor axes, residual paths and attention/vocabulary normalizations distinct. The deeper notes separately explain real grouped-query dimensions and other positional methods.

## 1. Decoder input and output

**Key terms.** Here **B** is batch size, **T** sequence length, **d** hidden width and **V** vocabulary size. A **hidden state** is the vector representing one position inside the model.

**Process.** IDs enter an embedding lookup, blocks refine the resulting vectors, and a vocabulary projection produces logits. Training sends them to a loss; generation instead selects a token and repeats.

```text
text → tokenizer → token IDs [B,T]
→ embedding lookup [B,T,d]
→ positional information + repeated Transformer blocks
→ final normalization → vocabulary projection [B,T,V]
→ logits → probabilities → selected next token
```

`B` is batch size, `T` sequence length, `d` hidden width and `V` vocabulary size. An embedding table `[V,d]` maps each integer ID to a row. During training, loss compares the vocabulary scores at a position with the next target token. During inference, the selected token extends the input.

We explain a common pre-normalized decoder block. Exact models differ in normalization, biases, positions, activations and attention variants. The original 2017 Transformer was encoder–decoder, not this exact modern decoder recipe.

## 2. Query, key and value

**Key terms.** A **query Q** is a matching request; a **key K** is what it matches against; **values U** are mixed information. **dₖ/dᵥ** are head widths; **M** is the attention mask.

**Process.** Token states enter three learned projections to produce Q, K and U. Query–key products become masked, normalized attention weights; those weights combine U and pass a new representation to the next operation.

Given token representations `X:[T,d]` for one sequence, compute:

\[
Q=XW_Q,\quad K=XW_K,\quad U=XW_V.
\]

We call the value matrix `U` here to avoid confusing it with vocabulary size `V`. For a single head, projections yield `[T,d_k]`, `[T,d_k]`, `[T,d_v]`.

A **query** represents what a position seeks; a **key** represents how a position can match that request; a **value** carries information to aggregate. These are useful analogies, not literal questions stored in the weights.

Attention is:

\[
S=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}+M,\quad
A=\operatorname{softmax}_{row}(S),\quad O=AU.
\]

`S:[T,T]` contains pairwise scores. `M` is zero for allowed positions and negative infinity for forbidden positions. Each row of `A` sums to one over allowed keys. Scaling controls score growth with feature width under useful initialization assumptions. Softmax operates over keys for each query, not across every entry of the matrix at once.

## 3. Calculate one attention row

**Key terms.** An **attention row** holds one query's weights over keys; **softmax** normalizes allowed scores to sum to 1; a **weighted sum** combines values using those weights.

**Process.** Compute dot products, divide by the square root of key width, mask forbidden keys, then apply softmax. Multiply the resulting row by the value vectors to obtain this query position's output.

Let the current query be `[1,0]`, two permitted keys be `[1,0]` and `[0,1]`, and values be `[2,0]` and `[0,4]`. With `d_k=2`, scaled scores are `[1/√2,0]≈[0.7071,0]`. Softmax gives approximately `[0.6698,0.3302]`.

The weighted value is:

```text
0.6698 × [2,0] + 0.3302 × [0,4] = [1.3395,1.3210]
```

Attention produced a mixture, not a selected source token. If the second key is causally forbidden, its probability becomes zero and the output becomes `[2,0]`. Mask **before** softmax; setting an output probability to zero afterwards without renormalizing is not the same calculation.

The static attention diagram shows this calculation's complete path. Compare the allowed two-key result with the one-key masked result above; no playback or parameter slider is required.

## 4. Multi-head attention and shapes

**Key terms.** An **attention head** is one learned projection subspace; **h** counts heads; **concatenation** joins features; **Wₒ** projects joined outputs back to hidden width.

**Process.** Split projected features into heads, compute each head's attention, join their outputs and project back. That final width must match the residual stream before the block can add the result.

With `h` heads, projected features are reshaped to `[B,h,T,d_k]`. Each head computes its own interactions. Concatenate head outputs, then apply an output projection `W_O` to return to `[B,T,d]`. In a common choice, `h d_k=d` and `d_v=d_k`.

Multiple heads give multiple learned interaction subspaces. They do not have guaranteed roles such as “grammar head” and “truth head.” Some behaviours may be studied empirically, and redundancy can occur.

For `B=2,T=4,d=8,h=2`, each head width is 4. Scores have shape `[2,2,4,4]`; concatenated outputs have shape `[2,4,8]`. Distinguish number of tokens from feature width at every reshape.

## 5. One decoder block

**Key terms.** **Norm** rescales each token's features; **MLP** is a feed-forward network; a **residual** adds the input back; **d_ff** is the MLP's intermediate width.

**Process.** Normalize the input, apply attention and add its residual. Normalize that result, apply the MLP and add the second residual. The unchanged outer shape lets the next decoder block repeat this sequence.

A common pre-norm block is:

\[
H=X+\operatorname{Attention}(\operatorname{Norm}(X)),
\qquad Y=H+\operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{Norm}(H)).
\]

The attention mixes positions. The MLP applies a learned nonlinear transformation separately at each position using shared weights. Residual additions preserve the shape. For a simple MLP, expand width `d→d_ff`, activate, then contract `d_ff→d`. Gated variants use another branch.

The residual stream is the evolving vector at each position across layers. Adding two same-shape tensors is not concatenation. Normalization generally acts over features per token, not over the batch's labels.

### Read a real grouped-query block by its dimensions

The locally prepared SmolLM2-360M configuration has width `d=960`, 15 query heads, 5 KV heads and head width `960/15=64`.

1. For input `[B,T,960]`, the query projection produces `[B,T,960]`, then reshapes to `[B,15,T,64]`.
2. Each key and value projection produces only `5×64=320` features: `[B,5,T,64]` after reshaping. Three query heads share each KV head. A kernel need not physically store three copies of the same cache entry.
3. Rotary position transformations modify Q/K coordinate pairs before their dot products; they are not learned absolute vectors added to the token embedding in this model.
4. Attention returns 15 head outputs and an output projection returns width 960. A gated feed-forward branch then uses intermediate width 2560 and projects back to 960.
5. The gated branch has three matrices: two input projections and one down projection. In row convention it is `SiLU(XW_gate) ⊙ (XW_up)`, followed by `W_down`. Here `⊙` is elementwise multiplication, not another matrix contraction.

Both residual additions preserve `[B,T,960]`. Check exact architecture fields instead of assuming every modern model uses a four-times-width GELU MLP. Sources: [local model's upstream configuration](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct/blob/main/config.json), [GQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245), [RoPE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864) and [gated feed-forward variants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202).

## 6. Position information

**Key terms.** A **position embedding** represents token location; **RoPE** rotates query/key coordinate pairs; **relative offset** is the distance between positions.

**Process.** Supply position information before or within token interactions. In RoPE models, transform Q and K before their dot products; the resulting scores can depend on relative position as well as content.

Without positional information, plain self-attention has strong permutation symmetry: it cannot generally distinguish reordered tokens in the desired way. Absolute positional embeddings add position vectors. Relative methods influence interactions based on distance. Rotary embeddings rotate pairs of query/key coordinates as a function of position, allowing their dot products to encode relative offsets. A causal mask adds directionality but does not replace every use of explicit position design.

Longer nominal context does not ensure reliable use of distant evidence. Position extrapolation, training-length distribution, distractors and retrieval all affect performance.

## 7. Output and generation

**Key terms.** A **vocabulary projection** maps hidden features to token scores; **weight tying** shares compatible input/output weights; the **KV cache** retains earlier keys and values.

**Process.** The final hidden state becomes vocabulary logits. Select a next token, append it, reuse cached earlier state where supported, and repeat until the stop condition.

After the blocks, a linear projection maps each hidden state to `V` logits. Weight tying can share embedding and output weights under compatible shapes. During generation, use the last relevant position's distribution, choose a token, append it and repeat until a stop rule or budget is reached.

The **KV cache** stores earlier keys and values so they need not be recomputed for every generated token. It is temporary inference state, not new model knowledge. R6 derives its memory cost.

## 8. Limits of attention visualization

**Key terms.** An **attention heatmap** displays mixing weights; a **causal intervention** changes computation to test an effect; a **control** rules out alternative explanations.

**Process.** Inspect a heatmap to form a hypothesis, then intervene under matched conditions and measure behaviour. Do not jump from a dark cell to a claim about why the complete model answered correctly.

An attention heatmap shows a component of computation, not a complete causal explanation. Residuals, MLPs, many heads and multiple layers all contribute. High weight on a passage does not establish that the final answer faithfully uses it. Intervention tests need carefully matched controls.

## Exercises and checks

1. Why is `QKᵀ` `[T,T]`? Each query compares with each key; the inner feature axis is summed out.
2. During causal training, can token 2 attend to token 4? **No**, even though token 4 is present in the batch.
3. What changes at inference versus training? Gold next tokens are not supplied; generation uses chosen outputs; cached state can avoid repeated work; dropout/gradient tracking settings differ.
4. Reproduce the numerical attention row above within 0.001 and explain every axis.

Primary sources: [original Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762), [GQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245), [RoPE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864) and [RMSNorm](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467). The numerical attention example is illustrative; the separately labelled checkpoint inspector displays actual model values.

# T3. Decoder Transformer architecture

A decoder Transformer predicts a token from a permitted prefix by repeatedly transforming one vector per input position. Attention mixes information between allowed positions, while feed-forward layers transform features within each position. Residual connections preserve direct paths around these transformations. Training compares predictions with known targets; generation instead chooses and appends tokens with fixed parameters.
