# DS04. Sampling with NumPy and SciPy

`np.random.default_rng(seed)` builds a pseudorandom generator. The seed fixes the sequence for this generator and this NumPy version. `integers(low, high, size=n)` draws `n` integers from `low` up to, and not including, `high`.

Sampling **with replacement** can draw the same position more than once. A bootstrap resample draws a new sample of the same size from the observed rows, with replacement, and recomputes a statistic. The item you resample has to match the study: a row, a patient, a document or a group. Resampling the wrong unit pretends that dependent rows were independent.

### Why SciPy

SciPy is the library of numerical routines that sit on NumPy arrays: statistics, optimization, sparse matrices, and special functions. People use it because those routines are shared and tested, so a standard error or a sparse count matrix does not have to be rederived in each project. `from scipy import stats` then `stats.sem(values)` is the call. SciPy computes the formula you select. It does not decide whether the rows are independent, and a standard error is not a bootstrap interval.

`scipy.stats.sem` estimates the standard error of the mean from the sample’s own spread. It is the standard error, which is different from the standard deviation of the observations. Sparse matrices from `scipy.sparse` appear in the last lesson of this chapter, for grids that are mostly zeros. That is the same library.

<!-- example: DS04-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

scores_a = np.array([1., 0., 1., 1.])
scores_b = np.array([0., 0., 1., 0.])
indices = np.array([0, 0, 2, 3])
paired_difference = scores_a[indices].mean() - scores_b[indices].mean()
print(f"paired difference={paired_difference:.2f}")
print(f"standard error={stats.sem([2., 4., 6.]):.3f}")
rng = np.random.default_rng(17)
print(rng.integers(0, 4, size=4).shape)
```

**Output**
```text
paired difference=0.75
standard error=1.155
(4,)
```

The index array `[0, 0, 2, 3]` is one chosen resample. Position 0 is used twice, and position 1 is unused. Both score arrays are indexed with those same positions, so paired rows stay paired. The printed difference is that one resample’s mean difference, not a confidence interval. `stats.sem([2., 4., 6.])` is a separate illustration on three fixed numbers. The last line only checks that a draw of four integers has shape `(4,)`. It does not print the integers, because the lesson is the draw’s shape and the paired index, not a particular random sequence.

Many resamples can describe how a statistic varies under that resampling scheme. They do not repair a biased sample. A seed that restarts training is a different experiment from a bootstrap of rows. Running several hypothesis tests and keeping the smallest p-value needs a plan that was chosen before looking at those p-values.

Sources: [SciPy bootstrap](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html), [SciPy standard error](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.sem.html), [Think Stats](https://allendowney.github.io/ThinkStats/).

People use it because those routines are shared and tested, so a standard error or a sparse count matrix does not have to be rederived in each project. `from scipy import stats` then `stats.sem(values)` is the call. SciPy computes the formula you select. It does not decide whether the rows are independent, and a standard error is not a bootstrap interval.

`scipy.stats.sem` estimates the standard error of the mean from the sample’s own spread. It is the standard error, which is different from the standard deviation of the observations. import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

scores_a = np.array([1., 0., 1., 1.])
scores_b = np.array([0., 0., 1., 0.])

paired_difference = scores_a[indices].mean() - scores_b[indices].mean()
print(f"paired difference={paired_difference:.2f}")
print(f"standard error={stats.sem([2., 4., 6.]):.3f}")

# DS04. Sampling with NumPy and SciPy

`np.random.default_rng(seed)` builds a pseudorandom generator. The seed fixes the sequence for this generator and this NumPy version. `integers(low, high, size=n)` draws `n` integers from `low` up to, and not including, `high`.

# DS05. pandas tables

### Why pandas

pandas is the library people use for tables in Python. A column has a name, a missing value has a place, and a filter can be written as a condition on the column rather than as a loop over row indexes. Spreadsheet files, CSV files, and database results are routinely loaded into the same object, which is why the library shows up in analysis code even when the model itself is NumPy or scikit-learn. After `import pandas as pd`, `table["score"]` selects a column. pandas aligns rows by index and will happily average a column that includes values you meant to exclude. It does not know which rows belong in the study.

A **DataFrame** is the table. A **Series** is one column, with the table’s row index attached. `type(table).__name__` and `type(table["score"]).__name__` show those two objects. `.tolist()` copies values into a Python list. `.shape` is `(rows, columns)`.

<!-- example: DS05-objects -->
```python
import pandas as pd

table = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["a", "b"], "score": [2, 6]})
print(type(table).__name__)
print(type(table["score"]).__name__)
print(table["score"].tolist())
print(tuple(table.shape))
```

**Output**
```text
DataFrame
Series
[2, 6]
(2, 2)
```

The dictionary keys become column names. The values become the columns. Row labels default to 0 and 1. Those labels are an index, separate from the integer position. Two rows and two columns give shape `(2, 2)`.

`pd.read_csv` builds a DataFrame from CSV text. A blank field becomes a missing value, which pandas prints as `NaN` and tests with `.isna()`. `.count()` counts values that are present. `.mean()` on a numeric Series skips missing values in its default behavior. Filling the gap with zero would include a zero in that mean, which answers a different question.

`io` comes with Python. `StringIO` wraps a string so a function written for a file can read it. The example uses it so the CSV stays on the page. `StringIO` supplies those characters. It does not find a file on disk and it does not decide how a blank field should be filled.

<!-- example: DS05-main -->
```python
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

table = pd.read_csv(StringIO("id,group,score\na,A,2\nb,A,\nc,B,6\n"))
print(table.shape)
print(table["score"].isna().tolist())
print(table["score"].count())
print(table["score"].mean())
```

**Output**
```text
(3, 3)
[False, True, False]
2
4.0
```

Three rows and three columns are present. The score column is missing in the second row, so `.isna()` is false, true, false. `.count()` is 2. The mean of the observed scores is `(2+6)/2 = 4`. The missing row still exists in the table.

CSV text does not store a full schema. A column of digits may arrive as text unless you convert it. Parquet can keep column types and read selected columns. Neither format means the rows are independent or licensed for redistribution. Looking at the test split while you decide how to fill missing values uses that split for design. Inspect columns, ranges, duplicate identifiers and units before a model sees the table.

**Practice.** `table["score"].count()` answers “how many scores are present?” `len(table)` answers “how many rows are present?” On this table those numbers are 2 and 3.

Sources: [pandas data structures](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/2.3/user_guide/dsintro.html), [pandas missing values](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/2.3/user_guide/missing_data.html).

# DS06. Selecting and updating rows

`.loc` selects by labels and by Boolean conditions. `.iloc` selects by integer position, starting at zero, and ignores the labels. Use `.loc` when you mean “the row named `a`” or “the rows where a condition is true.” Use `.iloc` when you mean “the row at position 1,” whatever its label is.

<!-- example: DS06-select -->
```python
import pandas as pd

table = pd.DataFrame({"score": [2.0, 6.0]}, index=["a", "b"])
print(table.loc["a", "score"])
print(table.iloc[1, 0])
```

**Output**
```text
2.0
6.0
```

`loc["a", "score"]` is the score on the row labeled `a`. `iloc[1, 0]` is the second row and the first column, which is 6.0. If the index were sorted differently, those two selections could stop referring to the same cell.

Assignment through `.loc` writes into the rows you selected. A Boolean Series such as `table["score"].isna()` has one true or false per row. Missing values are not numbers, so a later numeric step needs an explicit decision. Replacing them with −1 in the next example only makes the gap visible. It is not a general rule for model inputs.

Series arithmetic aligns by index label. Two Series can have the same length and still pair `a` with `a` rather than first position with first position.

<!-- example: DS06-main -->
```python
import pandas as pd

table = pd.DataFrame({"score": [2., None, 6.]}, index=["a", "b", "c"])
table.loc[table["score"].isna(), "score"] = -1
print(table.loc[["b", "c"], "score"].tolist())
print(table.iloc[0, 0])
first = pd.Series([10, 20], index=["a", "b"])
second = pd.Series([1, 2], index=["b", "a"])
print((first + second).tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
[-1.0, 6.0]
2.0
[12, 21]
```

Row `b` was missing and becomes −1. Row `c` stays 6. `iloc[0, 0]` is still row `a`, the value 2. `first + second` adds `a` to `a` (`10+2`) and `b` to `b` (`20+1`), so the result is 12 then 21 in `first`’s index order. Adding by position would have produced 11 and 22. Resetting an index without keeping the identifier can change which rows pair.

Write `table.loc[mask, "score"] = value` when you mean to update that column on those rows. An expression such as `table[mask]["score"] = value` can update a temporary object and leave the table unchanged. Nullable integer types can represent missing integers without converting the column to float. Dates need an explicit format and timezone when the order of events matters. A string that looks like a date is still a string until you parse it.

Sources: [pandas indexing](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/2.3/user_guide/indexing.html), [copy-on-write](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/2.3/user_guide/copy_on_write.html).

# DS07. Grouping and joins

`groupby("group")` splits the rows by the values in that column. Selecting `["score"]` and calling `.mean()` reduces each group to one number. The result is a Series whose index is the group label.

<!-- example: DS07-group -->
```python
import pandas as pd

scores = pd.DataFrame({"group": ["A", "A", "B"], "score": [2, 4, 8]})
print(scores.groupby("group")["score"].mean().to_dict())
```

**Output**
```text
{'A': 3.0, 'B': 8.0}
```

names = pd.DataFrame({"group": ["A", "B"], "name": ["alpha", "beta"]})
joined = scores.merge(names, on="group", validate="many_to_one")
print(joined.groupby("name")["score"].mean().to_dict())

except pd.errors.MergeError:

3
duplicate lookup keys rejected

# DS08. Matplotlib figures

### Why Matplotlib

Matplotlib is the plotting library the scientific Python stack draws with. pandas and seaborn can hand it an axes, and a saved figure is an ordinary image file. People use it because one script can draw the chart and write the file, with the labels in the same program as the numbers. `plt.subplots()` returns a **Figure**, the whole image, and an **Axes**, one plotting region. `axes.plot(x, y)` draws a line. `axes.set` adds the labels and the title. Matplotlib draws the pairs you give it. It does not check that the line answers the question in the title.

A line is appropriate when the horizontal value is an ordered quantity such as time. A bar chart compares separate categories. A histogram counts values that fall into bins. The chart type is part of the claim.

<!-- example: DS08-main -->
```python
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

minutes = [0, 10, 20]
records_read = [0, 4, 9]
figure, axes = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3), layout="constrained")
axes.plot(minutes, records_read, marker="o")
axes.set(xlabel="Time (minutes)", ylabel="Records read", title="Reading progress")
figure.savefig("progress.png", dpi=120)
print(axes.get_xlabel())
print(axes.lines[0].get_ydata().tolist())
plt.close(figure)
```

**Output**
```text
Time (minutes)
[0, 4, 9]
```

`matplotlib.use("Agg")` selects a backend that writes a file and does not open a window. It has to run before pyplot builds a figure. `figsize=(5, 3)` sets the size in inches. `plot` pairs 0 with 0, 10 with 4, and 20 with 9. The markers show those three observations. The straight segments between them are the line’s interpolation, not a measurement of what happened at minute 5. `get_xlabel` confirms the label that was set. `get_ydata` returns the vertical values that were plotted, which is a useful check that the picture and the table still match.

`figure.savefig` writes `progress.png` in the working directory. `plt.close` releases the figure. Creating figures in a loop without closing them holds on to their memory. The checked image for this lesson is [the progress figure](outputs/DS08-main-progress.png). Several panels are `fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols)`. Each panel still needs its own labels.

Sources: [Matplotlib quickstart](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/quick_start.html), [Matplotlib savefig](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.figure.Figure.savefig.html).

# DS09. Diagnostic plots

A confusion matrix is a table of counts before it is a picture. Rows are actual labels. Columns are predicted labels. You choose that orientation by passing `labels` in a fixed order and by labeling the axes the same way. Precision and recall are ratios of those counts. A heatmap only displays the table.

### Why seaborn

seaborn draws statistical charts on a Matplotlib axes. People use it because a heatmap, a distribution, or a comparison across groups is a few arguments once the table already exists. `sns.heatmap` paints a grid you already computed. Some other seaborn functions average the data and add error bars themselves. When a function does that, set the aggregation explicitly and say what the bar means: the spread of observations, a standard error, a bootstrap interval, or the spread across repeated runs. seaborn will draw the summary its function computed. It does not decide which rows were allowed into that summary.

### scikit-learn, first as a metric

`sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix` is this course’s first call into **scikit-learn**. The library is the usual Python toolkit for classical machine learning: prepare a table, fit an estimator, predict, and score the result with a named metric. Here only the metric appears. It counts pairs of actual and predicted labels. The machine-learning chapter explains why the library is organized around `fit`, `predict`, and `transform`. The function below counts. It does not train a model, and it does not know which label order you intended until you pass `labels`.

<!-- example: DS09-main -->
```python
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

actual = [0, 0, 1, 1]
predicted = [0, 1, 1, 1]
counts = confusion_matrix(actual, predicted, labels=[0, 1])
figure, axes = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3), layout="constrained")
sns.heatmap(counts, annot=True, fmt="d", cbar=False, ax=axes,
            xticklabels=["negative", "positive"], yticklabels=["negative", "positive"])
axes.set(xlabel="Predicted label", ylabel="Actual label")
figure.savefig("confusion.png", dpi=120)
print(counts.tolist())
plt.close(figure)
```

**Output**
```text
[[1, 1], [0, 2]]
```

`labels=[0, 1]` puts class 0 first and class 1 second. The printed grid is:

- actual 0, predicted 0: 1
- actual 0, predicted 1: 1
- actual 1, predicted 0: 0
- actual 1, predicted 1: 2

For class 1, the true positives are 2. The predicted positives are the column total `1+2 = 3`, so precision is `2/3`. The actual positives are the row total `0+2 = 2`, so recall is `2/2`. Swapping the axis labels would describe those same stored numbers as the opposite errors. The figure is [the confusion-matrix image](outputs/DS09-main-confusion.png). `annot=True` prints the counts in the cells. `fmt="d"` formats them as integers.

A precision–recall curve uses scores and a moving threshold, not one hard label list. A residual plot compares prediction errors with another quantity, such as the prediction itself. Training-loss curves from a real run belong on the lab’s results pages. This lesson plots a fixed matrix.

Sources: [sklearn confusion matrix](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix.html), [Seaborn error bars](https://seaborn.pydata.org/tutorial/error_bars.html).

# DS10. A small checked analysis

A small analysis should say how many values entered each number it reports. `groupby` splits the rows. `agg(["count", "mean"])` computes both reductions on the same groups, so the mean is next to the count that produced it. `scipy.sparse.csr_matrix` is SciPy’s compressed store for a grid that is mostly zeros. It records the shape and the stored entries. It does not fill in the zeros, and it does not decide what a nonzero count means.

<!-- example: DS10-main -->
```python
from io import StringIO
import pandas as pd
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix

table = pd.read_csv(StringIO("id,group,score\na,A,2\nb,A,4\nc,B,8\n"))
if table["id"].duplicated().any():
    raise ValueError("row IDs must be unique")
summary = table.groupby("group")["score"].agg(["count", "mean"])
print(summary.to_csv().strip())
sparse = csr_matrix([[0, 0, 2], [1, 0, 0]])
print(sparse.shape, sparse.nnz)
```

**Output**
```text
group,count,mean
A,2,3.0
B,1,8.0
(2, 3) 2
```

`duplicated()` marks repeated ids. `.any()` is true if at least one row is a repeat. This table has ids `a`, `b` and `c`, so the check passes. Group A contributes two scores whose mean is 3. Group B contributes one score, 8. `to_csv` turns that summary into text. `.strip()` removes the trailing newline so the print matches the two data lines. An actual program can write that text to a path from PY08.

The last two lines are a different object, a **sparse matrix** from SciPy. `csr_matrix` stores the nonzero values and their positions. This grid has shape `(2, 3)` and `nnz` equal to 2, because only two cells are nonzero. A wide vocabulary table is often sparse. Calling `.toarray()` on it builds the full grid, including the zeros, and can exhaust memory even when the sparse object was small enough.

For a larger file, read the columns you need and check row counts after every join or group. A join can still build the whole result in memory. Keep a short validation record: row count, duplicate ids, missing counts and the path that was read. The next chapter’s model code should start from a table whose shape and missing values you can already explain.

Sources: [pandas IO](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/2.3/user_guide/io.html), [SciPy sparse](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/sparse.html).

# SK01. Estimators

### Why scikit-learn

scikit-learn is the library this course uses for classical machine learning. It is widely used because many learning objects share one shape: you construct the object with settings, `fit` learns from fitting rows, and `predict` or `transform` applies what was learned. A logistic regression, a tree, and a scaler are that kind of object. A scaler is a transformer: `fit` learns a statistic and `transform` applies it. A metric function is a different kind of tool. `f1_score(actual, predicted)` is a function call on labels you already have. It is not constructed, fitted, and then asked to predict. The same estimator shape is why a pipeline can hold the scaler and the model together. After `import sklearn`, the classes live under short module names such as `sklearn.linear_model`. Constructing `LogisticRegression(C=0.5)` only stores the setting. The library will also let you call `predict` before `fit`, and it will raise an error rather than invent coefficients. It does not choose the split, the metric, or whether a higher score is the decision you wanted. Fitting stays in the training lab. Where a later example writes `coef_` or `mean_` by hand, that is an inspection fixture: a constructed state used so the method can be shown. It is not the supported way to prepare an arbitrary estimator.

In scikit-learn, an **estimator** is an object configured to learn something from data. `X` is the table of examples. Its shape is `(examples, features)`: each row is one example, and each column is one measurement. `y` contains the target for each row. The confusion-matrix lesson already used one metrics function from this same library.

<!-- example: SK01-shape -->
```python
import numpy as np

examples = np.array([[1.0, 0.2], [0.0, 1.5], [1.0, 0.4]])
targets = np.array([1, 0, 1])
print(examples.shape)
print(targets.shape)
```

**Output**
```text
(3, 2)
(3,)
```

Three rows mean three examples. Two columns mean two features. `targets` has one answer per row, so its shape is `(3,)`.

Constructing an estimator only stores settings. `fit` is the method that learns from examples and writes the learned numbers onto the object. `predict` uses those numbers. Calling `predict` first fails, because the learned numbers are not there yet.

<!-- example: SK01-unfitted -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.exceptions import NotFittedError
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

model = LogisticRegression()
try:
    model.predict(np.array([[1.0, 0.2]]))
except NotFittedError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__)
```

**Output**
```text
NotFittedError
```

`LogisticRegression()` created the object. It has not seen any examples. `predict` refuses to invent a decision, and the error names the missing step: `fit`.

This lesson does not call `fit`. The next example places the learned numbers by hand, so `predict` and `predict_proba` can show what they return. `coef_` holds one weight per feature. `intercept_` holds the added constant. The trailing underscore is scikit-learn’s mark for a value produced by learning. `classes_` records which column of `predict_proba` belongs to which class.

<!-- example: SK01-predict -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

model = LogisticRegression()
model.classes_ = np.array([0, 1])
model.coef_ = np.array([[1.0, -1.0]])
model.intercept_ = np.array([0.0])
model.n_features_in_ = 2
features = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 2.0]])
print(model.predict(features).tolist())
print(np.round(model.predict_proba(features), 3).tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
[1, 0]
[[0.119, 0.881], [0.881, 0.119]]
```

The first row has a larger score for class 1, so `predict` returns 1. The second row has a larger score for class 0. `predict_proba` returns a probability for each class, and each pair adds to 1. Those are class probabilities for the two rows, not a count of how many rows belong to each class. Column 0 belongs to class 0 because that is the order in `classes_`. The weights were written into the object so the method could be inspected. A real run would obtain them from `fit` on fitting rows only. Copying this assignment into a project is not how an estimator is trained. The existing training lab is where that call belongs.

<!-- example: SK01-main -->
```python
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier, DummyRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

models = [DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
          DummyRegressor(strategy="mean"), LogisticRegression(C=0.5)]
print([type(model).__name__ for model in models])
print(models[2].get_params()["C"])
training_targets = [2., 4., 6.]
mean_baseline = sum(training_targets) / len(training_targets)
print([mean_baseline] * 2)
```

**Output**
```text
['DummyClassifier', 'DummyRegressor', 'LogisticRegression']
0.5
[4.0, 4.0]
```

No estimator was fitted. The final line manually applies the mean rule to two future examples. A baseline asks whether a more complex model improves on a simple defensible rule. For classification, “always predict the most common fitting class” can have high accuracy on imbalanced data while finding none of the rare class.

Settings such as `C` are hyperparameters; learned coefficients are model parameters. Scikit-learn often names learned attributes with a trailing underscore, such as `coef_`. An unfitted estimator should not be treated as a trained predictor. Calling `predict` before fitting usually raises a not-fitted error. The distribution is installed as `scikit-learn`, but imported as `sklearn`.

Sources: [sklearn getting started](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/getting_started.html), [dummy estimators](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/model_evaluation.html#dummy-estimators).

# SK02. Pipelines

**Preprocessing** converts raw features into the representation a model expects. A scaler learns statistics; an imputer learns replacement values; an encoder may learn categories. `transform` applies statistics that were already learned. Like `predict`, it fails before that learning has happened.

<!-- example: SK02-transform -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.exceptions import NotFittedError
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
try:
    scaler.transform(np.array([[5.0, 2.0]]))
except NotFittedError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__)
scaler.mean_ = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
scaler.scale_ = np.array([2.0, 2.0])
scaler.var_ = np.array([4.0, 4.0])
scaler.n_features_in_ = 2
print(scaler.transform(np.array([[5.0, 2.0]])).tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
NotFittedError
[[2.0, 0.0]]
```

The first call has no stored mean, so it stops. The lesson then supplies the mean and the scale as an inspection fixture, the same kind of constructed state as the classifier weights above. `(5 − 1) / 2` is 2, and `(2 − 2) / 2` is 0. `fit` would have calculated that mean and scale from fitting rows. Using the same stored values on later rows is what keeps the representation stable. Recomputing them from the rows you are about to score would mix those rows into the transformation.

If these operations see test data while learning, evaluation can become optimistic. A Pipeline expresses the order and keeps those learned transformations with the estimator.

<!-- example: SK02-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

numeric = Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer()), ("scale", StandardScaler())])
prepare = ColumnTransformer([("numbers", numeric, [0, 1])])

# SK03. Linear regression

Linear regression predicts a weighted sum of features plus an intercept. `predict` on a `LinearRegression` object does that arithmetic with the stored `coef_` and `intercept_`. The weights below are an inspection fixture: the same arithmetic a fitted model would apply, written in by hand so the lesson can show it without calling `fit`. They are not a saved training result and not a recipe for rebuilding an estimator from a notebook.

<!-- example: SK03-predict -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = LinearRegression()
model.coef_ = np.array([2.0, -1.0])
model.intercept_ = np.array([1.0])
model.n_features_in_ = 2
features = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 1.0]])
print(model.predict(features).tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
[1.0, 4.0]
```

The first row is `2×1 + (−1)×2 + 1 = 1`. The second is `2×2 + (−1)×1 + 1 = 4`. `predict` returns one number per row. Ridge discourages large squared weights; lasso uses an absolute-value penalty that can set weights to zero; elastic net combines both. These penalties affect fitting, not the arithmetic used to apply a fixed linear predictor.

<!-- example: SK03-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, root_mean_squared_error

features = np.array([[1., 2.], [2., 1.]])
fixed_weights = np.array([2., -1.])
predicted = features @ fixed_weights + 1
actual = np.array([2., 3.])
print(predicted.tolist())
print(f"MAE={mean_absolute_error(actual, predicted):.1f}")
print(f"RMSE={root_mean_squared_error(actual, predicted):.1f}")
print([type(m).__name__ for m in [Ridge(alpha=1), Lasso(alpha=1), ElasticNet(alpha=1)]])
```

**Output**
```text
[1.0, 4.0]
MAE=1.0
RMSE=1.0
['Ridge', 'Lasso', 'ElasticNet']
```

The weights are teaching values, not fitted coefficients. Both predictions differ from their targets by one unit. MAE averages absolute errors; RMSE square-roots the mean squared error and penalizes large errors more strongly. R² compares squared error with a mean-target reference and can be negative; it is not a percentage accuracy.

Coefficient magnitudes depend on feature units. Standardizing a feature changes the coefficient scale and the effective regularization. PolynomialFeatures can create powers/interactions, but high degree can amplify overfitting and numerical problems. Inspect residuals—actual minus predicted values—and compare against a simple baseline rather than interpreting a complex equation as evidence of quality.

Sources: [sklearn linear models](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/linear_model.html), [ISLP book](https://www.statlearning.com/).

# SK04. Thresholds

Logistic regression produces class scores that can be mapped to probabilities. `predict_proba` lines those probabilities up in the order stored in `classes_`. The positive class is whichever position matches the label you care about. It is not automatically the last column.

<!-- example: SK04-column -->
```python
import numpy as np

classes = np.array(["premise", "claim"])
probabilities = np.array([[0.8, 0.2], [0.3, 0.7]])
claim_column = int(np.where(classes == "claim")[0][0])
print(claim_column)
print(probabilities[:, claim_column].tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
1
[0.2, 0.7]
```

`"claim"` is position 1 in `classes`. The claim probabilities are therefore 0.2 and 0.7, not the first column. A **threshold** then turns one of those probabilities into a label. Evaluation must distinguish the numerical scores from the decisions made using them.

<!-- example: SK04-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

actual = [0, 1, 0, 1]
fixed_positive_probabilities = np.array([0.1, 0.9, 0.6, 0.4])
predicted = (fixed_positive_probabilities >= 0.5).astype(int)
print(predicted.tolist())
print(confusion_matrix(actual, predicted, labels=[0, 1]).tolist())
print(precision_score(actual, predicted), recall_score(actual, predicted), f1_score(actual, predicted))
```

**Output**
```text
[0, 1, 1, 0]
[[1, 1], [1, 1]]
0.5 0.5 0.5
```

These are constructed probabilities. There is one true positive, one false positive and one false negative. Precision is `1/(1+1)` and recall is `1/(1+1)`; F1 is their harmonic mean. In actual `predict_proba` output, locate the positive-class column through the estimator's `classes_`; do not assume column 1 always means the concept you want.

For several classes, macro F1 gives each class equal weight, weighted F1 weights by support and micro averaging pools counts. Multilabel tasks allow several simultaneous labels and differ from multiclass tasks with exactly one class per example. A higher F1 after changing a threshold does not prove better calibrated probabilities. Threshold choice belongs to validation, not repeated optimization on the final test set.

Sources: [sklearn classification metrics](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/model_evaluation.html#classification-metrics), [threshold tuning](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/classification_threshold.html).

# SK05. Neighbours

A nearest-neighbour rule stores examples and predicts the label of the closest one. Distance is the absolute difference here.

<!-- example: SK05-near -->
```python
reference = [0.0, 2.0, 5.0]
labels = [0, 1, 0]
query = 1.8
distances = [abs(point - query) for point in reference]
nearest = distances.index(min(distances))
print([round(distance, 1) for distance in distances])
print(labels[nearest])
```

**Output**
```text
[1.8, 0.2, 3.2]
1
```

The query 1.8 is 0.2 away from the stored value 2, and farther from 0 and 5. The label stored with 2 is 1, so that is the prediction. No model was fitted. An SVM learns a separating rule instead of storing every neighbour. Naive Bayes combines class evidence under a conditional-independence assumption. Similar method names do not make those mechanisms the same.

<!-- example: SK05-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB, MultinomialNB

reference = np.array([0., 2., 5.])
labels = np.array([0, 1, 0])
distance = np.abs(reference - 1.8)
print(labels[distance.argmin()].item())
models = [KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=1), SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1), GaussianNB(), MultinomialNB()]
print([type(model).__name__ for model in models])
```

**Output**
```text
1
['KNeighborsClassifier', 'SVC', 'GaussianNB', 'MultinomialNB']
```

The nearest-reference calculation is manual and performs no fitting. Changing feature units can change which point is nearest; this is why distance-based methods often need scaling. Larger `k` smooths local decisions. For an RBF SVM, `gamma` controls locality and `C` the regularization trade-off; tune them together under a valid selection protocol.

GaussianNB models numerical class-conditional feature distributions. MultinomialNB is appropriate for nonnegative count-like features, not arbitrary centered measurements. A large predicted probability from an assumption-heavy model is not automatically a reliable confidence estimate. Current lab training includes Gaussian NB, kNN classification and SVM classification/regression—not every variant constructed here.

# SK06. Trees

A decision tree asks a yes-or-no question about one feature. Several trees can vote, and the majority wins.

<!-- example: SK06-vote -->
```python
feature = 1.5
print("claim" if feature >= 1 else "premise")
votes = [0, 1, 1]
print(1 if sum(votes) > len(votes) / 2 else 0)
```

**Output**
```text
claim
1
```

`1.5` is at least 1, so this one question answers `"claim"`. The three votes contain two 1s, which is more than half, so the vote is 1. A random forest combines randomized trees. Stacking learns another model from predictions that were kept separate from the rows used to make them.

<!-- example: SK06-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, ExtraTreesClassifier

fixed_tree_votes = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 1], [1, 0]])
print((fixed_tree_votes.mean(axis=0) > 0.5).astype(int).tolist())
models = [DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3), RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=30), ExtraTreesClassifier()]
print([type(model).__name__ for model in models])
```

**Output**
```text
[1, 1]
['DecisionTreeClassifier', 'RandomForestClassifier', 'ExtraTreesClassifier']
```

Rows here are three fixed trees' binary votes; columns are two examples. Both examples receive two positive votes. This illustrates hard voting, not necessarily a forest library's probability-averaging implementation. A tree's depth and minimum leaf size limit complexity; the number of trees controls ensemble size and cost. More trees are not the same as deeper trees.

Bagging fits models to randomized samples and aggregates them. Stacking needs out-of-fold predictions to train the combining model without giving it unrealistically easy fitting-set outputs. Tree importance values can favor some feature types and split credit across correlated features. The ML lab supports its defined tree and forest routes; ExtraTrees and stacking remain code/theory comparisons, not advertised training options.

Sources: [sklearn trees](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/tree.html), [sklearn ensembles](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/ensemble.html).

# SK07. Boosting

Boosting starts with a prediction and then adds a small correction. The learning rate shrinks that correction before it is added.

<!-- example: SK07-step -->
```python
prediction = 2.0
correction = 1.0
learning_rate = 0.2
print(prediction + learning_rate * correction)
```

**Output**
```text
2.2
```

The correction is 1. Only a fifth of it is added, so the prediction moves from 2.0 to 2.2. The next component would look at the error that remains. The number of rounds and the size of each tree both change how far the model can move, and they are not the same setting.

<!-- example: SK07-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor, AdaBoostClassifier

initial_prediction = np.array([2., 2.])
fixed_corrections = np.array([[1., -1.], [0.5, 0.5]])
print((initial_prediction + 0.2 * fixed_corrections.sum(axis=0)).tolist())
models = [HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=20), GradientBoostingRegressor(), AdaBoostClassifier()]
print([type(model).__name__ for model in models])
```

**Output**
```text
[2.3, 1.9]
['HistGradientBoostingRegressor', 'GradientBoostingRegressor', 'AdaBoostClassifier']
```

The corrections are supplied numbers; they were not learned here. The first example receives `0.2×(1+0.5)=0.3`, while the second receives `0.2×(−1+0.5)=−0.1`. Classification boosting combines scores according to its objective; do not blindly apply a regression calculation to class labels.

Histogram boosting bins numerical values to make split search efficient. AdaBoost uses a different reweighting mechanism from gradient boosting. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost offer additional implementations/features but are not needed to understand the additive idea. The existing lab implements histogram boosting with a fixed round budget, not an exposed early-stopping or every-library comparison service.

Sources: [sklearn gradient boosting](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/ensemble.html#gradient-boosting), [ISLP tree methods](https://www.statlearning.com/).

# SK08. Splits

A score answers the question defined by which rows were used to learn and which rows were held out. If two rows come from the same person, putting one in each side lets the model see that person before the test.

<!-- example: SK08-group -->
```python
groups = ["a", "a", "b", "b"]
train = [0, 1]
valid = [2, 3]
train_groups = {groups[i] for i in train}
valid_groups = {groups[i] for i in valid}
print(sorted(train_groups), sorted(valid_groups))
print(train_groups.isdisjoint(valid_groups))
```

**Output**
```text
['a'] ['b']
True
```

Rows 0 and 1 both belong to person `a` and stay in training. Rows 2 and 3 belong to person `b` and stay in validation. The two sets of people do not overlap. Time splitting instead keeps earlier rows on the fitting side. Cross-validation rotates those subsets. It does not repair a split that mixes one person across both sides.

<!-- example: SK08-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, ParameterGrid

features = np.zeros((6, 2))
groups = np.array(["a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c"])
folds = list(GroupKFold(n_splits=3).split(features, groups=groups))
print([(len(train), len(valid)) for train, valid in folds])
print(all(set(groups[train]).isdisjoint(groups[valid]) for train, valid in folds))
print(len(ParameterGrid({"C": [0.1, 1.0], "kernel": ["linear", "rbf"]})))
```

**Output**
```text
[(4, 2), (4, 2), (4, 2)]
True
4
```

The splitter only creates indices; no model is fitted. The grid enumerates four configurations; it does not run four experiments. A search would fit each candidate inside valid training folds. Any learned preprocessing must be refitted within those folds too. If a final performance estimate is required after tuning, use an untouched test set or an appropriately nested procedure.

Repeatedly selecting a configuration from test scores changes the test set's role into development data. Training seeds assess fitted-model variation; bootstrap resampling assesses specified sampling variability. Neither justifies inventing tiny error bars from repeated visits to the same table. The current lab supports manual compatible-run comparisons, not a full automated cross-validation/search interface.

Sources: [sklearn cross-validation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/cross_validation.html), [parameter search](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/grid_search.html).

# SK09. Clustering

Clustering assigns a point to the nearest center. Those centers are not class labels supplied by a teacher.

<!-- example: SK09-center -->
```python
point = 1.0
centers = [0.0, 10.0]
distances = [abs(point - center) for center in centers]
print(distances)
print(distances.index(min(distances)))
```

**Output**
```text
[1.0, 9.0]
0
```

The point is 1 away from center 0 and 9 away from center 10, so it joins center 0. PCA instead returns coordinates along directions of large spread. Anomaly detection returns an unusualness score. A cluster number, a coordinate and a score are different kinds of output.

<!-- example: SK09-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, DBSCAN, AgglomerativeClustering
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, TruncatedSVD
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest

points = np.array([[1., 0.], [8., 0.]])
fixed_centers = np.array([[0., 0.], [10., 0.]])
distances = ((points[:, None, :] - fixed_centers[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)
print(distances.argmin(axis=1).tolist())
print((points @ np.array([[1.], [0.]])).tolist())
print([type(m).__name__ for m in [KMeans(), DBSCAN(), AgglomerativeClustering(), PCA(), TruncatedSVD(), GaussianMixture(), IsolationForest()]])
```

**Output**
```text
[0, 1]
[[1.0], [8.0]]
['KMeans', 'DBSCAN', 'AgglomerativeClustering', 'PCA', 'TruncatedSVD', 'GaussianMixture', 'IsolationForest']
```

The centers and projection are supplied for illustration, not fitted K-means/PCA outputs. K-means minimizes within-cluster squared distance; DBSCAN uses density connectivity and may mark noise as −1. A Gaussian mixture offers component probabilities, not known semantic classes. Cluster IDs can be permuted without changing the grouping.

PCA's high-variance directions are not guaranteed to contain the best predictive information. TruncatedSVD is useful with sparse features without the same centering requirement. Isolation Forest's contamination setting helps set a decision threshold, not discover a verified true anomaly prevalence. DBSCAN lacks a native held-out prediction method in this lab: its fitting-set diagnostics must not be presented as equivalent to a held-out supervised score.

Sources: [sklearn clustering](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/clustering.html), [decomposition](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/decomposition.html), [outlier detection](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/outlier_detection.html).

# SK10. Calibration

**Calibration** asks whether events assigned a probability occur at about that frequency. One way to score a single probability is the square of its distance from what happened: 1 if the event happened, 0 if it did not.

<!-- example: SK10-one -->
```python
probability = 0.8
happened = 0
print(round((probability - happened) ** 2, 2))
```

**Output**
```text
0.64
```

The model said 0.8 and the event did not happen. `(0.8 − 0)²` is 0.64. A lower number would mean the stated probability was closer to the outcome. A useful ranking can still have badly calibrated probabilities. A decision also depends on what a false alarm or a miss costs.

<!-- example: SK10-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss, confusion_matrix

actual = np.array([0, 1, 0, 1])
probabilities = np.array([0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.9])
print(f"Brier={brier_score_loss(actual, probabilities):.4f}")
for threshold in [0.3, 0.8]:
    predicted = (probabilities >= threshold).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(actual, predicted, labels=[0, 1]).ravel()
    print(threshold, "false alarms", fp, "misses", fn)
```

**Output**
```text
Brier=0.2625
0.3 false alarms 1 misses 0
0.8 false alarms 1 misses 1
```

The Brier score averages squared probability errors: `(.04+.36+.64+.01)/4`. Lower is better for the same task/protocol. Raising this threshold creates an extra miss without reducing false alarms in these four constructed cases. That is an observed trade-off for this fixture, not a general theorem about all models.

Calibration fitting and threshold selection are learned choices and require a proper development protocol. Slice metrics can expose group/domain failures hidden by an overall mean, but tiny groups have unstable estimates. Permutation importance changes a feature in a frozen model's input and measures the resulting difference; correlation can complicate interpretation, and it is not a causal-effect estimate. These concepts do not imply dedicated calibration/threshold-fitting controls already exist in the lab.

Sources: [sklearn calibration](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/calibration.html), [permutation importance](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/permutation_importance.html).

# SK11. Time and ranking

A forecast predicts a later value from information available earlier. The input is the past. The target is the next observation.

<!-- example: SK11-lag -->
```python
observations = [10.0, 12.0, 11.0]
print(observations[:-1], observations[1:])
```

**Output**
```text
[10.0, 12.0] [12.0, 11.0]
```

`10` is used to predict `12`, and `12` is used to predict `11`. The future is not used to predict the past. A recommender instead ranks candidate items. Shuffling rows as if they were ordinary classification examples answers a different question.

<!-- example: SK11-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

observations = np.array([10., 12., 11., 15., 14., 18.])
lagged_input = observations[:-1]
next_value = observations[1:]
print(lagged_input.tolist(), next_value.tolist())
print(all(train.max() < test.min() for train, test in TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=2).split(observations)))
relevance = [1, 0, 1]
print(f"precision@2={sum(relevance[:2]) / 2:.1f}")
```

**Output**
```text
[10.0, 12.0, 11.0, 15.0, 14.0] [12.0, 11.0, 15.0, 14.0, 18.0]
True
precision@2=0.5
```

The first pair uses time `t` to predict `t+1`, not the future to predict the past. Real forecasts may require a gap, horizon-aware features and rolling evaluation. The recommendation example counts relevant items in the first two ranks; it needs known relevance judgments and a declared candidate set.

`partial_fit` updates supported estimators incrementally; it is still learning and is not called here. Semi-supervised methods use unlabeled as well as labeled data, while Gaussian processes represent functions with a probabilistic prior/kernel. Sequential decision problems additionally need actions, transitions and rewards, not only target labels. These are scope extensions, not currently runnable time-series/recommender/RL lab trainers. See the extension register for code still to be expanded.

Sources: [sklearn TimeSeriesSplit](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit.html), [scaling strategies](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/computing/scaling_strategies.html).

### A sequential decision adds transitions and rewards

In a Markov decision model, an action can change the next state as well as produce an immediate reward. Given fixed transition probabilities and state values, calculate one action's expected return without learning a policy:

<!-- example: SK11-return -->
```python
import numpy as np

next_state_probabilities = np.array([0.25, 0.75])
fixed_next_state_values = np.array([2., 5.])
immediate_reward, discount = 1., 0.9
expected_return = immediate_reward + discount * (next_state_probabilities @ fixed_next_state_values)
print(f"expected return={expected_return:.3f}")
```

**Output**
```text
expected return=4.825
```

The expected next value is `.25×2+.75×5=4.25`; discounting and adding reward gives 4.825. These values are provided, not learned. A classification label does not encode this action-dependent future. The existing ML lab has no sequential-decision trainer. Source: [Sutton and Barto, author's book page](http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html).

# SK12. The fitting workflow

This is a **read-only walkthrough**, not an output-bearing example or another training interface. The existing ML lab selects a supported dataset/task/model, obtains fixed fitting/development/test indices, fits preprocessing only on fitting rows, fits the estimator and evaluates under its task-specific protocol.

The function below is a simplified supervised illustration of that order, not a verbatim replacement for `model_lab.py`. Its caller supplies the configured pipeline and already separated arrays. It intentionally has no call and no training-output block.

```python walkthrough
def fit_and_evaluate_supervised(pipeline, x_train, y_train, x_dev, y_dev, x_test, y_test):
    from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
    pipeline.fit(x_train, y_train)
    development_predictions = pipeline.predict(x_dev)
    test_predictions = pipeline.predict(x_test)
    return {
        "development_accuracy": accuracy_score(y_dev, development_predictions),

# PT01. PyTorch

PyTorch is the library this course uses for neural networks, and it is the library behind most current research code and behind the Hugging Face models in the LLM lessons. People keep using it because the numbers, the derivatives, and the network live in one Python process.

### Why it is widely used

A paper can publish a model as ordinary Python. A reader can run the same functions, print a value in the middle, and change one layer. The deep-learning trainer in this lab is written against the same objects: tensors and `nn.Module`. When a later lesson loads a language model, that model is a PyTorch module with stored weights. Learning these objects once is what makes the rest of the code readable.

Three pieces do the work:

- A **tensor** holds the numbers. Arithmetic and indexing look like the NumPy arrays from the data lessons.
- **Autograd** stores how those numbers were computed. You write the forward calculation. `backward` fills in the gradient. You do not differentiate each layer by hand.
- A **module** is a class. `forward` is a method. A new layer is the same `class` and `def` you already wrote in the Python chapter.

The library will also add two tensors of the wrong shape, score the wrong tokens, or train on a leaked split. It runs the calculation you wrote. It does not know which task you meant, and it does not decide that a result is good.

### Why the first lines stay short

The operations are the math. `+` adds. `@` multiplies and adds, which for two vectors is a dot product. A mistake is an ordinary Python traceback, so you can print the tensor that caused it. Moving the same tensor to a GPU, when the machine has one, changes where the arithmetic runs. The formula in the next line stays the same. These lessons stay on the CPU so the printed numbers do not depend on a graphics chip.

<!-- example: PT01-add -->
```python
import torch

first = torch.tensor([1., 2.])
second = torch.tensor([3., 4.])
print((first + second).tolist())
print((first @ second).item())
```

**Output**
```text
[4.0, 6.0]
11.0
```

`1+3` and `2+4` are the pair `[4, 6]`. The dot product is `1×3 + 2×4 = 11`. Those are the same operations you would write for an array. These two tensors only demonstrate that arithmetic. `requires_grad` is false unless you ask for tracking, so this addition does not record a graph and `backward` has nothing to fill in. The gradient lesson turns tracking on.

<!-- example: PT01-track -->
```python
import torch

plain = torch.tensor([1., 2.])
tracked = plain.clone().requires_grad_(True)
print(plain.requires_grad)
print(tracked.requires_grad)
```

**Output**
```text
False
True
```

`plain` is the same kind of tensor as the addition above. `clone` makes another tensor with the same numbers. `requires_grad_(True)` marks that copy so a later `backward` can fill its `.grad`. The original stays unmarked. No weight is updated here.

### A tensor

A tensor carries a shape, a storage type, and a device. `shape` says how many values sit along each axis. `dtype` says how each value is stored. `device` says whether those values live on the CPU or on a GPU.

<!-- example: PT01-shape -->
```python
import torch

values = torch.tensor([1., 2., 3.])
print(tuple(values.shape), str(values.dtype), values.device.type)
print(values[0].item())
```

**Output**
```text
(3,) torch.float32 cpu
1.0
```

Three numbers along one axis give shape `(3,)`. The dtype is a 32-bit float. This tensor is on the CPU. `.item()` reads one stored number back out as an ordinary Python float.

A tensor can share storage with a NumPy array. Automatic differentiation can additionally record how some tensors were calculated.

<!-- example: PT01-main -->
```python
import numpy as np
import torch

array = np.array([1., 2.], dtype=np.float32)
shared = torch.from_numpy(array)
independent = shared.clone()
shared[0] = 9
print(array.tolist())
print(independent.tolist())
print(tuple(shared.shape), str(shared.dtype), shared.device.type)
```

**Output**
```text
[9.0, 2.0]
[1.0, 2.0]
(2,) torch.float32 cpu
```

`from_numpy` shares compatible CPU storage; `clone` makes separate tensor storage. Moving a tensor with `.to(device)` returns a tensor on the chosen device; do not assume every conversion mutates the original in place. Tensor shape alone does not tell you whether an axis is batch, time or channels.

Use integer tensors for token/class IDs and floating tensors for features or probabilities as required by the operation. CUDA is NVIDIA's execution platform; MPS is Apple's Metal backend; CPU works without either. Availability and available memory are different questions. These examples deliberately use CPU so interpreting a shape does not require a GPU.

Sources: [PyTorch tensor tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/tensorqs_tutorial.html), [torch.from_numpy](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.from_numpy.html).

# PT02. Gradients

A **gradient** tells us how a small local change in a weight would change a result. `requires_grad=True` asks PyTorch to remember the operations that used the weight. `backward` writes the gradient into `.grad`. It does not change the weight.

<!-- example: PT02-scale -->
```python
import torch

weight = torch.tensor(2., requires_grad=True)
result = weight * 3
result.backward()
print(result.item(), weight.grad.item())
```

**Output**
```text
6.0 3.0
```

`2 × 3` is 6. The derivative of `3w` with respect to `w` is 3, so `.grad` is 3. The weight is still 2, because nothing subtracted the gradient from it.

The next calculation uses a squared error, which is the usual shape of a loss. Autograd applies the chain rule. Calling `backward` still only calculates the gradient.

<!-- example: PT02-main -->
```python
import torch

weight = torch.tensor(2., requires_grad=True)
prediction = 3 * weight
loss = (prediction - 1) ** 2
loss.backward()
print(loss.item(), weight.grad.item())
print(prediction.detach().requires_grad)
```

**Output**
```text
25.0 30.0
False
```

The prediction is 6, so the squared error is `(6−1)²=25`. The derivative is `2×(3w−1)×3`, which equals 30 at `w=2`. The weight remains 2: no optimizer step ran. `detach` creates a tensor disconnected from this gradient history; it does not train or improve the prediction.

Gradients accumulate by default. Repeating backward calculations without clearing or intentionally accumulating them changes the meaning. An optimizer later uses the gradients, but a gradient is not itself a claim of feature importance or causal influence in the real world. This isolated calculation teaches the mechanism; PT05 explains how the actual loop uses it.

Sources: [PyTorch autograd](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/notes/autograd.html), [D2L automatic differentiation](https://d2l.ai/chapter_preliminaries/autograd.html).

# PT03. Modules

`nn.Linear` stores a weight and a bias and computes one weighted sum per output. The numbers below are written in by hand, so the result is arithmetic you can check.

<!-- example: PT03-linear -->
```python
import torch
from torch import nn

layer = nn.Linear(2, 1)
with torch.no_grad():
    layer.weight.copy_(torch.tensor([[1., 2.]]))
    layer.bias.fill_(0.5)
with torch.inference_mode():
    print(layer(torch.tensor([[1., 1.]])).tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
[[3.5]]
```

`1×1 + 1×2 + 0.5 = 3.5`. `nn.Module` organizes a neural component and its parameters. A new module starts in training mode. `.eval()` switches it to evaluation mode. That switch changes layers such as dropout. It does not run the layer and it does not change the weights.

<!-- example: PT03-mode -->
```python
from torch import nn

model = nn.Linear(2, 1)
print(model.training)
model.eval()
print(model.training)
```

**Output**
```text
True
False
```

`model.training` is true immediately after construction. After `.eval()` it is false. Several layers are used in order. An activation adds a nonlinear transformation. Without nonlinearities, several linear layers can collapse into one linear map.

<!-- example: PT03-main -->
```python
import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 3), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(3, 1))
with torch.no_grad():
    for parameter in model.parameters():
        parameter.fill_(0.5)
model.eval()
with torch.inference_mode():
    output = model(torch.tensor([[1., 2.]]))
print(output.tolist())
print(sum(parameter.numel() for parameter in model.parameters()))
```

**Output**
```text
[[3.5]]
13
```

All weights/biases are explicitly set to 0.5; none was learned. Each first-layer unit computes `1×.5+2×.5+.5=2`. ReLU keeps it positive. The final layer computes `3×2×.5+.5=3.5`. Parameter count is `(2×3+3)+(3×1+1)=13`.

A custom model subclasses `nn.Module`, calls `super().__init__()`, stores submodules as attributes and defines `forward`. Invoke `model(inputs)`, not a direct `forward` call that bypasses module call machinery/hooks. Parameters are learned tensors registered with the module; buffers are state such as running statistics that are not ordinary optimizer parameters. `.eval()` changes mode-dependent layers; it does not, by itself, disable gradient recording.

Sources: [PyTorch model tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/buildmodel_tutorial.html), [D2L layers/modules](https://d2l.ai/chapter_builders-guide/model-construction.html).

### Define your own module when the computation needs a name

<!-- example: PT03-custom -->
```python
import torch
from torch import nn

class MeanEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, feature_count):
        super().__init__()
        self.feature_count = feature_count

    def forward(self, inputs):
        if inputs.shape[-1] != self.feature_count:
            raise ValueError("unexpected feature width")
        return inputs.mean(dim=1)

encoder = MeanEncoder(2)
print(encoder(torch.tensor([[[1., 2.], [3., 4.]]])).tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
[[2.0, 3.0]]
```

The input is one example, two positions and two features. Reducing `dim=1` averages positions and retains both features. This module has no learned parameters, demonstrating that `nn.Module` is an organizational interface, not a synonym for “trained neural layer.” A padded sequence would additionally need masked averaging as shown in NC03.

# PT04. Batches

A batch is several examples kept together with their own targets. The feature row and the label at the same position belong to one example.

<!-- example: PT04-pair -->
```python
import torch

features = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
labels = torch.tensor([0, 1])
print(tuple(features.shape), labels.tolist())
print(features[0].tolist(), int(labels[0]))
```

**Output**
```text
(2, 2) [0, 1]
[1.0, 2.0] 0
```

The feature table has two examples and two measurements. The first example's features are `[1, 2]` and its label is 0. A **Dataset** defines how to obtain those pairs. A **DataLoader** groups them into batches and can schedule loading work. Shuffling the feature rows without shuffling the labels in the same order would attach the wrong answer to an example.

<!-- example: PT04-main -->
```python
import torch
from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader

features = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.], [5., 6.]])
labels = torch.tensor([0, 1, 0])
dataset = TensorDataset(features, labels)
loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=2, shuffle=False, num_workers=0)
for inputs, targets in loader:
    print(tuple(inputs.shape), targets.tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
(2, 2) [0, 1]
(1, 2) [0]
```

The final batch contains one example, not two. Averaging batch means equally would overweight that batch when calculating an example-weighted epoch mean. Variable-length text additionally needs a `collate_fn` that pads/organizes several examples and creates masks/targets correctly.

Map-style datasets support indexed access; iterable datasets supply a stream. More loader workers can improve throughput but add process/memory complexity, and streaming workers must avoid duplicating data. Samplers determine which indices are visited; they are not a substitute for defining independent train/validation/test groups before loading. This code only inspects batches and performs no training.

Sources: [PyTorch data tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/data_tutorial.html), [PyTorch data loading](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/data.html).

# PT05. The training loop

This **read-only walkthrough** describes the order used by the supported neural lab. It is intentionally not executed and has no training-output panel. The caller supplies a model, optimizer, loaders, loss and device. It is a simplified classification example, not a replacement for the full lab worker/checkpoint/cancellation code.

```python walkthrough
def supervised_epoch(model, optimizer, train_loader, validation_loader, device):
    import torch
    from torch.nn import functional as F
    model.train()
    for inputs, targets in train_loader:
        inputs, targets = inputs.to(device), targets.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        logits = model(inputs)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    model.eval()
    validation_sum, validation_count = 0.0, 0
    with torch.inference_mode():
        for inputs, targets in validation_loader:
            logits = model(inputs.to(device))
            validation_sum += F.cross_entropy(logits, targets.to(device), reduction="sum").item()
            validation_count += len(targets)
    if validation_count == 0:
        raise ValueError("validation needs at least one example")
    return validation_sum / validation_count
```

Mode first: training enables behavior such as dropout. Clearing gradients prevents accidental carry-over; forward produces logits (raw class scores); cross-entropy compares those scores with the correct class IDs; backward calculates gradients; the optimizer changes parameters. PT06 works through this loss numerically. Validation changes mode and suppresses gradient recording. Its summed loss is divided by the number of examples, not the number of unequal batches.

The real DL lab adds settings, logs, best-development checkpoint selection, early stopping and saved evaluation. The test set must not choose the checkpoint. A weights-only save supports inference; exact resume additionally needs optimizer/scheduler/random/sampling state and cannot be assumed from a weights file.

**Run it in the existing lab:** **Deep learning → Training lab** (`dl-lab`) supports linear/MLP, CNN/residual CNN and its dense image autoencoder under compatible tasks. **Saved results** and **Compare models** own measured outputs. Local installation is required; reading this function never starts a job.

Sources: [PyTorch optimization](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/optimization_tutorial.html), [saving/loading](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/saveloadrun_tutorial.html). Local reference: `src/training_lab/model_lab.py`.

# PT06. Losses

A **logit** is an unnormalized score. Softmax turns one row of logits into fractions that add to 1. Equal logits become equal fractions.

<!-- example: PT06-softmax -->
```python
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F

logits = torch.zeros(1, 3)
print([round(value, 3) for value in F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)[0].tolist()])
```

**Output**
```text
[0.333, 0.333, 0.333]
```

Three equal scores become about one third each. A classification head produces logits, and the loss compares them with the target under a specific convention. Applying softmax yourself before `cross_entropy` is unnecessary for the usual class-index case, because that loss already includes the normalization.

<!-- example: PT06-main -->
```python
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F

class_logits = torch.zeros(2, 3)
class_targets = torch.tensor([0, 2])
binary_logits = torch.zeros(2)
binary_targets = torch.tensor([0., 1.])
print(f"class loss={F.cross_entropy(class_logits, class_targets).item():.6f}")
print(f"binary loss={F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(binary_logits, binary_targets).item():.6f}")
```

**Output**
```text
class loss=1.098612
binary loss=0.693147
```

Equal three-class logits assign each class probability `1/3`, giving loss `−log(1/3)`. A zero binary logit assigns probability one half. Multiclass class-index targets are typically integer IDs; BCE targets are floating values aligned to logits. Multilabel classification uses independent binary targets, not a single mutually exclusive class ID.

For token/segmentation losses, keep the class axis and ignored/padded targets correct. Regression uses numerical targets and a suitable loss such as MSE. Initialization, normalization, learning rate and optimizer affect training; gradient clipping cannot fix a wrong target or leaked feature. A useful debugging procedure is checking whether a supported model can overfit a very small subset—but that experiment belongs in the lab, not a fabricated output here.

# PT07. Convolution

An image tensor in this lesson is arranged as batch, channels, height and width. A filter looks at a small window of that image.

<!-- example: PT07-window -->
```python
import torch

image = torch.arange(1., 10.).reshape(1, 1, 3, 3)
print(tuple(image.shape))
print(image[0, 0, :2, :2].tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
(1, 1, 3, 3)
[[1.0, 2.0], [4.0, 5.0]]
```

Shape `(1, 1, 3, 3)` is one image, one channel, three rows and three columns. The upper-left 2×2 window holds 1, 2, 4 and 5. A **convolutional filter** reuses the same numbers on every window. Stride controls how far the window moves. Padding controls the boundary. Pooling summarizes nearby outputs.

<!-- example: PT07-main -->
```python
import torch
from torch import nn

image = torch.arange(1., 10.).reshape(1, 1, 3, 3)
convolution = nn.Conv2d(1, 1, kernel_size=2, bias=False)
with torch.no_grad():
    convolution.weight.fill_(1.)
with torch.inference_mode():
    features = convolution(image)
    pooled = nn.MaxPool2d(2)(features)
print(features[0, 0].tolist())
print(tuple(features.shape), pooled.item())
```

**Output**
```text
[[12.0, 16.0], [24.0, 28.0]]
(1, 1, 2, 2) 28.0
```

The upper-left window sums `1+2+4+5=12`. The fixed all-one filter is a teaching choice, not a trained detector. Pooling selects the maximum from the 2×2 feature map. Increasing stride reduces output resolution; flattening later turns spatial features into classifier inputs, while adaptive pooling can produce a defined spatial size.

A residual block adds a compatible input path to a learned correction, helping information/gradients travel through deeper networks. A pretrained torchvision model needs its declared input transforms and weight revision; constructing an architecture with random weights does not give pretrained visual competence. Freezing parameters and switching evaluation mode do different jobs. Current lab CNN/residual training is supported; arbitrary torchvision transfer-learning training is not.

Sources: [PyTorch Conv2d](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.Conv2d.html), [D2L convolutions](https://d2l.ai/chapter_convolutional-neural-networks/conv-layer.html), [torchvision models](https://docs.pytorch.org/vision/stable/models.html).

# PT08. Recurrent models

An RNN reads a sequence one position at a time and carries a hidden vector forward. With `batch_first=True`, the input shape is batch, positions, features.

<!-- example: PT08-rnn -->
```python
import torch
from torch import nn

inputs = torch.zeros(1, 3, 2)
model = nn.RNN(2, 4, batch_first=True)
model.eval()
with torch.inference_mode():
    output, hidden = model(inputs)
print(tuple(output.shape), tuple(hidden.shape))
```

**Output**
```text
(1, 3, 4) (1, 1, 4)
```

One example, three positions and two features go in. The output has four features at each of the three positions. The hidden state has one layer, one example and four features. The values are zeros in and an untrained network out, so only the shapes are the lesson. A GRU adds gates. An LSTM also carries a cell state. Bidirectionality runs a second pass from the other end of the sequence.

<!-- example: PT08-main -->
```python
import torch
from torch import nn

inputs = torch.zeros(2, 5, 4)
for kind in [nn.RNN, nn.GRU, nn.LSTM]:
    model = kind(4, 3, batch_first=True, bidirectional=True)
    model.eval()
    with torch.inference_mode():
        output, state = model(inputs)
    hidden = state[0] if isinstance(state, tuple) else state
    print(kind.__name__, tuple(output.shape), tuple(hidden.shape))
```

**Output**
```text
RNN (2, 5, 6) (2, 2, 3)
GRU (2, 5, 6) (2, 2, 3)
LSTM (2, 5, 6) (2, 2, 3)
```

The input is two examples, five positions and four features. Two directions each provide three hidden features, giving six features per output position. The returned hidden state's first axis indexes layer×direction, not batch; LSTM also returns a matching cell-state tensor. Random initialization affects numerical values, but the displayed dimensions are fixed by this configuration. No meaningful labels are predicted.

For padded sequences, length handling/packing prevents padding from being mistaken for real sequence content. In a bidirectional model, `output[:, -1]` is not generally the desired concatenation of both complete-sequence final states. A backward direction also sees future tokens and is unsuitable for an ordinary causal next-token predictor. The current DL lab has no recurrent trainer; these are forward-interface examples.

Sources: [PyTorch LSTM](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.LSTM.html), [GRU](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html), [D2L bidirectional RNNs](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/bi-rnn.html).

# PT09. Attention

Attention replaces each position with a mix of the value vectors it is allowed to read. With a causal rule, the first position can read only itself. The second can read both. When those two are allowed equally, the mix is their average.

<!-- example: PT09-mix -->
```python
values = [[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 4.0]]
print(values[0])
print([(values[0][i] + values[1][i]) / 2 for i in range(2)])
```

**Output**
```text
[2.0, 0.0]
[1.0, 2.0]
```

The first value stays `[2, 0]`. The average of `[2, 0]` and `[0, 4]` is `[1, 2]`. Queries and keys produce the scores that decide those weights. The output is mixed information, not automatically a class prediction.

<!-- example: PT09-main -->
```python
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F

queries = torch.zeros(1, 1, 2, 2)
keys = torch.zeros(1, 1, 2, 2)
values = torch.tensor([[[[2., 0.], [0., 4.]]]])
output = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(queries, keys, values,
                                        is_causal=True, dropout_p=0.0)
print(output[0, 0].tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
[[2.0, 0.0], [1.0, 2.0]]
```

All allowed scores are equal. Position zero can read only the first value. Position one can read both and averages them: `([2,0]+[0,4])/2=[1,2]`. Multiple heads perform several projections/mixes before combining results. Residual paths preserve earlier representations, normalization controls feature scale and a feed-forward block transforms each position's features.

Encoder self-attention can read both directions; decoder causal attention cannot. Encoder–decoder cross-attention uses decoder queries with source-side keys/values. PyTorch attention APIs differ in Boolean-mask conventions: check the exact function instead of reusing a mask blindly. SDPA applies its specified dropout probability, so pass zero explicitly for evaluation. The existing architecture diagram owns the detailed Transformer explanation; this code links its mask/mix operations to actual tensors.

Sources: [PyTorch SDPA](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html), [D2L attention](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/attention-scoring-functions.html).

# PT09. Attention

Attention replaces each position with a mix of the value vectors it is allowed to read. With a causal rule, the first position can read only itself. The second can read both. When those two are allowed equally, the mix is their average.

<!-- example: PT09-mix -->
```python
values = [[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 4.0]]
print(values[0])
print([(values[0][i] + values[1][i]) / 2 for i in range(2)])
```

**Output**
```text
[2.0, 0.0]
[1.0, 2.0]
```

The first value stays `[2, 0]`. The average of `[2, 0]` and `[0, 4]` is `[1, 2]`. Queries and keys produce the scores that decide those weights. The output is mixed information, not automatically a class prediction.

<!-- example: PT09-main -->
```python
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F

queries = torch.zeros(1, 1, 2, 2)
keys = torch.zeros(1, 1, 2, 2)
values = torch.tensor([[[[2., 0.], [0., 4.]]]])
output = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(queries, keys, values,
                                        is_causal=True, dropout_p=0.0)
print(output[0, 0].tolist())
```

**Output**
```text
[[2.0, 0.0], [1.0, 2.0]]
```

All allowed scores are equal. Position zero can read only the first value. Position one can read both and averages them: `([2,0]+[0,4])/2=[1,2]`. Multiple heads perform several projections/mixes before combining results. Residual paths preserve earlier representations, normalization controls feature scale and a feed-forward block transforms each position's features.

Encoder self-attention can read both directions; decoder causal attention cannot. Encoder–decoder cross-attention uses decoder queries with source-side keys/values. PyTorch attention APIs differ in Boolean-mask conventions: check the exact function instead of reusing a mask blindly. SDPA applies its specified dropout probability, so pass zero explicitly for evaluation. The existing architecture diagram owns the detailed Transformer explanation; this code links its mask/mix operations to actual tensors.

Sources: [PyTorch SDPA](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.html), [D2L attention](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/attention-scoring-functions.html).
