notes.title: Topology, features and neighbour exchange
notes.markdown:
An MLP treats feature rows independently. A graph network introduces relational structure, which can help only if that structure is useful and available. Sum and mean aggregation encode different size information. The canonical normalized GCN rule uses degree-normalized adjacency with self loops; a simple mean-neighbour example is not numerically identical to that rule.

Node classification on one known graph can be transductive, with unlabelled test-node features/edges visible. Inductive evaluation instead asks about unseen nodes/graphs under stated access. Using test labels in messages is leakage in either case unless the task explicitly grants those labels. Too many layers can oversmooth representations; graph topology shortcuts can dominate genuine feature reasoning.

notes.title: Choosing a graph aggregation rule
notes.markdown: Compare an MLP on identical node features, a graph-only reference and message passing. This separates useful attributes from useful edges. Graph attention learns neighbour weights under a different rule; it does not prove that its largest edge caused a correct prediction.

notes.title: Example: legitimate graph access
notes.markdown: Use an authored graph with known edges and planted label leakage first. Public graph datasets need a later dataset/rights/split review; do not invent a default downloadable graph benchmark.

notes.title: Degree-normalized graph convolution
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** A is adjacency, I adds self loops, and D̃ records degrees after adding them. Symmetric normalization weights an edge by both endpoint degrees. H contains node features.

Read the formula from right to left as a feature transformation combined with graph-based mixing, followed by an activation. A+I supplies edges including self loops. The degree factors on both sides rescale contributions using each endpoint's connection count; this is a different layer from the walkthrough's simple self-plus-neighbour mean/sum update.

\[
H^{(\ell+1)}=\sigma\!\left(\widetilde D^{-1/2}(A+I)
\widetilde D^{-1/2}H^{(\ell)}W^{(\ell)}\right).
\]

In a two-node graph with one undirected edge, both self-looped degrees are two. Every normalized coefficient is 1/2; each node initially receives half its own features plus half its neighbour's. For a three-node chain, the endpoint self-weight is 1/2, the middle self-weight 1/3 and an endpoint-middle edge weight 1/√6. This is not simply a mean over each node's own neighbourhood.

### Evaluate the graph access policy

A train/test split over nodes can expose test-node features and edges during fitting in a transductive task while withholding labels. An inductive task with new graphs has a different information boundary. Neither can use test labels as features.

Compare an MLP using the same permitted attributes before attributing improvement to graph relations. No graph trainer or public graph-data download is silently enabled by reading this lesson.

notes.title: GraphSAGE: learn an aggregation function, not just node identities
notes.markdown:
**Read the degree-normalized GCN section first.** A GCN mixes neighbors under its specified normalization. GraphSAGE instead emphasizes learning reusable neighborhood-aggregation functions, often with bounded neighbor sampling, so new nodes can be represented from permitted features and neighborhoods. “Inductive” does not mean the model works on every unseen graph without compatible features or topology.

A mean-aggregation variant calculates a neighborhood summary, concatenates it with the node's own representation, then applies a learned transformation:

\[
m_v=\operatorname{mean}_{u\in N(v)}h_u,\qquad
h'_v=\sigma\left(W[h_v\Vert m_v]\right).
\]

N(v) is the specified neighbor set and the parallel symbol denotes concatenation, not addition. Normalization, nonlinearities and whether self-features enter the aggregation vary by implementation. Sampling is a computational choice and also changes which information a particular forward pass sees.

For own scalar feature 2 and neighbor features 1 and 3, the mean is 2. Concatenation gives [2,2]. With row-compatible projection weights [0.5,1] and ReLU, the output is max(0,0.5×2+1×2)=3. A neighborhood [1,1,3,3] has the same mean despite twice as many entries. This illustrates lost multiplicity; sum aggregation would distinguish their totals, but changing aggregation also changes scale and model assumptions.

With ten sampled neighbors at each of two layers, one seed can require up to 1+10+100 sampled positions before overlap/deduplication. This is not necessarily 111 distinct nodes. Sampling prevents full-neighborhood expansion but can miss important rare neighbors. State train/evaluation sampling and graph access rules.

**Practice.** Can a learned identity embedding for an unknown node be looked up automatically? **Answer.** Not if it has no trained row. A feature-based aggregator can compute a representation when suitable new-node features and allowed neighbors are supplied. Compare it with a feature-only baseline to establish whether edges help.

[GraphSAGE](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02216) · [Aggregation expressivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826).

notes.title: Graph attention: learn weights within the allowed neighborhood
notes.markdown:
A graph attention network (GAT) calculates different mixing weights for a node's permitted neighbors. Unlike averaging all neighbors equally, a learned scoring function uses node features before normalizing the scores over that neighborhood. Connectivity still determines which candidates can contribute.

One original-style attention head forms projected features, concatenates a target/neighbor pair, scores it with a learned vector and a LeakyReLU, then applies neighbor softmax:

\[
e_{vu}=\operatorname{LeakyReLU}(a^\top[Wh_v\Vert Wh_u]),\quad
\alpha_{vu}=\frac{\exp(e_{vu})}{\sum_{j\in N(v)}\exp(e_{vj})},\quad
h'_v=\sigma\left(\sum_u\alpha_{vu}Wh_u\right).
\]

If supplied scores are log 3 and 0, weights are 0.75 and 0.25. Supplied projected scalar values 2 and 6 then mix to 3. These numbers illustrate normalization and mixing; they are not the result of fitting a GAT. Add a self-loop only under the declared graph convention. Multiple heads may concatenate or average outputs, affecting shapes and cost.

Follow the dependencies: permitted edges/features → projected pairs → scores → neighbor softmax → weighted values. These are learned neighbor weights, not a guarantee that the largest weight identifies a causal explanation of the final prediction. Degree, alternate paths and later layers also matter.

**Practice.** Does adding attention let a one-layer local GAT directly read an unconnected distant node? **Answer.** No. It reweights the allowed neighborhood. Additional layers or changed connectivity expand access, with different compute and leakage implications. Too many mixing layers can make node features indistinguishable (oversmoothing); narrow paths can also bottleneck distant information (oversquashing). These are distinct issues.

[GAT primary paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10903).

notes.title: Node, link and whole-graph predictions
notes.markdown:
The same message-passing backbone can feed different tasks. A node head predicts one output per selected node. A link decoder scores a pair. A graph readout converts a variable number of node representations into one whole-graph representation before its prediction head. The data split and metric must match the task, not just the tensor shape.

For a simple link decoder, logit h_u dot h_v becomes a score after sigmoid. If h_u=[1,0] and h_v=[0.5,1], the logit is 0.5 and sigmoid is 0.6225. This formula does not establish calibration or prove that an edge exists. Negative sampling defines which nonedges are compared, and filtered candidate sets can make evaluation easier than deployment.

For whole-graph prediction, sum/mean/max pooling are invariant to node order, but retain different information. Scalar nodes [1,3] and [1,1,3,3] both have mean 2; their sums are 4 and 8. Mean loses multiplicity, while sum scales with graph size. Choose a readout compatible with whether size itself carries legitimate signal.

Keep held-out link targets outside the message-passing graph unless the benchmark explicitly permits that information. Handle reversed undirected edges consistently. Transductive access to unlabeled nodes/topology is not the same as permission to read held-out labels. Temporal tasks must not receive future edges or target-derived node features.

**Practice.** A link predictor sees its positive test edge during neighborhood aggregation. Is this harmless because the test label was removed? **Answer.** Not necessarily: the edge itself can disclose the target. Rebuild the allowed graph from the intended protocol, then repeat evaluation. Test graph-level splits on entire graphs or source groups where required.

[OGB link protocols](https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/linkprop/) · [OGB graph protocols](https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/graphprop/).

notes.title: Settings: Graph message-passing layers, Neighbour aggregation
notes.markdown:
### Graph message-passing layers

Number of successive neighbourhood aggregation stages.

k rounds can expose k-hop information under the specific graph/update.

More layers broaden access but can oversmooth or increase structural shortcuts.

Interactions: graph split; aggregation; hidden_width.

Permitted graph information is part of the protocol, not a free implementation detail.

### Neighbour aggregation

Order-independent combination of neighbour messages.

Mean divides by neighbour count; sum preserves a count-dependent magnitude.

Changes sensitivity to degree and multiset size.

Interactions: self-loop policy; normalization.

A simple mean aggregator is not the canonical degree-normalized GCN operator.

reading.title: Graph neural networks
reading.definition: A graph represents objects as nodes and relationships as edges. A graph neural network, or GNN, updates node features by collecting messages from connected neighbours. Its calculation therefore depends on both the feature values and which connections are present; merely listing nodes in a table would omit important information.
reading.example: The graph is A—B—C, with scalar features [1,2,4]. We calculate B's update using mean or sum neighbour messages and its own feature. A separate readout section applies the same rule to all nodes and shows a whole-graph sum.
reading.connection: CNNs share local filters on a regular image grid. Message-passing GNNs generalize local information exchange to an explicit graph; neighbour order should not arbitrarily change an invariant aggregation.

steps.title: Graph connections and original features
steps.prose: Node B is connected to A and C. This declared neighbour set does not include B itself; its own feature is added separately. A directed edge or explicit self-loop convention would describe a different calculation.
steps.terms: Nodes are objects with features; edges specify relationships or permitted message routes. All updates here use original states synchronously.
steps.next: Read neighbour features for B while preserving its own original feature.

steps.title: Messages from neighbours
steps.prose: A sends feature 1 and C sends feature 4 to B. These are identity messages in the small example; a learned GNN may transform neighbour features first. Do not overwrite A before C's update if all nodes are meant to use the same previous layer.
steps.terms: Synchronous updating uses one common old-state snapshot for a layer. It prevents node iteration order from changing results.
steps.next: Aggregate the two incoming messages using the selected rule.

steps.title: Mean or sum aggregation
steps.prose: Summing gives 5; taking their mean gives 2.5. Mean reduces direct dependence on neighbour count, while sum can retain information related to that count. Neither choice is universally better; it changes the model's assumptions.
steps.terms: A permutation-invariant aggregation is unaffected by the order in which the same messages are listed.
steps.next: Combine this summary with B's original feature.

steps.title: Update node B
steps.prose: Add B's original feature 2 to its neighbour summary, multiply by 0.5, then apply ReLU. This is the declared layer, not a universal GNN formula. Other networks use learned projections, normalized neighbours, concatenation or attention.
steps.terms: ReLU keeps the positive value here. Self information and neighbour information are separate inputs to the update.
steps.next: The next section is a separate graph-readout example, not another learned update to B.

steps.title: Separate node updates from graph readout
steps.prose: A node-level task can predict from each updated node. For a whole-graph task, first update all nodes with the same synchronous rule, then pool their representations. The fixed sum shown here adds A', B' and C'; it is independent of whether neighbour messages used mean or sum.
steps.terms: A graph readout produces one representation from a set of node features. Edge-level tasks need another appropriate head.
steps.next: The deeper notes discuss normalization, multi-layer reach and limitations without implying that one pooled number solves a graph task.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A graph represents entities as nodes and relations as edges. Node features describe each entity; adjacency describes which entities can exchange messages. A graph network updates a node using its neighbours' representations, usually with shared learned transformations and a permutation-invariant aggregation such as sum or mean.

Suppose node B has value 2 and neighbours with values 1 and 4. Their mean is 2.5. A simple update $h'_B=\operatorname{ReLU}(0.5(h_B+\operatorname{mean}_{j\in N(B)}h_j))$ gives 2.25. Using a sum instead gives 3.5. These are different choices: sum retains information about neighbour count, while mean normalises it away. This teaching update is not the exact normalisation rule of every GCN.

One message-passing layer reaches one-hop neighbours; two can use neighbours of neighbours. Repeated mixing may make representations too similar, called oversmoothing. Graph-level prediction additionally needs a readout pooling node representations; node classification predicts separately at each node.

The graph's edge meaning is a modelling decision, not proof that those relations are causal. Check whether evaluation nodes or labels were available during fitting and whether the intended setting is transductive or inductive. The site computes a small graph example but has no GNN-training button.

Sources: [Kipf and Welling: GCN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907), [PyTorch Geometric: message passing](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/create_gnn.html).

# DL12. Prediction heads, targets and losses

A prediction head maps learned features to the outputs a task needs. One class for a whole example, one label for each token, a numerical value and a segmentation map need different shapes and objectives. The head, target alignment, loss reduction and evaluation metric must agree with one another.

The hidden representation has shape [B,T,D] = [1,3,4]: one example, three positions and four features per position. Choose a target type to inspect its output shape and a separate authored score/loss calculation; no trained head is loaded.

Earlier architectures produce features. This lesson connects those features to an actual prediction task without treating softmax as the right operation for every output. The shared metrics lesson explains general evaluation; a deeper note adds segmentation-specific IoU and Dice.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: DL05, DL08, ML10.

## 1. Target shapes and valid scoring units

**Key terms.** A **task head** maps features to outputs; **multiclass** selects one class; **multilabel** permits several; **segmentation** predicts per-pixel labels; **detection** predicts object classes and locations. A **mask** can mean a target image or a scoring/visibility rule, so name which.

**Process.** Define the target shape and meaning before constructing the output layer. Produce matching logits/coordinates, apply the correct loss and reduction, then evaluate with metrics that match the task and independent units.

A single image label commonly uses [B,C] logits and [B] integer targets. Semantic segmentation commonly uses [B,C,H,W] logits and [B,H,W] hard-label targets. Multilabel classification commonly uses independent binary logits with matching target indicators. Feeding softmax probabilities into a loss expecting raw logits changes the computation.

Detection adds box representation, matching/assignment, class scores and localization penalties; it is not classification with more categories. Class imbalance can affect sampling, loss weighting and thresholds. A rare-class recall gain can cost false positives, so report both. Aggregate at patient/source/image level when pixels or patches are correlated.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** IoU is intersection size divided by union size for a declared pair of regions. C is class count, B batch, and H/W spatial dimensions. Per-class and averaged IoU require explicit absent-class handling.

### Region overlap: IoU and Dice

For segmentation, foreground is the set of pixels assigned to the object or region of interest. Intersection counts pixels both prediction and reference include; union counts pixels included by either. Intersection over union (IoU) and the Dice coefficient summarize the same overlap with different denominators, so their values should not be compared as though they were one metric.

If predicted foreground has 7 pixels, reference foreground has 5 and their overlap is 3, union=7+5−3=9 and IoU=3/9=0.3333. Dice overlap is 2×3/(7+5)=0.5: same regions, different metric. A ten-class [8,10] output contains 80 logits, not 80 independent target examples.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Choosing task-specific heads and objectives

Choose the simplest head matching the annotation. Weighted cross-entropy, focal-style objectives and Dice losses have different targets/normalizations and need a specific derivation before implementation. They should not appear as unexplained dropdown names.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: image-level independence

Use authored image masks for arithmetic and shape tests. The first lab can remain image classification; segmentation/detection are bounded theory branches until real datasets, target loaders and metrics are implemented.

**Check.** Why is treating every segmentation pixel as an independent case for uncertainty suspect?

**Answer.** Nearby pixels and pixels in one source image are correlated. Resample independent images or higher-level source groups under the stated protocol.

## 5. Object detection: predict locations and labels together

Object detection returns a variable-size set of object boxes, class labels and scores for an image. A box can use corner coordinates or center/width/height; declare the convention before calculating overlap or losses. Training must match predictions to annotations and combine classification with localization terms. Detection is not image classification with extra class names.

Many detectors propose dense or region-based candidates and use score filtering plus **non-maximum suppression (NMS)**. NMS keeps a high-scoring box and suppresses lower-scoring overlapping boxes under a stated class/overlap rule. It is postprocessing, not an evaluation metric, and not every architecture requires it: DETR uses a set-prediction/matching formulation rather than ordinary NMS.

For continuous-coordinate boxes A=(0,0,2,2) and B=(0.5,0,2.5,2), both areas are 4. Their intersection is 3 and union is 5, giving IoU=0.6. If same-class scores are 0.9 and 0.8 and NMS threshold is 0.5, B is suppressed. Do not add an inclusive-pixel “+1” to this continuous convention. A ground-truth matching threshold is a separate evaluation choice, even if it also uses IoU.

At evaluation, match predictions to ground truth under the benchmark's one-to-one rules, score ordering and overlap thresholds. Unmatched predictions can become false positives, including duplicate detections of one object. Average precision summarizes a precision/recall relationship under specified interpolation, classes and IoU settings. Its value is not interchangeable with a classification accuracy or a single F1.

**Practice.** Could aggressive NMS improve precision but reduce recall? **Answer.** Yes, especially for nearby same-class objects. Inspect the retained boxes and full precision/recall trade-off. Train/validation image or source splits must preserve independence; correlated video frames should not be randomly divided without justification.

[Official NMS definition](https://docs.pytorch.org/vision/main/generated/torchvision.ops.nms.html) · [DETR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.12872).

## 6. Semantic and instance segmentation: retain spatial detail

Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each pixel. Instance segmentation additionally distinguishes separate objects of the same category. A third variant, panoptic segmentation, combines instance-aware objects with semantic background regions under a stated label policy. The required annotations and evaluation are different.

A U-Net-style encoder compresses spatial resolution while building features; a decoder upsamples and combines compatible encoder features through skip connections. These spatial skip connections preserve detail and differ from the residual addition introduced in DL06. Concatenating encoder/decoder maps increases feature channels; adding requires matching shapes. Cropping, padding and resize alignment affect which output pixel corresponds to which input location.

For a two-class semantic task on a 64×64 image, one convention returns logits [B,2,64,64] and integer targets [B,64,64]. Cross-entropy consumes the raw logits, not another softmax first. A binary sigmoid formulation instead uses one logit per pixel with a compatible binary loss. State ignored labels and reduction. Weighted losses or soft overlap losses change the optimization target, not the underlying annotation quality.

Use the earlier IoU/Dice note for their denominators rather than defining them twice. To see why pixel accuracy can mislead, suppose only 10 of 1,000 pixels are foreground. Predicting background everywhere gives 99% accuracy but zero foreground recall. A per-class metric, foreground errors and absent-class convention are needed to interpret this result.

Mask R-CNN predicts instance-specific masks associated with detected objects; it is not the same output as one semantic map. Evaluate object matching and mask quality under a compatible protocol. Medical or geographic patches may share a patient/scene; reserve independent sources and resample at that level for uncertainty.

**Practice.** Does a perfectly shaped output tensor prove spatial labels are aligned? **Answer.** No. Inspect input/target pairs after all transforms and test known landmark positions through crop/resize/flip operations. Data augmentation must transform masks and boxes consistently with the image.

[U-Net](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.04597) · [Mask R-CNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06870).

## 7. Tracking: keep an identity across video frames

Tracking connects observations across time. A multi-object tracker takes detections, predicts motion, associates new observations with existing tracks and handles track creation, missed detections and termination. It is not another name for detecting the same class independently in every frame. This extension concerns video association, not robotics/control.

SORT supplies a useful baseline built around motion estimation and assignment. Deep SORT adds an appearance representation to help associate detections. An association cost can combine geometry/motion and appearance under a declared gating policy; assigning each detection greedily to its nearest track can conflict with a globally consistent one-to-one assignment.

For an illustrative two-track/two-detection cost table, let costs be [[1,2],[1.1,100]], where lower is better. Greedily giving track 1 its cheapest detection can force track 2 to cost 100, totaling 101. The other one-to-one assignment costs 2+1.1=3.1. This arithmetic illustrates assignment constraints, not a complete tracker. No identity decision is justified from this cost table without knowing how costs were constructed.

Two people can be correctly detected in every frame while their IDs swap when they cross. Detection quality can remain high even though association is wrong. Track metrics therefore need localization/detection and identity continuity; HOTA is one framework for evaluating multiple aspects. Report dataset conventions, matching thresholds and treatment of missing/occluded objects, rather than claiming that image-level accuracy measures tracking.

**Practice.** Should a track disappear permanently after one missing detection? **Answer.** That is a policy choice. A bounded missing-frame allowance may preserve identity through occlusion but can also keep false tracks alive. Choose it on validation sequences and evaluate full held-out sequences, not shuffled individual frames.

sections.markdown:
# DL12. Prediction heads, targets and losses

A prediction head maps learned features to the outputs a task needs. One class for a whole example, one label for each token, a numerical value and a segmentation map need different shapes and objectives. The head, target alignment, loss reduction and evaluation metric must agree with one another.

The hidden representation has shape [B,T,D] = [1,3,4]: one example, three positions and four features per position. Choose a target type to inspect its output shape and a separate authored score/loss calculation; no trained head is loaded.

Earlier architectures produce features. This lesson connects those features to an actual prediction task without treating softmax as the right operation for every output. The shared metrics lesson explains general evaluation; a deeper note adds segmentation-specific IoU and Dice.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: DL05, DL08, ML10.

sections.title: Target shapes and valid scoring units
sections.markdown:
## 1. Target shapes and valid scoring units

**Key terms.** A **task head** maps features to outputs; **multiclass** selects one class; **multilabel** permits several; **segmentation** predicts per-pixel labels; **detection** predicts object classes and locations. A **mask** can mean a target image or a scoring/visibility rule, so name which.

**Process.** Define the target shape and meaning before constructing the output layer. Produce matching logits/coordinates, apply the correct loss and reduction, then evaluate with metrics that match the task and independent units.

A single image label commonly uses [B,C] logits and [B] integer targets. Semantic segmentation commonly uses [B,C,H,W] logits and [B,H,W] hard-label targets. Multilabel classification commonly uses independent binary logits with matching target indicators. Feeding softmax probabilities into a loss expecting raw logits changes the computation.

Detection adds box representation, matching/assignment, class scores and localization penalties; it is not classification with more categories. Class imbalance can affect sampling, loss weighting and thresholds. A rare-class recall gain can cost false positives, so report both. Aggregate at patient/source/image level when pixels or patches are correlated.

sections.title: A worked calculation
sections.markdown:
## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** IoU is intersection size divided by union size for a declared pair of regions. C is class count, B batch, and H/W spatial dimensions. Per-class and averaged IoU require explicit absent-class handling.

### Region overlap: IoU and Dice

For segmentation, foreground is the set of pixels assigned to the object or region of interest. Intersection counts pixels both prediction and reference include; union counts pixels included by either. Intersection over union (IoU) and the Dice coefficient summarize the same overlap with different denominators, so their values should not be compared as though they were one metric.

If predicted foreground has 7 pixels, reference foreground has 5 and their overlap is 3, union=7+5−3=9 and IoU=3/9=0.3333. Dice overlap is 2×3/(7+5)=0.5: same regions, different metric. A ten-class [8,10] output contains 80 logits, not 80 independent target examples.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

sections.title: Choosing task-specific heads and objectives
sections.markdown:
## 3. Choosing task-specific heads and objectives

Choose the simplest head matching the annotation. Weighted cross-entropy, focal-style objectives and Dice losses have different targets/normalizations and need a specific derivation before implementation. They should not appear as unexplained dropdown names.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

sections.title: Example: image-level independence
sections.markdown:
## 4. Example: image-level independence

Use authored image masks for arithmetic and shape tests. The first lab can remain image classification; segmentation/detection are bounded theory branches until real datasets, target loaders and metrics are implemented.

**Check.** Why is treating every segmentation pixel as an independent case for uncertainty suspect?

**Answer.** Nearby pixels and pixels in one source image are correlated. Resample independent images or higher-level source groups under the stated protocol.

sections.title: Object detection: predict locations and labels together
sections.markdown:
## 5. Object detection: predict locations and labels together

Object detection returns a variable-size set of object boxes, class labels and scores for an image. A box can use corner coordinates or center/width/height; declare the convention before calculating overlap or losses. Training must match predictions to annotations and combine classification with localization terms. Detection is not image classification with extra class names.

Many detectors propose dense or region-based candidates and use score filtering plus **non-maximum suppression (NMS)**. NMS keeps a high-scoring box and suppresses lower-scoring overlapping boxes under a stated class/overlap rule. It is postprocessing, not an evaluation metric, and not every architecture requires it: DETR uses a set-prediction/matching formulation rather than ordinary NMS.

For continuous-coordinate boxes A=(0,0,2,2) and B=(0.5,0,2.5,2), both areas are 4. Their intersection is 3 and union is 5, giving IoU=0.6. If same-class scores are 0.9 and 0.8 and NMS threshold is 0.5, B is suppressed. Do not add an inclusive-pixel “+1” to this continuous convention. A ground-truth matching threshold is a separate evaluation choice, even if it also uses IoU.

At evaluation, match predictions to ground truth under the benchmark's one-to-one rules, score ordering and overlap thresholds. Unmatched predictions can become false positives, including duplicate detections of one object. Average precision summarizes a precision/recall relationship under specified interpolation, classes and IoU settings. Its value is not interchangeable with a classification accuracy or a single F1.

**Practice.** Could aggressive NMS improve precision but reduce recall? **Answer.** Yes, especially for nearby same-class objects. Inspect the retained boxes and full precision/recall trade-off. Train/validation image or source splits must preserve independence; correlated video frames should not be randomly divided without justification.

[Official NMS definition](https://docs.pytorch.org/vision/main/generated/torchvision.ops.nms.html) · [DETR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.12872).

sections.title: Semantic and instance segmentation: retain spatial detail
sections.markdown:
## 6. Semantic and instance segmentation: retain spatial detail

Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each pixel. Instance segmentation additionally distinguishes separate objects of the same category. A third variant, panoptic segmentation, combines instance-aware objects with semantic background regions under a stated label policy. The required annotations and evaluation are different.

A U-Net-style encoder compresses spatial resolution while building features; a decoder upsamples and combines compatible encoder features through skip connections. These spatial skip connections preserve detail and differ from the residual addition introduced in DL06. Concatenating encoder/decoder maps increases feature channels; adding requires matching shapes. Cropping, padding and resize alignment affect which output pixel corresponds to which input location.

For a two-class semantic task on a 64×64 image, one convention returns logits [B,2,64,64] and integer targets [B,64,64]. Cross-entropy consumes the raw logits, not another softmax first. A binary sigmoid formulation instead uses one logit per pixel with a compatible binary loss. State ignored labels and reduction. Weighted losses or soft overlap losses change the optimization target, not the underlying annotation quality.

Use the earlier IoU/Dice note for their denominators rather than defining them twice. To see why pixel accuracy can mislead, suppose only 10 of 1,000 pixels are foreground. Predicting background everywhere gives 99% accuracy but zero foreground recall. A per-class metric, foreground errors and absent-class convention are needed to interpret this result.

Mask R-CNN predicts instance-specific masks associated with detected objects; it is not the same output as one semantic map. Evaluate object matching and mask quality under a compatible protocol. Medical or geographic patches may share a patient/scene; reserve independent sources and resample at that level for uncertainty.

**Practice.** Does a perfectly shaped output tensor prove spatial labels are aligned? **Answer.** No. Inspect input/target pairs after all transforms and test known landmark positions through crop/resize/flip operations. Data augmentation must transform masks and boxes consistently with the image.

[U-Net](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.04597) · [Mask R-CNN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06870).

Objective whose expected output/target shapes match the declared task.

reading.title: Prediction heads, targets and losses
reading.definition: A prediction head maps learned features to the outputs a task needs. One class for a whole example, one label for each token, a numerical value and a segmentation map need different shapes and objectives. The head, target alignment, loss reduction and evaluation metric must agree with one another.
reading.example: The hidden representation has shape [B,T,D] = [1,3,4]: one example, three positions and four features per position. Choose a target type to inspect its output shape and a separate authored score/loss calculation; no trained head is loaded.
reading.connection: Earlier architectures produce features. This lesson connects those features to an actual prediction task without treating softmax as the right operation for every output. The shared metrics lesson explains general evaluation; a deeper note adds segmentation-specific IoU and Dice.

steps.title: What receives a target?
steps.prose: Decide whether the label belongs to the whole example, each valid position or a numerical measurement. Example-level classification usually summarizes positions first; token labelling preserves them. A span or structured target can require additional alignment or constraints.
steps.terms: B counts examples, T positions and D feature dimensions. These axes are not interchangeable just because their sizes match.
steps.next: Choose a projection whose output axes match the target unit.

steps.title: Projection and output dimensions
steps.prose: A task head transforms hidden features into the necessary scores or numbers. Three mutually exclusive classes require three scores at the relevant unit. Regression may require one number; token classification requires a class-score vector for every labelled token.
steps.terms: A head is a learned mapping. Pooling summarizes positions for an example-level target; it is not appropriate when each position needs its own label.
steps.next: Interpret these outputs according to the task before calculating a loss.

steps.title: Class probabilities or numerical values
steps.prose: For exclusive classes, softmax normalizes each unit's class scores. For regression, keep the numerical prediction instead of forcing it into a class probability. Independent binary labels would use a different probability/objective setup.
steps.terms: Logits are unnormalized class scores. Token softmax works across classes separately at each position.
steps.next: Compare the prediction with the aligned observed target using a suitable loss.

steps.title: Loss, valid positions and reduction
steps.prose: Choose the objective for the target type, then score only valid labelled positions. Padding and unlabelled positions may be excluded. The displayed token-classification arithmetic concerns one token; a full sequence objective needs an explicit aggregation over valid positions.
steps.terms: A loss mask controls scored targets and is different from an attention mask. A sum and a mean use different denominators.
steps.next: The retained task notes compare regression, multilabel, span and segmentation conventions before evaluation.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A representation becomes a prediction only after an output head assigns the required meaning. First specify the target unit and which outcomes may coexist. Then choose a head and objective, rather than selecting a loss because its name is familiar.

For one of K mutually exclusive classes, produce K logits and use categorical cross-entropy. For independent binary labels that can coexist, produce one logit per label and use binary cross-entropy. A sequence with one tag at every position is still categorical at each position, with logits shaped conceptually `[batch, positions, tags]`; it is not automatically multilabel. A CRF additionally models a joint score over allowed tag sequences.

For a numerical target, a linear output can be trained with squared or absolute error. For language modelling, each scored position predicts one vocabulary token. Ignore masks determine which targets contribute. For reconstruction, the observation model determines an appropriate output distribution and loss.

Training loss and task metric answer related but different questions. Cross-entropy can improve without changing any thresholded labels. Segmentation overlap metrics count regions: if intersection is 3 and union is 9, IoU is 1/3. Dice instead divides twice the intersection by the total sizes of both regions. Define the counted sets before comparing them.

Sources: [PyTorch: CrossEntropyLoss](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss.html), [PyTorch: BCEWithLogitsLoss](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss.html).

question.prompt: An image can contain both a bicycle and a pedestrian. You need one presence score for each label, and both labels may be true. Which output/loss design fits that target?

options.text: Two independent logits trained with a binary loss for each label.
options.feedback: Multilabel targets allow multiple positive indicators, unlike mutually exclusive softmax classes.

options.text: One two-class softmax that forces exactly one label per image.
options.feedback: A softmax competition would incorrectly force the two labels to exclude one another.

options.text: A single number interpreted as the coordinates of both objects.
options.feedback: Object presence and localization are different targets; one scalar cannot encode both stated presence indicators.

options.text: A per-pixel segmentation mask, because all image tasks require one.
options.feedback: Segmentation needs spatial annotations and answers a different question from image-level presence.

question.explanation: Start from target meaning: several labels can be present, so the outputs should not be forced to sum to one. Localization or segmentation would require additional targets and heads.
question.skill: Match a task head and loss to label semantics

question.prompt: A predicted foreground region contains 8 pixels, the reference region contains 6 pixels, and their intersection contains 4 pixels. What is intersection-over-union (IoU)?

options.feedback: 4/8 is precision for this foreground prediction, not intersection divided by union.
Union size is 8+6−4=10, so IoU=4/10=0.40.
4/6 is recall against the reference foreground, not IoU.
2×4/(8+6) is Dice overlap, a different metric from IoU.

question.explanation: Subtract the intersection once when forming the union to avoid counting shared pixels twice. Naming the metric matters because precision, recall, Dice, and IoU use different denominators.
question.skill: Calculate segmentation overlap

question.prompt: Two same-class boxes have IoU=0.6 and scores 0.9 and 0.8. Standard greedy NMS uses threshold 0.5. What happens?
question.explanation: NMS removes lower-scoring overlapping candidates under this convention; it is not a ground-truth evaluation metric.
question.skill: Apply the advanced section

options.text: Keep the higher-scoring box and suppress the lower one
options.feedback: NMS removes lower-scoring overlapping candidates under this convention; it is not a ground-truth evaluation metric.

options.text: Average the two boxes automatically
options.feedback: Greedy NMS suppression is not the same as box fusion.

options.text: Declare both true positives
options.feedback: Truth matching requires ground-truth annotations and a separate evaluation protocol.

options.text: Both must remain because IoU is below 1
options.feedback: The stated suppression threshold is 0.5, not exact equality.

question.prompt: Only 10 of 1,000 pixels are foreground. Predicting background everywhere gives what warning?
question.explanation: Background dominance makes accuracy insufficient; examine per-class errors and compatible overlap metrics.
question.skill: Apply the advanced section

options.text: 99% accuracy proves useful foreground segmentation
options.feedback: No foreground pixels were recovered in this prediction.

options.text: 99% pixel accuracy can coexist with zero foreground recall
options.feedback: Background dominance makes accuracy insufficient; examine per-class errors and compatible overlap metrics.

options.text: Foreground recall is also 99%
options.feedback: Recall uses actual foreground pixels, all of which were missed.

options.text: The tensor shape must be invalid
options.feedback: A correctly shaped output can still make completely unhelpful predictions.

question.prompt: In each frame two people are detected perfectly, but their track IDs swap after crossing. What failed?
question.explanation: Tracking evaluates continuity across frames; correct boxes alone do not establish correct persistent identities.
question.skill: Apply the advanced section

options.text: Necessarily image-level object classification
options.feedback: The identities can swap even if both object classes and boxes are correct.

options.text: Nothing, because detection is perfect
options.feedback: Per-frame detection omits the defining cross-frame association task.

options.text: Identity association, despite good per-frame detection
options.feedback: Tracking evaluates continuity across frames; correct boxes alone do not establish correct persistent identities.

options.text: The camera must have changed resolution
options.feedback: No such cause follows from the described identity error.

# DL13. The neural training loop and its system state

Training is a repeated procedure: fetch a batch, calculate predictions and loss, compute gradients and update trainable parameters. The data loader, device, optimizer state and checkpoint rules are part of that procedure, not extra neural-network layers. Validation checks a model without fitting on those cases; saving state makes selected results or later resumption possible.

We have 32 examples with 16 float32 features each. Change batch size to see input-memory bytes and updates per epoch under one-update-per-batch training. These calculations exclude other memory costs and do not launch a job.

The earlier lessons explain individual model operations. Here we connect them to data movement, training/evaluation modes, gradient clearing, periodic validation and recoverable state.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: DL04, DL05.

## 1. Training state, devices and data movement

**Key terms.** **Parameters** are learned state; **gradients** hold derivatives; **optimizer state** stores update history; **activations** are forward intermediates. A **checkpoint** may contain only weights or a complete resumable state; these are different contracts.

**Process.** Load permitted data and a configuration, allocate compatible tensors, run bounded forward/backward/update steps and record actual progress. Validate separately, save complete state if resuming is supported, then measure inference without training.

Dataset → DataLoader → tensor batch → model → loss → backward → optimizer is the core loop. A scheduler has declared step units. Gradient accumulation combines microbatches before an update and needs the correct denominator; clipping occurs at the specified update boundary. Train/eval modes and gradient-recording modes solve different problems.

CPU is the correctness reference; Mac MPS is a possible accelerator, not CUDA. Unsupported operations or mixed-precision paths need explicit handling, not silent fallback that invalidates timing. DataLoader workers, thread counts and device transfers can dominate small models. Synchronize correctly when timing asynchronous work, and distinguish startup from steady-state latency.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** N is parameter count and b bytes per value. Raw parameter storage is N×b, before all other states. Effective batch is microbatch size times accumulation count under the declared equal-size single-device convention.

One million FP32 parameters occupy 4,000,000 bytes, about 3.81 MiB. FP32 parameters plus gradients plus two FP32 Adam moments alone occupy about 16,000,000 bytes, before activations, buffers and overhead; other precision recipes differ. Microbatch 16 with accumulation 4 supplies 64 examples per update only if all four batches contain 16 included examples.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Batching, throughput and deployment metadata

More batching can improve throughput and increase memory while changing optimization. A small model can run faster on CPU than GPU when transfer/launch costs dominate. Do not make speed claims before a representative bounded pilot. Deployment also needs feature/token mappings, preprocessing and task metadata.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: save enough state to resume

Use existing app logging concepts, but keep the new ML/DL artifacts in their own versioned task namespace. A classical estimator's final fit and a neural optimizer update must not be given fabricated identical progress curves.

**Check.** Why are weights alone insufficient to reproduce the next training update?

**Answer.** The optimizer, scheduler, random generators, sampler/data position and compatible configuration may all affect it. Save/restore the complete state and test continuation under declared tolerances.

## 5. Microbatch weighting and memory accounting

**Key terms.** A microbatch is one forward/backward calculation. An optimizer update can accumulate several such calculations. Effective batch size counts examples contributing before that update.

**Process.** Zero gradients, accumulate correctly weighted losses over microbatches, clip once after accumulation and then update once. If using mixed precision, unscale gradients before clipping.

For microbatch target counts 12 and 4, loss means L₁ and L₂ combine as (12L₁+4L₂)/16. Simply averaging the two means gives the smaller microbatch disproportionate influence. For equal-sized classification batches, division by the number of accumulated microbatches is equivalent; the final partial group needs its actual denominator.

### Memory has several owners

Weights, gradients, optimizer moments and saved activations are different allocations. For P float32 parameters, weights alone use 4P bytes; gradients add about 4P, and two Adam moments add about 8P, before activations, temporary buffers and allocator overhead. Freezing parameters removes their gradient/moment needs but not necessarily all activations used by trainable downstream layers.

The current image lab runs one batch per update in float32 with bounded width and rows. It does not pretend to implement accumulation, mixed precision, distributed execution or compiled kernels. The LLM scratch path separately exposes accumulation. Record actual hardware and elapsed time rather than extrapolating a theoretical FLOP estimate into a speed claim.

## 6. Export a prediction pipeline, not an isolated weight file

A deployable prediction pipeline includes everything needed to turn an allowed input into the intended output: parsing, feature order, resizing/scaling, vocabularies or category maps, model parameters, output interpretation and any decision threshold. The serving code must use compatible versions and the same relevant conventions as evaluation.

First save a small non-sensitive set of input/output fixtures from the approved pipeline. Export the declared artifact, load it in an isolated supported runtime, and compare outputs within a chosen tolerance. Record artifact hash, data/model revision, dependencies, input schema, expected units and supported hardware. A hash detects changed bytes but does not authenticate an untrusted publisher by itself.

Training mode and inference mode remain separate: disable unwanted dropout and state updates, and choose appropriate derivative-recording settings. A model export format such as ONNX can support another runtime but does not guarantee that every operator, dynamic shape or preprocessing step transfers correctly. Loading arbitrary pickle/joblib files can execute code; accept only trusted artifacts under an explicit policy, not anonymous uploads.

Measure an end-to-end boundary as well as model-only time. If parsing/preprocessing takes 8 ms, model computation 12 ms and postprocessing 5 ms, serial service work totals 25 ms before network and queueing. That is not automatically 40 requests/second under concurrent traffic: batching, overlap, hardware contention and tail effects must be measured. Report input sizes, batch, precision, warm-up, synchronization and measurement distribution.

**Practice.** Exported weights give the same tensor outputs on a synthetic input, but live predictions change. What else should be inspected? **Answer.** Feature ordering, normalization, token/label maps, resize alignment, thresholds, mode and runtime precision. Test the full raw-input path before blaming the model architecture.

The next section handles changes after deployment. Existing LLM serving lessons add prefill/decoding/KV specifics; they do not replace these general pipeline checks. [scikit-learn persistence/security](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/model_persistence.html) · [PyTorch export documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/export.html).

## 7. Monitor data, predictions and outcomes; recover deliberately

Monitoring asks whether the deployed system still meets its intended contract. **Data drift** is a change in input distribution; **prediction drift** is a change in outputs; **performance degradation** concerns quality against outcomes. A shift in an input histogram does not by itself prove failure, and unchanged inputs do not prove the target relationship stayed stable.

Log permitted aggregate distributions, schema failures, latency/errors, confidence or score distributions and outcomes when available. Real labels may arrive late or only for selected cases. Preserve that selection context and group-level counts; do not report apparent accuracy from a convenient unrepresentative slice as the whole service's performance.

If 10 of 1,000 baseline requests fail but 40 of 1,000 later requests fail, the failure rate rose from 1% to 4%. That is +3 percentage points and a fourfold rate, not +3%. Explain denominators and time windows. Investigate request mix, data sources, dependencies and resource saturation before automatically retraining. Drift alarms need validation and accountable response rules to avoid alert fatigue.

A **shadow** deployment compares a candidate on copied permitted inputs without affecting decisions; ensure it does not duplicate external side effects. A **canary** routes a limited portion of eligible live traffic to a candidate under a defined allocation policy. Neither is automatically a randomized quality experiment. Maintain an approved prior version, compatible data/schema state and a rollback path; replacing the model file alone may not undo downstream effects.

**Practice.** When an alarm fires, should the pipeline immediately fit on all new requests? **Answer.** No. First validate labels, privacy/consent, source changes and evaluation boundaries. Quarantine suspect data, stop unsafe actions where appropriate, investigate and re-run the agreed regression checks before approving a new version.

These are system-design exercises, not a production service running behind this local application. Use ML16's risk/reporting criteria and R8 for the additional risks of LLM-generated instructions and tool actions. [NIST AI RMF](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework).

## Sources

- [PyTorch training workflow](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/intro.html).
- [CS231n practical neural-network training notes](https://cs231n.github.io/neural-networks-3/).

notes.title: Settings: Microbatch examples, Training epochs, Compute device
notes.markdown:
### Microbatch examples

Examples processed by one forward/backward calculation.

Tensor leading dimension B; final batch may be smaller.

Changes memory, throughput and gradient noise.

Interactions: learning_rate; accumulation; BatchNorm.

Epoch counts are not update counts when batch size changes.

### Training epochs

Planned full passes through the declared fitting dataset.

Without dropping: batches per epoch=ceil(n/B).

More exposure can help or overfit and costs work.

Interactions: batch_size; early_stopping; schedule.

Sampled-window training may not correspond to exact passes; report actual exposures.

### Compute device

Local hardware backend used for tensor operations.

Device placement is separate from dtype and model structure.

May change throughput and numerical behaviour; measure actual work.

Interactions: operator support; dtype; transfer cost.

MPS is not CUDA; do not silently mix backends in a benchmark.

notes.title: Settings: Numeric format, Data-loader workers, Microbatches per update
notes.markdown:
### Numeric format

Representation of model/computation values; initial planned path is FP32.

Raw storage=element_count×bytes_per_value.

Reduced formats can save storage but require separately tested support.

Interactions: device; stable reductions; optimizer state.

Do not expose FP16/BF16 as working options before correctness and backend checks.

### Data-loader workers

Processes helping prepare batches.

Worker count changes input preparation concurrency, not gradient averaging.

Can help input throughput or add startup/memory overhead.

Interactions: Mac spawn semantics; dataset size; memory.

A larger worker count is not automatically faster; begin with 0 for debugging.

### Microbatches per update

Combines gradients across small batches before one optimizer step.

Use the intended valid-example/target-weighted denominator over each window.

Supports a larger effective batch without storing all forward graphs simultaneously.

Interactions: batch_size; scheduler units; gradient_clip.

Final partial windows need the actual denominator; BatchNorm/stochastic layers can break large-batch equivalence.

reading.definition: Training is a repeated procedure: fetch a batch, calculate predictions and loss, compute gradients and update trainable parameters. The data loader, device, optimizer state and checkpoint rules are part of that procedure, not extra neural-network layers. Validation checks a model without fitting on those cases; saving state makes selected results or later resumption possible.
reading.example: We have 32 examples with 16 float32 features each. Change batch size to see input-memory bytes and updates per epoch under one-update-per-batch training. These calculations exclude other memory costs and do not launch a job.
reading.connection: The earlier lessons explain individual model operations. Here we connect them to data movement, training/evaluation modes, gradient clearing, periodic validation and recoverable state.

steps.title: Fetch the next training batch
steps.prose: A data loader selects a batch and applies the declared training-data transformations. Its size controls how many examples are processed together. Multiplying input entries by bytes per value estimates input-tensor storage only, not the total memory needed to train.
steps.terms: A batch is a group of examples. An epoch is one pass over this finite training set; float32 uses four bytes per value.
steps.next: Move the batch and model to compatible devices/types before their forward calculation.

steps.title: Forward calculation and loss
steps.prose: Use the current parameters to compute predictions and compare them with training targets. Training mode can affect dropout and running statistics. Retain the operations needed for differentiation, but do not keep every old computation graph unnecessarily.
steps.terms: Device and numeric type must be compatible. CUDA is an NVIDIA backend; Apple MPS is a different backend, not a CUDA setting.
steps.next: The scalar training objective supplies the backward pass and optimizer update.

steps.title: Backward pass and parameter update
steps.prose: Clear old gradients for an independent batch update, or deliberately accumulate appropriately weighted microbatch contributions. Backward computes derivatives; the optimizer changes parameters and updates its own stored state. The next iteration fetches the next batch without resetting learned weights.
steps.terms: Gradient accumulation changes the update schedule. It does not mean every microbatch should be averaged equally when valid-target counts differ.
steps.next: Continue with the next batch; at chosen intervals, separately evaluate current weights on validation data.

steps.title: Periodic validation and checkpoints
steps.prose: Switch mode appropriately and evaluate separate validation cases without optimizer updates. Use the declared validation rule to choose a checkpoint. For resumption, save optimizer/progress/random/sampler state as needed, not only model weights; then restore training mode before continuing.
steps.terms: A selected inference checkpoint and an exactly resumable training checkpoint have different state requirements.
steps.next: The system notes explain accumulation denominators, device limits, serving and which runtime features are actually implemented.

links: Move this training batch to the compatible model device and compute predictions/loss.
Differentiate the training objective and apply the intended optimizer update.
Fetch the next batch using updated weights and preserved optimizer state.
training
At chosen intervals, evaluate current weights on separate validation data and apply the checkpoint rule.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A training loop changes a model in a controlled sequence. Load a batch, clear or deliberately retain gradient buffers, run the forward computation, calculate the intended scalar loss, backpropagate, and apply one optimizer update. An epoch counts a pass through training data; a step here means an optimizer update. Gradient accumulation can combine several microbatches into one such step.

The system contains more than weights. Adam has moment estimates; the data sampler has a position and random state; a scheduler has progress. A checkpoint for exact continuation needs this state and the compatible model, tokenizer, preprocessing, and data. Saving only weights can support inference without supporting faithful resumption.

Validation should use evaluation behaviour and avoid parameter updates. The local neural and scratch trainers select their best checkpoint using development loss before reporting test performance. Best and last checkpoints can differ: last means most recent, not necessarily best on validation.

Memory holds parameters, gradients, optimizer state, activations, and temporary buffers. Hardware availability does not imply every operation or precision is supported efficiently. The lab probes a small neural forward/backward path when choosing a device; classical scikit-learn fits remain CPU-based. A live loss chart reports saved measurements, not a promise that the next point will fall.

Sources: [PyTorch: saving and loading models](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html), [D2L: parameter management](https://d2l.ai/chapter_builders-guide/parameters.html).

question.prompt: You save only model weights and later want to reproduce the exact next training update from an interrupted Adam run. What is missing from the continuation contract?

options.text: Nothing; weights fully determine the next update for every training setup.
options.feedback: The next data batch, optimizer moments, schedules, and randomness can all affect continuation.

options.text: Only the final test score.
options.feedback: A test score does not restore the training computation or its state.

options.text: A screenshot of the learning curve.
options.feedback: A chart records observations, not optimizer buffers or sampler position.

options.text: Optimizer and scheduler state, random-generator state, data position, and compatible settings as applicable.
options.feedback: These states can change the next gradient or update even when the starting weights match.

question.explanation: An inference weights file and a resumable training checkpoint serve different purposes. Exact continuation needs the relevant state and a tested restoration procedure under stated numerical tolerances.
question.skill: Define a reproducible training checkpoint

question.prompt: You accumulate gradients over two microbatches using per-example mean losses. The first has 6 examples with mean loss 2; the second has 2 examples with mean loss 6. What combined mean matches one batch of all 8 examples?

options.feedback: The weighted mean is (6×2+2×6)/8=24/8=3; each example receives equal weight.
An unweighted average of the two means overweights each example in the smaller microbatch.
Adding batch means does not account for either their sizes or the total example count.
This is the total loss sum over the examples, not the requested per-example mean.

# DL14. Compare neural and classical models

A useful neural-model experiment asks whether it improves a real outcome over a strong classical alternative. Both candidates need the same target definition and held-out evaluation cases. Their preprocessing and fitting procedures may differ, but each must use legitimate training information and a declared selection budget.

The worked comparison uses hypothetical final scores 0.82 and 0.80 to illustrate a difference of 0.02. They are not measured evidence that deep learning wins. The actual lab's saved results keep their own dataset, protocol and configuration information.

The ML capstone defined a complete experiment. This DL capstone applies that plan to a cross-family comparison, including tuning effort, errors, uncertainty and compute cost rather than just architecture labels.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: ML16, DL06, DL13.

## 1. Evidence for a cross-family comparison

**Key terms.** A **matched comparison** controls the intended question; an **inductive bias** is a model's structural preference; a **tuning budget** is allowed selection work; **pretraining exposure** is extra prior data, not free architecture capacity.

**Process.** Choose a shared task/split, freeze preprocessing and evidence rules, tune each model within its allowed budget and save selected configurations. Compare independent outcomes, errors and measured costs, then explain which change the evidence actually supports.

On images, linear classifiers, MLPs and CNNs test different representation assumptions. On tabular data, ridge or boosted trees remain necessary competitors. Comparing only weakly tuned classical methods with an extensively tuned neural network measures more than model family.

Equal parameter counts are not equal training work; equal epochs are not equal updates; equal wall time is not equal hyperparameter exploration. Report these trade-offs instead of claiming one universal fairness definition. Repeat selected conditions across seeds where relevant and use paired independent-unit comparisons. A null or reversed result is informative if the protocol is sound.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** For N training cases, batch size B and E full epochs without dropping cases, optimizer steps per epoch are ceil(N/B) without accumulation. Parameter count, exposure, latency and metric difference are separate measurements.

For 1,000 cases and batch size 64, one full epoch needs 16 batches, with a final batch of 40. Ten epochs give 160 optimizer updates without accumulation. With accumulation 4 and a defined partial-window rule, they give 40 updates; the same epoch count no longer implies the same optimizer schedule. Count actual cases rather than assume 16×64 unique cases.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Comparison budgets and baselines

A prediction-quality study, resource-efficiency study and teaching demonstration deserve different result tables. Scratch and pretrained models need separate exposure labels. Model-size or architecture changes that alter compute should be documented, not hidden by one averaged score.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: report a useful negative result

Run the future digits progression first; only then move to Fashion-MNIST and a tabular contrast. Show confusion matrices, selected examples, measured curves where available, and a compact comparison table. No outcome is predetermined and no new results are claimed by these drafts.

**Check.** If a CNN fails to beat a linear baseline on a small subset, is the project a failure?

**Answer.** No. Check correctness, uncertainty, tuning and sample-size effects, then report the supported limitation. The learning goal is to understand the comparison, not manufacture a deep-learning victory.

## Sources

- [Stanford CS230, Fall 2026 syllabus](https://cs230.stanford.edu/syllabus/).
- [scikit-learn cross-validation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html).
- [CS231n practical neural-network training notes](https://cs231n.github.io/neural-networks-3/).

reading.lesson_markdown:
Choosing a neural model is an empirical decision, not a reward for using a more advanced architecture. A small numerical table may favour a tree ensemble; a spatial image task may benefit from convolution. Compare methods on the same target and held-out cases, while documenting what each fit is allowed to learn.

Start with a baseline, then compare plausible candidates with a declared tuning budget. A linear classifier on scaled features and a neural network on raw features differ in both learner and representation. That may be a useful system comparison, but it does not isolate architecture alone. Decide which question you mean.

For a one-point accuracy gain, inspect changed predictions, sample size, seed variation, cost, and important subgroups. A conditional bootstrap interval over test predictions addresses sample sensitivity for that fitted pair; it does not include every training or search choice. Fit time and inference latency are also measurements with hardware and workload attached.

Save unsuccessful fits and explain what they ruled out. A larger network that increases training accuracy while reducing validation accuracy is evidence about that configuration, not evidence that deep learning fails. Likewise, a neural win on one dataset is not proof of a general ranking. The comparison pages should help answer which fitted system is useful for this task and budget.

Sources: [scikit-learn: statistical comparisons of models](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/auto_examples/model_selection/plot_grid_search_stats.html), [D2L: generalisation in deep learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_multilayer-perceptrons/generalization-deep.html).
