reading.lesson_markdown:
Information extraction turns text into structured records. Entity recognition finds typed mentions; relation extraction links mentions; event extraction identifies an event and its participants. Each extra stage introduces a question about what the source actually states.

In “Mira joined Acme in June,” an entity system may find Mira as a person and Acme as an organisation. A relation could represent employment; an event record could attach a person, organisation, and time to a joining event. The text does not specify Mira's later job title or whether she still works there. A plausible completion would be an unsupported addition.

Choose whether records use mention spans, canonical entities, or both. Two names can refer to one entity, and one name can refer to different entities. Relations may be directed; swapping participants can change the meaning. Define the schema and missing-value policy before evaluating generated JSON.

Measure exact spans, types, participant roles, and source support separately where useful. A schema-valid record can still be wrong. Pipeline errors accumulate, so compare end-to-end records as well as individual stage scores. Preserve source offsets to make every extracted claim inspectable.

Sources: [SLP: information extraction](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/21.pdf), [SLP: coreference and entity linking](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/24.pdf).

# N18. Machine translation and BLEU evaluation

Machine translation produces a target-language sequence intended to preserve a source's meaning. Automatic reference-based metrics compare a candidate with permitted reference translations, but they test different kinds of agreement. BLEU combines clipped n-gram precision with a brevity penalty; the simple example here isolates unigram BLEU-1 rather than implementing standard corpus BLEU.

The reference is 'the cat sat down'. Choose a short candidate, a repeated word or the exact reference. Clipping stops a repeated sat from gaining unlimited credit, and the brevity penalty reduces the score of an otherwise matching short fragment.

Encoder–decoder attention and search explain how a translation may be produced. This lesson asks how to evaluate the resulting text without confusing lexical overlap with preserved meaning or full translation quality.

## 1. Translation objectives and overlap metrics

Translation can use recurrent attention models, encoder–decoders or instructed generative models, but the source/target task must stay fixed. Segmentation, script, morphology, domain terminology and document context all affect what a correct translation means. Teacher forcing and beam search are explained in the sequence-to-sequence lesson rather than repeated here.

BLEU combines clipped n-gram precisions with a brevity penalty. The browser deliberately computes unigram BLEU-1 for transparency; it is not standard four-order corpus BLEU. Corpus BLEU aggregates counts before applying its formula, not by averaging sentence BLEU scores. Smoothing, effective order, reference count and tokenization affect the result.

chrF compares character n-gram overlap; COMET uses a learned evaluation model. A fluent or high-overlap output can still reverse a fact or omit a critical condition.

## 2. Scorer configuration and meaning preservation

Report the SacreBLEU signature or equivalent full configuration, corpus split, reference set, model/tokenizer revision and decoding settings. Learned metrics require their exact checkpoint and input configuration. Reference translations are not the only valid wording.

Inspect meaning preservation, omissions, additions, names, numbers and negation. Human review and targeted challenge sets can expose errors missed by aggregate overlap. Match language pairs and domain before interpreting an apparent improvement. This course does not download a multilingual translation model or claim a measured translation benchmark.

## Sources

[SacreBLEU official implementation](https://github.com/mjpost/sacrebleu) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) · [BLEU](https://aclanthology.org/P02-1040/) · [COMET](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.213/)

Automatic reference-based metrics compare a candidate with permitted reference translations, but they test different kinds of agreement. reading.example: The reference is 'the cat sat down'. Choose a short candidate, a repeated word or the exact reference. Clipping stops a repeated sat from gaining unlimited credit, and the brevity penalty reduces the score of an otherwise matching short fragment.
reading.connection: Encoder–decoder attention and search explain how a translation may be produced. This lesson asks how to evaluate the resulting text without confusing lexical overlap with preserved meaning or full translation quality.

steps.title: Fix the candidate, reference and token units
steps.prose: Use the same tokenizer to count both texts. The worked example uses whitespace-separated words and one reference. A real evaluation must specify tokenization, references and aggregation before comparing scores across systems or language pairs.
steps.terms: A reference is an accepted target wording, not necessarily the only valid translation. BLEU-1 uses unigrams rather than the standard multi-order recipe.
steps.next: Count allowed word matches using reference occurrence limits.

steps.title: Clip repeated word matches
steps.prose: Each candidate occurrence can match only an available occurrence in the reference. Repeating sat therefore cannot create another reference match. Divide the clipped count by candidate length to obtain this unigram precision.
steps.terms: Clipping caps a candidate word's matched count at its reference count. Higher-order n-grams additionally check local word order.
steps.next: Use candidate and reference lengths to penalize omission by an overly short output.

steps.title: Apply the brevity penalty
steps.prose: A short fragment could otherwise obtain precision one by avoiding difficult words. Multiply the unigram precision by the displayed length penalty. Standard corpus BLEU aggregates counts across sentences before scoring rather than averaging these toy sentence values.
steps.terms: In the length penalty c is candidate length and r reference length. BP is at most one; scoring also needs its n-gram, smoothing and aggregation conventions.
steps.next: Check meaning preservation separately and document the real scorer used for any reported benchmark.

steps.title: Audit meaning and report scorer settings
steps.prose: Inspect names, numbers, negation, omissions and added claims. Character-overlap chrF and learned COMET contribute different evidence from BLEU. Neither a fluent output nor one high score guarantees suitability for every translation use.
steps.terms: A scorer signature records configuration. Learned metric versions/checkpoints must also be pinned to interpret a comparison.
steps.next: Question answering next uses span and answer-token matching rather than translation n-gram precision.

links: Count candidate/reference tokens under the fixed tokenizer and clip matches.
Their lengths supply the brevity-penalty calculation.
bypass
Multiply clipped unigram precision by the stated brevity factor.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Translation generates a target-language sequence preserving the source's meaning. Several target sentences may be valid, so exact string equality is often too strict. Encoder–decoder models condition generation on the source while the target decoder uses its permitted prefix.

BLEU counts modified n-gram precision against reference translations, combining different n-gram orders and a brevity penalty. Clipping prevents a repeated candidate word from earning more matched occurrences than the reference allows. The brevity penalty discourages a very short output that matches only easy words.

Corpus BLEU aggregates counts across a corpus; it is not generally the mean of sentence BLEU. Tokenisation, reference choice, smoothing, and implementation affect the number. A candidate with good overlap can still reverse a fact or omit a crucial negation, while a valid paraphrase can lose overlap.

Report the evaluation signature and inspect meaning, names, numbers, and omissions. Learned semantic metrics and human judgements offer additional evidence but also have assumptions and biases. Changing decoding or the reference set is not the same experiment as improving the model under a fixed evaluation protocol.

Sources: [SLP: machine translation](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/13.pdf), [Papineni et al.: BLEU](https://aclanthology.org/P02-1040/).

options.text: All sentence lengths and n-gram counts are always identical.
options.feedback: Real corpora contain differing lengths and count distributions.

options.text: BLEU directly certifies every translation's factual correctness.
options.feedback: Lexical matching does not establish adequacy or all semantic details.

options.text: A learned COMET model makes BLEU's implementation irrelevant to reporting.
options.feedback: Every reported metric still requires its own named configuration and interpretation.

options.text: Its corpus counts and brevity components are aggregated before the final scoring formula.
options.feedback: Different aggregation order generally changes the result, especially for short or uneven examples.

# N19. Question answering, answer spans and abstention

Question answering predicts an answer to a question under a defined information-access setting. An extractive reader chooses a span in supplied context; a generative system may produce new wording. Answer correctness, source support and deciding when no answer is available are separate requirements, with different evaluation rules.

The context tokens are 'The red car stopped .', and the gold answer is red car. Select car, red car or The red car to compare exact answer matching with partial token credit. All span coordinates here use inclusive token ends.

Translation metrics compare generated wording with references. Question answering additionally needs a question, a permissible evidence source and an answerability decision; it must not reuse an unrelated classification or entity-matching score.

## 1. Answer spans, generated answers and missing answers

An extractive reader assigns start/end scores to context positions. A valid decoder enforces start ≤ end, permitted context positions and any maximum answer length. Independently choosing the two highest logits can produce an illegal span. A retrieval step can fail before the reader ever sees useful context.

A generative QA model may return words not present verbatim in a passage. Correctness, answerability and evidence support then require separate tests. An explicit null/abstain decision should be selected using development data and a declared cost/metric, not hidden test labels.

The small diagram uses an exact context-token alignment and three candidate spans. Its answer-token F1 is not classification macro-F1 or entity span F1. A real SQuAD-style evaluator also specifies normalization and multiple-reference handling.

## 2. Exact match, token overlap and source support

Exact match asks whether the normalized answer matches a reference; token-overlap F1 rewards partial matches under that evaluator's tokenizer/normalizer. A partial entity name may receive answer-token credit while failing exact entity extraction. That is a metric definition, not a contradiction.

SQuAD 2 introduces unanswerable questions; closed-book factual QA and source-grounded QA test different information access. Evaluate retrieval recall, reader correctness, abstention and source support separately. A plausible span in a retrieved passage does not establish that the passage answers the actual question. Keep source offsets and truncated-context coverage visible.

## Sources

[SQuAD 2 original paper](https://aclanthology.org/P18-2124/) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

## 1. Answer spans, generated answers and missing answers

An extractive reader assigns start/end scores to context positions. A valid decoder enforces start ≤ end, permitted context positions and any maximum answer length. Independently choosing the two highest logits can produce an illegal span. A retrieval step can fail before the reader ever sees useful context.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Extractive question answering selects a span from a supplied passage. Open-domain QA first has to find a relevant passage; generative QA may produce an answer not present as one contiguous span. These settings provide different evidence and require different failure checks.

A span model scores start and end positions, then chooses a valid span under a stated decoding rule. Independent maximum start and end scores can produce an invalid order, so constraints matter. An unanswerable question should not force an arbitrary extraction.

Exact match checks equality after a defined normalisation. SQuAD token F1 compares token overlap as a multiset: “19 August” versus “August 19” has F1 1 but exact match 0 under its official evaluator. Abstention trades coverage against errors among answered questions. At zero coverage that conditional error is undefined, not zero. Choose an operating threshold on validation data and test it unchanged. A model can remain confidently wrong under domain shift, so confidence-based abstention is not proof that every answered question is supported.

document.markdown:
# N20. Summarization, dialogue and source faithfulness

Summarization selects and compresses source content, either by extracting passages or generating new wording. Source faithfulness asks whether the output preserves what the source supports; external truth asks a different question. Dialogue adds an interaction goal: helping a user may require clarification, correction or abstention rather than simply producing agreeable text.

The supplied source says 'trial improved symptoms'. Replacing improved with worsened leaves two of three reference words unchanged while reversing the main claim. The control reveals why lexical overlap alone cannot certify a faithful summary.

Generation scores and QA matching test limited forms of agreement. This lesson examines their blind spots and connects language-model outputs to source claims and actual interaction usefulness, without treating style as correctness.

## 1. Source faithfulness and summary evaluation

Extractive summarization selects source material; abstractive summarization generates new wording. Compression requires selecting what to omit, while faithfulness requires avoiding unsupported changes. A source-faithful summary may repeat a false source; a true external statement may still be unsupported by the supplied source.

ROUGE variants compare lexical or sequence overlap and use different matching/reduction rules. The example replaces “improved” with “worsened”: two of three unigrams still match even though the direction of the finding reverses. That toy recall is not a full implementation of every ROUGE variant and cannot certify factuality.

Evaluate claims, numbers, entities, scope, uncertainty and omitted qualifications. Do not turn a high overlap score or fluent style into proof that an answer is trustworthy.

## 2. Dialogue usefulness and correction

A dialogue system can manage intent/slots, retrieve a response, generate a response or combine those stages. Multi-turn state should reflect the actual user goal and evidence, not just the most recent wording. A satisfying response can agree with a false premise or avoid challenging an incorrect assumption.

Measure task completion, grounding, correction of false premises and appropriate uncertainty alongside preference judgements. LLM judges can inherit verbosity, order or agreement biases; the shared evaluation lesson covers judge auditing. Reducing unsupported content may require abstention or questions, not simply a longer reasoning trace. Keep evaluation examples independent from prompt iteration.

## Sources

[ROUGE original paper](https://aclanthology.org/W04-1013/) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) · [Evaluation and interpretability](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness)

reading.lesson_markdown:
A summary compresses source information for a purpose. Extractive summaries select source passages; abstractive summaries generate new wording. Fluent new wording can omit a qualification, merge incompatible claims, or introduce an unsupported statement. Readability and faithfulness are separate evaluation targets.

ROUGE measures forms of reference overlap, such as shared n-grams or a longest common subsequence. It is useful for a stated comparison but does not prove factual support. A summary can preserve many reference words while reversing “did not improve” into “improved.” Check claims against the source and consider important omissions as well as additions.

Dialogue adds an interaction history and user goal. A helpful response should advance that goal, respect the user's constraints, and remain supported. Agreement or polite tone alone is not evidence of usefulness. Evaluate complete turns or tasks, not only whether a response sounds confident in isolation.

Keep generation settings, available context, reference policy, and human evaluation instructions explicit. If a system uses a generated summary as an intermediate representation, assess both whether that representation is faithful and whether it improves the final task. A downstream gain does not automatically validate every intermediate statement.

Sources: [Lin: ROUGE](https://aclanthology.org/W04-1013/), [Maynez et al.: faithfulness in abstractive summarisation](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.173/), [SLP: conversation](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/26.pdf).

document.markdown:
# N21. Inference, discourse and argument mining

Language understanding involves more than classifying a sentence in isolation. Natural-language inference compares a premise with a hypothesis; discourse analysis relates text units; argument mining identifies claims, reasons and support or attack relations under a specified scheme. These tasks share language evidence but do not define the same output or universal argument label.

Three authored units have roles claim, premise and other. One toy guideline counts only claims as positive; another counts claims and premises. The same premise therefore changes binary label when the policy changes, even though its text and supplied role stay fixed.

Source faithfulness asks whether a statement is supported; this lesson distinguishes semantic inference, discourse roles and argumentative structure. It also shows why a successful intermediate representation must be tested against the actual target guideline.

## 1. Inference, context and argumentative structure

Natural-language inference distinguishes entailment, contradiction and an unresolved/neutral relation under a specified premise. A contradiction can come from negation, quantification, time or incompatible entities; lexical overlap alone does not identify it. Pragmatics also considers speaker intention and context, which can make irony or indirect requests difficult.

Discourse relations connect units such as reasons, contrasts and elaborations. Argument mining may identify argumentative units, assign claim/premise roles and extract support/attack relations. Those are separate prediction targets. A role label is not automatically a universal binary definition of an argument.

The diagram compares two explicitly declared annotation policies on three authored units. It demonstrates how the same text/role can map to different labels. It does not assert that all real datasets use either of these policies.

## 2. Intermediate representations and target definitions

A generated role, claim or explanation can help a downstream predictor, introduce errors or restate an annotation shortcut. Compare direct text, context/guideline access and structured fields under controlled information and selection budgets.

A role-only rule that works on claim-oriented annotations may fail where premises, conversational implications or other definitions matter. State that scope without dismissing the diagnostic. Evaluate role accuracy, relation quality and the final task separately where gold data permit it. External discussion can motivate a hypothesis; it is not a substitute for a held-out comparison.

## Sources

[Argument mining survey](https://aclanthology.org/J19-4006/) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

reading.lesson_markdown:
Argument mining identifies claims, reasons, and relationships such as support or attack. Discourse analysis also studies how statements connect across a text. The positive label “argument” can mean a standalone claim in one dataset and a claim with explicit justification in another. Define the policy before comparing transfer scores.

“Close the road” states a position. “Close the road because the bridge is unsafe” additionally supplies a reason. Context may reveal the missing justification, but it may also introduce irrelevant evidence. A generated abstraction might expose a claim–reason relation or invent one. These are empirical possibilities, not automatic benefits of structure.

Separate component detection from relation prediction and end-to-end structure recovery. A rule that treats every predicted claim role as a positive label can perform well when the dataset's label is largely claim-based; that does not establish a universal argument-identification rule. Test the mapping against contrasting guidelines and inspect individual disagreements.

For cross-dataset experiments, distinguish text changes, source-domain changes, label-policy changes, and generator changes. A controlled comparison holds the relevant conditions fixed. The central question is which evidence supports the label under this policy, not which representation looks most linguistically elaborate.

Sources: [Lippi and Torroni: argument mining survey and open manuscript](https://cris.unibo.it/handle/11585/523460), [SLP: discourse coherence](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/25.pdf).

# N22. Cross-lingual and cross-domain transfer

Transfer evaluation tests whether a system developed under one condition works under another. Cross-lingual transfer changes language; cross-domain transfer changes the source or content distribution; annotation-policy changes can alter the label meaning itself. These shifts can coexist, so a score drop alone does not explain its own cause.

A two-by-two authored table uses fine-tuning sources as rows and evaluation targets as columns. Selecting source A or B changes the highlighted row. The scores are invented for interpretation practice, not measurements of real languages or named models.

Earlier lessons fixed targets, representations and evaluation units. Transfer now asks which parts remain compatible across conditions, including whether a base multilingual model had already encountered target-language text during pretraining.

## 1. Transfer protocols and types of shift

A cross-lingual experiment may fine-tune on one language and evaluate another, while the base model has already seen both languages during pretraining. That is not zero exposure to the target language. Translate-train, translate-test, multilingual joint training and target-language adaptation are different protocols.

Domain shift changes source/content conditions; annotation-policy shift changes what the label means. Those can coexist, but a score gap alone does not identify which caused it. Report per-language/domain outcomes and relevant data characteristics, not only one grand mean.

The diagram's 2 × 2 source–target score matrix is authored for interpretation practice. Its off-diagonal drops are not empirical claims about English, German or any model. Row and column meaning must remain explicit.

## 2. Low-resource conditions and target adaptation

Consider token coverage, morphology, script, code switching, dialect, annotation availability and community-specific meaning. Character/subword features, adapters, translation and data augmentation each add assumptions and cost. Synthetic labels require review and can preserve a teacher's biases.

Avoid letting translated or near-duplicate versions of one example cross training/test groups. Use a development protocol that matches the intended transfer scenario; tuning on target test labels is adaptation, not untouched transfer. XLM-R and XTREME are useful original references, but neither establishes coverage of every language, task or social context.

## Sources

[XLM-R original paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.747/) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

steps.prose: Diagonal entries evaluate a model on its source condition; off-diagonal entries test another target. Compare per-target values before the row mean. The A-to-B and B-to-A differences need not be symmetric, and a grand average hides that pattern.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Transfer evaluates a model beyond its fitted source distribution. Cross-lingual transfer changes language; cross-domain transfer may change topic, style, population, or annotation policy. A multilingual encoder supplies shared parameters, not a guarantee that these changes are harmless.

A source–target matrix makes the comparison visible: train on each source row, evaluate on each target column. Diagonal entries describe within-dataset performance; off-diagonal entries describe transfer. Keep label mappings and evaluation metrics explicit. A lower off-diagonal score may reflect an altered definition of the target, not merely unfamiliar words.

Leave-one-dataset-out training pools several sources and holds one dataset out. It tests whether evidence from multiple environments helps a new one, but does not make the held-out dataset independent if its results guided feature or prompt choices. Translate-train and translate-test introduce translation quality as another condition.

Inspect tokenisation efficiency, rare labels, named entities, and cultural or stylistic differences. A shared embedding space can align some meanings while leaving task conventions mismatched. Report per-target outcomes rather than allowing a large easy dataset to dominate an average and hide failed transfer.

Sources: [Conneau et al.: XLM-R](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02116), [D2L: distribution shift](https://d2l.ai/chapter_linear-classification/environment-and-distribution-shift.html).

document.markdown:
# N23. Long-document encoding and evidence coverage

A long-document system must specify how distant text can influence a prediction. Chunking encodes local windows and combines their representations; a hierarchical encoder adds a second level; sparse attention changes token-to-token connections within a sequence. These are different information paths, not interchangeable ways of increasing a context-length setting.

Eight token positions are processed in four-token windows. An answer needs positions 3 and 4 together. Overlap two makes that boundary jointly visible while increasing processed positions from eight to twelve; a separate control illustrates local versus global sparse-attention connections.

The earlier sequence encoders assumed the relevant input was accessible. Long documents expose a new failure: evidence can be lost at truncation or window boundaries before an otherwise capable model can combine it.

## 1. Chunking, hierarchy and sparse attention

Chunking fits local windows into an encoder, then aggregates their outputs. A hierarchical model can encode tokens into sentence vectors and sentences into document features. Mean pooling, attention pooling and a recurrent second level preserve different information. A bag of chunk vectors does not automatically know the order or cross-chunk relations.

Overlapping windows can preserve a span crossing one boundary but duplicate token exposure and computation. The example counts both eight unique tokens and twelve processed positions when four-token windows overlap by two. That distinction matters for fair comparisons and aggregation weights.

Sparse attention changes which token pairs can interact. A local window limits direct reach; designated global tokens add paths. It is not the same operation as independently encoding chunks and averaging them.

## 2. Evidence boundaries and fair comparison

For classification, some evidence may be local while the decision is document-wide. For extraction, a gold span crossing a hard window boundary can become unrecoverable unless windows overlap or another mechanism connects them. For retrieval, a good chunk may omit the document qualification needed to interpret it.

Longformer-style local/global attention, hierarchical encoders and retrieval-assisted reading are alternative designs, not free extensions to a model's trained context length. Match truncation, evidence access, number of windows and token budget. The diagram computes masks/coverage only; it does not execute a pretrained long-context encoder or claim end-to-end quality gains.

## Sources

[Longformer original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05150) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

steps.title: Locate the evidence the task requires
steps.prose: The example needs positions three and four together. A model that sees only the first four positions cannot recover that relationship from this truncated input. Decide whether the task needs a local span, several distant facts or a whole-document summary.
steps.terms: Evidence coverage means the required text is accessible through the chosen input path. It does not establish that a model understands that evidence.
steps.next: For a chunking design, construct windows and account for repeated processing.
steps.node: Locate the evidence the task requires

steps.title: Build windows and count repeated exposure
steps.prose: Window stride is width minus overlap. With width four, overlap two creates three windows over eight unique positions. Twelve processed positions count repeated appearances, not twelve distinct tokens or additional training examples.
steps.terms: Overlap repeats positions across adjacent windows. Independent encodings do not share hidden state unless a separate mechanism connects them.
steps.next: Check whether any valid window contains all positions required by the example.
steps.node: Build windows and count repeated exposure

steps.title: Check span coverage across boundaries
steps.prose: Without overlap, no window contains both positions three and four. With overlap two, the middle window does. This repairs this particular accessibility problem at extra computation, but says nothing yet about prediction quality.
steps.terms: A coverage test is a structural check before model evaluation. A longer answer or distant relation may require more than this local repair.
steps.next: Sparse attention offers a separate alternative; compare its connectivity rather than placing it after chunking as another step.

steps.title: Compare local and global attention paths
steps.prose: The mask selects allowed query–key pairs in one sequence. Local connections limit direct access; a global token connects to all positions in this illustration. This differs from encoding separate chunks, and pair counts are not measured runtime or quality.
steps.terms: Sparse attention changes the computation graph. A_ij indicates whether query position i may read key position j; a global token adds permitted connections.
steps.next: Choose an aggregation method explicitly if the design instead produces several chunk or sentence vectors.
steps.node: Compare local and global attention paths

steps.title: Combine representations for the required output
steps.prose: A hierarchical design can encode tokens into sentence or chunk vectors and then combine them. Mean pooling discards order; ordered or attention-based second levels add other assumptions. Record truncation, overlap and aggregation before comparing systems.
steps.terms: A hierarchical encoder adds representation levels. Increasing a configured input limit does not prove trained long-context capability.
steps.next: The final NLP lesson assembles task definitions, matched metrics and reproducible artifacts into a complete study.
steps.node: Combine representations for the required output

reading.lesson_markdown:
A model's context limit bounds what it can read at once. Truncation may discard the only sentence answering a question. Increasing the context window changes capacity to include evidence, but does not guarantee that the model will use it correctly.

Sliding windows encode overlapping pieces. A length-100 document with window 40 and stride 30 yields starts at 0, 30, and 60 under a suitable end policy; overlap preserves some boundary context but repeats content. A hierarchical model first represents chunks, then combines chunk representations. Sparse-attention architectures restrict communication patterns to reduce cost, sometimes adding global positions.

Define how predictions from multiple windows are combined and how offsets map back to the original text. Double-counting overlapping tokens can distort loss or evaluation. A document-level label attached to every chunk can also create noisy supervision when only one chunk contains the needed evidence.

Measure evidence coverage alongside downstream accuracy: was the required passage available, retained, and used? Distinguish a retrieval miss from a reader failure. The long-document worked view illustrates coverage, not a claim that a local sparse-attention model was trained by the application.

Sources: [Longformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05150), [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172).

document.markdown:
# N24. NLP evaluation and a complete study

An NLP evaluation counts matches between predicted and reference objects under a declared task rule. Token tags, complete entity spans, answer tokens and generated sequences are different objects, even when some metrics share a familiar name. A complete study also records preprocessing, model selection, source groups and failures so the result can be interpreted and reproduced.

Two gold entities and two predicted entities have one exact span-and-type match, giving one correct match, one false positive and one false negative. A separate six-token example has five correct tags. The scores differ because the evaluated objects differ.

The task lessons introduced distinct outputs and error sources. This final lesson connects them to the shared metric formulas and an executable research workflow without inventing one universal NLP accuracy.

## 1. Task-specific matching and metric units

For exact NER evaluation, both the entity span and type must match under a declared scheme/scorer. A wrong boundary can produce one false positive and one false negative even if most token labels are correct. POS token accuracy, NER entity F1 and QA answer-token F1 evaluate different objects.

The authored example has two gold entities and two predictions, only one of which exactly matches: precision=recall=F1=0.5. A separately defined six-token labelling example has five correct tags, or 0.8333 token accuracy. These are not alternative calculations of the same metric. Use the right record-level matcher before invoking a shared count formula.

For generation, BLEU/chrF/ROUGE, semantic similarity and human/learned factuality checks add different evidence. Their scores must not be mixed into one unexplained universal accuracy.

## 2. Reproducible NLP studies and practice routes

Build one source-grouped text-classification study: lexical baseline, masked sentence-vector classifier and an optional fine-tuned encoder, keeping splits and selection budgets explicit. Then build a separate token/span study so pooling and sequence decoding are not confused. Record data/model licenses, revision IDs, seeds, preprocessing, label policies and per-case outputs.

Use scikit-learn for sparse pipelines; PyTorch for sequence tensors/packing; spaCy or NLTK for linguistic processing; Transformers/Tokenizers/Datasets for pinned encoders and data alignment; Sentence Transformers for pooling and retrieval; seqeval and SacreBLEU for task-specific scoring. These links describe an implementation route, not libraries automatically installed or new web trainers. Verify dataset access/licences and dependencies before downloading anything.

Inspect important slices and valid counterfactuals, report conditional uncertainty with appropriate groups, and distinguish development exploration from final checking. Dataset/model cards document intended use and limitations; they are not safety certificates.

### Data routes for progressively harder exercises

| Task | First-party route | What to preserve or inspect |

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

]

```

## 1. Task-specific matching and metric units

For exact NER evaluation, both the entity span and type must match under a declared scheme/scorer. A wrong boundary can produce one false positive and one false negative even if most token labels are correct. POS token accuracy, NER entity F1 and QA answer-token F1 evaluate different objects.

Use the right record-level matcher before invoking a shared count formula.

For generation, BLEU/chrF/ROUGE, semantic similarity and human/learned factuality checks add different evidence. Their scores must not be mixed into one unexplained universal accuracy.

reading.lesson_markdown:
An NLP study should connect its annotation policy, representation, training objective, and reported output metric. Token accuracy, exact entity F1, retrieval recall, and summary faithfulness count different things. A complete report names the unit, the split, and the model-selection process before interpreting the score.

For two gold entities, predicting one exact typed span and one wrong span gives one True Positive, one False Positive, and one False Negative: precision and recall are both 0.5. A token-level metric can give a different impression because many non-entity tokens are easy. Show a concrete error, not only a leaderboard.

Behavioural testing complements a representative held-out sample. CheckList-style tests ask whether capabilities such as negation handling or name invariance behave as intended. They are test suites, but do not automatically estimate performance on a naturally sampled deployment population. A successful template test also does not prove the broader capability is solved.

Keep a baseline, meaningful ablations, uncertainty with the right independent unit, and evidence for generated intermediate records. Save prompts, preprocessing, data versions, and evaluation scripts. When a result fails to transfer, narrow the conclusion rather than hiding the target. That is a scientific outcome, not a reason to replace the metric after seeing the answer.

Sources: [Ribeiro et al.: CheckList](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.442/), [scikit-learn: evaluation metrics](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/model_evaluation.html).

# T0. The language-model training loop

Training changes a language model's parameters using examples. A batch supplies input tokens and known targets; the model predicts, a loss measures mistakes, backpropagation computes gradients and an optimizer updates the parameters. Validation and generation use the model differently: they do not apply these training updates.

A sequence [3,7,2,9] supplies inputs [3,7,2] and next-token targets [7,2,9]. One supplied target probability illustrates loss, while a separate scalar gradient illustrates an update. They explain the stages but are not one fully differentiated numerical model.

The foundations and DL course introduced loss, gradients and updates. This lesson assembles them for token sequences, keeping the repeated training path separate from periodic validation, checkpoint selection and fixed-weight use.

## 1. Training, validation and generation

**Key terms.** A **batch** is a group of training examples; **weights** are learned numbers; an **update** changes them; **validation** checks separate examples without updates.

**Process.** Preparation produces batches and starting weights. Training repeats prediction, loss, gradients and updates; periodic validation selects a saved checkpoint. Generation then uses that checkpoint without the training loop.

There are three parts: prepare once, repeat training, then check/save/use. They are connected but are not the same loop.

```text
Prepare: sources → clean and split → tokenizer → batches → initial weights

Repeat:  batch → predictions → loss → gradients → optimizer update
            ↑                                      |
            +--------------- next batch ------------+

Check:   validation text → measure without updates → choose checkpoint
Use:     chosen checkpoint → prompt → generate → inspect the output
```

A batch supplies many next-token targets. After enough batches the program checks progress, saves state and continues if the planned budget allows it. Validation is periodic, not necessarily after every update.

## 2. Text preparation

**Key terms.** A **corpus** is a collection of text; a **split** assigns independent sources to training, development or test; a **tokenizer** converts text to IDs.

**Process.** Choose permitted sources, clean and split them, then fit a tokenizer only on training text or reuse the pretrained model's tokenizer. The output is compatible token sequences for building batches.

Choose permitted text that suits the goal. A story model needs many varied stories; 24 repeated teaching paragraphs are not a substitute. Remove broken documents and obvious duplicates, then assign whole documents or related groups to training, validation and test splits.

Training supplies weight updates. Validation, also called development text, helps choose settings/checkpoints. Test is the final reserved check. If we keep changing the design after seeing test, it is no longer independent.

A tokenizer turns text into pieces and gives each piece a number. Fit a new tokenizer on training text only. A pretrained model instead needs its compatible existing tokenizer: changing IDs without changing their learned meanings breaks that compatibility.

## 3. Inputs and next-token targets

**Key terms.** A **target** is the answer to predict; a **causal mask** blocks future input; a **loss mask** excludes positions from scoring.

**Process.** Take a token sequence and align each input position with its next token. Mask forbidden attention and unscored targets, then send the aligned inputs to the model and targets to the loss.

```text
Original: <start> The cat sat <end>
Input:    <start> The cat sat
Target:   The     cat sat <end>
```

The target at each position is the next piece. That is where labels come from; someone does not label every word by hand. Some libraries shift internally, so our code must not shift twice.

Training processes many positions together. A causal attention mask still blocks future input: when predicting `cat`, the model cannot read it from a future position. A separate loss mask decides which targets count towards the grade. Padding is ignored. In our conversation adapter, the prompt provides context but only response targets contribute to loss.

## 4. Forward pass

**Key terms.** An **embedding** maps an ID to a vector; **attention** mixes allowed positions; an **MLP** transforms features; a **logit** is a raw vocabulary score.

**Process.** Token IDs become vectors, Transformer blocks transform those vectors, and the output layer produces vocabulary scores. These forward calculations precede loss and do not themselves update weights.

IDs select learned vectors, called embeddings. Position information represents order. Transformer blocks mix permitted earlier information through attention and transform it through feed-forward networks. Residual connections carry earlier information around a sublayer; normalization controls the scale of intermediate values.

The final layer produces a raw score for each vocabulary token: a logit. Softmax turns logits into probabilities summing to one. This is the forward pass. Predictions exist, but weights have not changed yet.

## 5. Cross-entropy loss

**Key terms.** **Cross-entropy loss** is the negative log probability of the correct target; a **nat** uses the natural logarithm; **N** counts scored targets; **pᵢ** is each correct-target probability.

**Process.** Combine vocabulary scores with the known targets, calculate a penalty at each included position and average those penalties. This scalar loss is the starting point for the backward calculation.

If the correct token gets probability 0.5, its penalty is about 0.693 nats. At probability 0.1, the penalty is about 2.303. Average over valid target tokens, not padding.

\[
L=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_i
\]

`N` is the included target count; `p_i` is the probability of correct target `i`. A nat is the unit from a natural logarithm. Lower loss means better prediction on that text/tokenization, not automatic truthfulness or useful conversation.

## 6. Backpropagation

**Key terms.** A **gradient** is a loss derivative; **backpropagation** applies the chain rule backwards; **sigmoid** maps a scalar score to a probability between 0 and 1.

**Process.** Start from the scalar loss and follow recorded operations backwards to each trainable parameter. The result is a set of gradients waiting for an optimizer, not a new set of weights.

Backpropagation follows the calculation backwards to find how a small change in each trainable weight would locally affect loss. These derivatives are gradients. They describe an adjustment direction; they are not updated weights yet.

As a separate numerical check, let a two-choice model use probability `sigmoid(w)` for a correct target of 1. At scalar weight zero the probability is 0.5 and the cross-entropy gradient is −0.5. Increasing that weight would locally reduce this loss. A real LLM has many interacting weights, with gradients through the complete computation.

## 7. Accumulation and optimizer updates

**Key terms.** A **microbatch** fits one forward/backward pass; **accumulation** combines gradients; **clipping** limits their overall length, called the gradient norm; **η** denotes learning rate; **g** denotes gradient.

**Process.** Accumulate correctly weighted microbatch gradients, unscale if needed, clip if configured, then apply one optimizer step. Clear gradients at the declared boundary before collecting the next update's evidence.

A microbatch is a small group that fits in memory. Gradient accumulation combines several microbatches before one optimizer update. It does not apply an update after each small batch.

With 10 valid targets in one microbatch and 90 in another, a token-average objective weights their mean losses by 0.1 and 0.9, not half each. The denominator matters. Gradient clipping can then reduce an excessively large overall gradient norm; it does not normally clip every weight separately.

The simple SGD update is:

\[
w_{\text{new}}=w-\eta g
\]

`w` is the learned number, `g` its gradient and `η` the learning rate. Weight 0, gradient −0.5 and rate 0.2 give new weight 0.1. In the two-choice example, correct-token probability becomes about 0.525 and loss falls from 0.693 to 0.644. This checked calculation is not a promise that every large-model update improves validation. AdamW also uses running statistics and weight decay rather than this bare SGD rule.

Clear gradients at the appropriate boundary so unrelated updates do not accidentally accumulate. Advance the schedule in its declared units, fetch another batch and repeat. An update is not an epoch: an epoch is a pass over a dataset, whereas our sampler can practise examples repeatedly.

### Check the complete update boundary

Before calling an experiment reproducible, trace one update with these checks:

1. Save the exact input IDs, target IDs and scoring mask of a small non-sensitive test batch. Count valid targets after shifting.
2. Compute a summed cross-entropy and divide by the intended update's target count. A response-only objective and an all-token objective are different even with the same input text.
3. Confirm that expected trainable parameters have finite gradients, frozen parameters stay frozen, and no training graph is retained accidentally in logging.
4. Apply one optimizer update and verify that the expected weights changed. Record learning rate and gradient norm, with an explicit before/after-clipping convention.
5. Restore a complete checkpoint and compare the next few CPU updates against uninterrupted training. Approximate continuation and identical replay are different acceptance criteria.

The saved-run inspector's optional scratch update is a separate diagnostic: it uses its own short text batch and SGD, not the original run's optimizer state. Do not treat it as a replay of the training trajectory. For implementation details, consult [PyTorch autograd](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/notes/autograd.html) and [checkpoint restoration](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

## 8. Validation and checkpoints

**Key terms.** **Evaluation mode** changes behaviours such as dropout; **no-grad mode** stops recording derivative history; a **checkpoint** saves model state.

**Process.** Pause training updates, measure separate validation text and choose whether to save the current state. Resume training only afterwards; validation results select checkpoints but supply no training gradient.

Periodically use separate validation text in evaluation mode, with gradient recording disabled. Dropout is off in evaluation mode. There is no backward pass or optimizer update. Validation helps choose a checkpoint, not the training gradient.

Training loss can fall while validation rises. That can indicate overfitting, although noisy checks, data changes and evaluation mistakes also matter. The lab's saved-run curves show recorded observations; the teaching process diagram is not a measured validation curve.

A checkpoint saves weights. Proper training resume also needs optimizer/schedule position, random/sampler state and compatible data/configuration. Our scratch path supports this continuation. The adapter path saves selected/final adapters but does not yet promise resumable optimizer state.

## 9. Generation with saved weights

**Key terms.** A **prompt** is starting text; **decoding** selects tokens from predicted probabilities; a **stop rule** ends generation.

**Process.** Load a chosen checkpoint, process the prompt, choose and append a token, then predict again. Generated tokens become the next inputs; no correct future targets or optimizer steps are supplied.

Process a prompt, choose a next token, append it and repeat until an end token or length limit. No weights change. Temperature and top-k affect selection, not learned knowledge. A story-completion model is not automatically an instruction-following assistant.

Training has known targets and uses gradients. Generation does not receive the true future answer and normally performs no backward pass. Inspect unedited outputs as well as loss: our adapter example became wrong about melting despite a better average loss.

## 10. Scratch training versus adaptation

**Key terms.** **Scratch training** starts from random weights; **adaptation** starts from pretrained weights; an **adapter** is a small trainable addition to a frozen base.

**Process.** Choose the learning goal before the training path. That choice determines the starting knowledge and updated parameters; evaluate success against the same starting point rather than comparing unlike training budgets.

| Path | Starting weights | Updated weights | Intended success |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scratch mechanics | Random | All weights | Correct, inspectable masking, gradients and controlled tests |
| Current language adapter | Pretrained SmolLM2 | Small LoRA matrices | Audited change against that same starting model |
| Proposed story model | Random | All weights of a roughly 14M decoder | Held-out prediction gains plus coherent completions on fixed new story beginnings |

The story model is a proposed next run, not trained already. It needs a tokenizer/corpus pipeline, throughput benchmark and approved budget. More parameters on the same tiny fixture would not supply missing language exposure.

## Quick checks

1. Does a forward pass change weights? No: it makes predictions.
2. Does backward apply the update? No: it computes gradients; the optimizer updates.
3. Does validation call the optimizer? No: that would train on the check.
4. Is lower training loss enough? No: check held-out prediction and intended behaviour.
5. Is adapting pretrained weights equivalent to learning from random weights? No: starting knowledge and compute requirements differ.

References: [PyTorch optimization](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/optimization_tutorial.html), [TinyStories paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07759), [TinyStories data/license](https://huggingface.co/datasets/roneneldan/TinyStories).

## 1. Training, validation and generation

**Key terms.** A **batch** is a group of training examples; **weights** are learned numbers; an **update** changes them; **validation** checks separate examples without updates.

**Process.** Preparation produces batches and starting weights. Training repeats prediction, loss, gradients and updates; periodic validation selects a saved checkpoint. Generation then uses that checkpoint without the training loop.

There are three parts: prepare once, repeat training, then check/save/use. They are connected but are not the same loop.

```text
Prepare: sources → clean and split → tokenizer → batches → initial weights

Repeat:  batch → predictions → loss → gradients → optimizer update
            ↑                                      |
            +--------------- next batch ------------+

Check:   validation text → measure without updates → choose checkpoint
Use:     chosen checkpoint → prompt → generate → inspect the output
```

A batch supplies many next-token targets. After enough batches the program checks progress, saves state and continues if the planned budget allows it. Validation is periodic, not necessarily after every update.

sections.title: Text preparation
sections.markdown:
## 2. Text preparation

**Key terms.** A **corpus** is a collection of text; a **split** assigns independent sources to training, development or test; a **tokenizer** converts text to IDs.

**Process.** Choose permitted sources, clean and split them, then fit a tokenizer only on training text or reuse the pretrained model's tokenizer. The output is compatible token sequences for building batches.

Choose permitted text that suits the goal. A story model needs many varied stories; 24 repeated teaching paragraphs are not a substitute. Remove broken documents and obvious duplicates, then assign whole documents or related groups to training, validation and test splits.

Training supplies weight updates. Validation, also called development text, helps choose settings/checkpoints. Test is the final reserved check. If we keep changing the design after seeing test, it is no longer independent.

A tokenizer turns text into pieces and gives each piece a number. Fit a new tokenizer on training text only. A pretrained model instead needs its compatible existing tokenizer: changing IDs without changing their learned meanings breaks that compatibility.

sections.title: Inputs and next-token targets
sections.markdown:
## 3. Inputs and next-token targets

**Key terms.** A **target** is the answer to predict; a **causal mask** blocks future input; a **loss mask** excludes positions from scoring.

**Process.** Take a token sequence and align each input position with its next token. Mask forbidden attention and unscored targets, then send the aligned inputs to the model and targets to the loss.

```text
Original: <start> The cat sat <end>
Input:    <start> The cat sat
Target:   The     cat sat <end>
```

The target at each position is the next piece. That is where labels come from; someone does not label every word by hand. Some libraries shift internally, so our code must not shift twice.

Training processes many positions together. A causal attention mask still blocks future input: when predicting `cat`, the model cannot read it from a future position. A separate loss mask decides which targets count towards the grade. Padding is ignored. In our conversation adapter, the prompt provides context but only response targets contribute to loss.

sections.title: Forward pass
sections.markdown:
## 4. Forward pass

**Key terms.** An **embedding** maps an ID to a vector; **attention** mixes allowed positions; an **MLP** transforms features; a **logit** is a raw vocabulary score.

**Process.** Token IDs become vectors, Transformer blocks transform those vectors, and the output layer produces vocabulary scores. These forward calculations precede loss and do not themselves update weights.

IDs select learned vectors, called embeddings. Position information represents order. Transformer blocks mix permitted earlier information through attention and transform it through feed-forward networks. Residual connections carry earlier information around a sublayer; normalization controls the scale of intermediate values.

The final layer produces a raw score for each vocabulary token: a logit. Softmax turns logits into probabilities summing to one. This is the forward pass. Predictions exist, but weights have not changed yet.

sections.title: Cross-entropy loss
sections.markdown:
## 5. Cross-entropy loss

**Key terms.** **Cross-entropy loss** is the negative log probability of the correct target; a **nat** uses the natural logarithm; **N** counts scored targets; **pᵢ** is each correct-target probability.

**Process.** Combine vocabulary scores with the known targets, calculate a penalty at each included position and average those penalties. This scalar loss is the starting point for the backward calculation.

If the correct token gets probability 0.5, its penalty is about 0.693 nats. At probability 0.1, the penalty is about 2.303. Average over valid target tokens, not padding.

\[
L=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_i
\]

`N` is the included target count; `p_i` is the probability of correct target `i`. A nat is the unit from a natural logarithm. Lower loss means better prediction on that text/tokenization, not automatic truthfulness or useful conversation.

sections.title: Backpropagation
sections.markdown:
## 6. Backpropagation

**Key terms.** A **gradient** is a loss derivative; **backpropagation** applies the chain rule backwards; **sigmoid** maps a scalar score to a probability between 0 and 1.

**Process.** Start from the scalar loss and follow recorded operations backwards to each trainable parameter. The result is a set of gradients waiting for an optimizer, not a new set of weights.

Backpropagation follows the calculation backwards to find how a small change in each trainable weight would locally affect loss. These derivatives are gradients. They describe an adjustment direction; they are not updated weights yet.

As a separate numerical check, let a two-choice model use probability `sigmoid(w)` for a correct target of 1. At scalar weight zero the probability is 0.5 and the cross-entropy gradient is −0.5. Increasing that weight would locally reduce this loss. A real LLM has many interacting weights, with gradients through the complete computation.

sections.title: Accumulation and optimizer updates
sections.markdown:
## 7. Accumulation and optimizer updates

**Key terms.** A **microbatch** fits one forward/backward pass; **accumulation** combines gradients; **clipping** limits their overall length, called the gradient norm; **η** denotes learning rate; **g** denotes gradient.

**Process.** Accumulate correctly weighted microbatch gradients, unscale if needed, clip if configured, then apply one optimizer step. Clear gradients at the declared boundary before collecting the next update's evidence.

A microbatch is a small group that fits in memory. Gradient accumulation combines several microbatches before one optimizer update. It does not apply an update after each small batch.

With 10 valid targets in one microbatch and 90 in another, a token-average objective weights their mean losses by 0.1 and 0.9, not half each. The denominator matters. Gradient clipping can then reduce an excessively large overall gradient norm; it does not normally clip every weight separately.

The simple SGD update is:

\[
w_{\text{new}}=w-\eta g
\]

`w` is the learned number, `g` its gradient and `η` the learning rate. Weight 0, gradient −0.5 and rate 0.2 give new weight 0.1. In the two-choice example, correct-token probability becomes about 0.525 and loss falls from 0.693 to 0.644. This checked calculation is not a promise that every large-model update improves validation. AdamW also uses running statistics and weight decay rather than this bare SGD rule.

Clear gradients at the appropriate boundary so unrelated updates do not accidentally accumulate. Advance the schedule in its declared units, fetch another batch and repeat. An update is not an epoch: an epoch is a pass over a dataset, whereas our sampler can practise examples repeatedly.

### Check the complete update boundary

Before calling an experiment reproducible, trace one update with these checks:

1. Save the exact input IDs, target IDs and scoring mask of a small non-sensitive test batch. Count valid targets after shifting.
2. Compute a summed cross-entropy and divide by the intended update's target count. A response-only objective and an all-token objective are different even with the same input text.
3. Confirm that expected trainable parameters have finite gradients, frozen parameters stay frozen, and no training graph is retained accidentally in logging.
4. Apply one optimizer update and verify that the expected weights changed. Record learning rate and gradient norm, with an explicit before/after-clipping convention.
5. Restore a complete checkpoint and compare the next few CPU updates against uninterrupted training. Approximate continuation and identical replay are different acceptance criteria.

The saved-run inspector's optional scratch update is a separate diagnostic: it uses its own short text batch and SGD, not the original run's optimizer state. Do not treat it as a replay of the training trajectory. For implementation details, consult [PyTorch autograd](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/notes/autograd.html) and [checkpoint restoration](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

sections.title: Validation and checkpoints
sections.markdown:
## 8. Validation and checkpoints

**Key terms.** **Evaluation mode** changes behaviours such as dropout; **no-grad mode** stops recording derivative history; a **checkpoint** saves model state.

**Process.** Pause training updates, measure separate validation text and choose whether to save the current state. Resume training only afterwards; validation results select checkpoints but supply no training gradient.

Periodically use separate validation text in evaluation mode, with gradient recording disabled. Dropout is off in evaluation mode. There is no backward pass or optimizer update. Validation helps choose a checkpoint, not the training gradient.

Training loss can fall while validation rises. That can indicate overfitting, although noisy checks, data changes and evaluation mistakes also matter. The lab's saved-run curves show recorded observations; the teaching process diagram is not a measured validation curve.

A checkpoint saves weights. Proper training resume also needs optimizer/schedule position, random/sampler state and compatible data/configuration. Our scratch path supports this continuation. The adapter path saves selected/final adapters but does not yet promise resumable optimizer state.

sections.title: Generation with saved weights
sections.markdown:
## 9. Generation with saved weights

**Key terms.** A **prompt** is starting text; **decoding** selects tokens from predicted probabilities; a **stop rule** ends generation.

**Process.** Load a chosen checkpoint, process the prompt, choose and append a token, then predict again. Generated tokens become the next inputs; no correct future targets or optimizer steps are supplied.

Process a prompt, choose a next token, append it and repeat until an end token or length limit. No weights change. Temperature and top-k affect selection, not learned knowledge. A story-completion model is not automatically an instruction-following assistant.

Training has known targets and uses gradients. Generation does not receive the true future answer and normally performs no backward pass. Inspect unedited outputs as well as loss: our adapter example became wrong about melting despite a better average loss.

sections.title: Scratch training versus adaptation
sections.markdown:
## 10. Scratch training versus adaptation

**Key terms.** **Scratch training** starts from random weights; **adaptation** starts from pretrained weights; an **adapter** is a small trainable addition to a frozen base.

**Process.** Choose the learning goal before the training path. That choice determines the starting knowledge and updated parameters; evaluate success against the same starting point rather than comparing unlike training budgets.

| Path | Starting weights | Updated weights | Intended success |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scratch mechanics | Random | All weights | Correct, inspectable masking, gradients and controlled tests |
| Current language adapter | Pretrained SmolLM2 | Small LoRA matrices | Audited change against that same starting model |
| Proposed story model | Random | All weights of a roughly 14M decoder | Held-out prediction gains plus coherent completions on fixed new story beginnings |

The story model is a proposed next run, not trained already. It needs a tokenizer/corpus pipeline, throughput benchmark and approved budget. More parameters on the same tiny fixture would not supply missing language exposure.

sections.title: Quick checks
sections.markdown:
## Quick checks

1. Does a forward pass change weights? No: it makes predictions.
2. Does backward apply the update? No: it computes gradients; the optimizer updates.
3. Does validation call the optimizer? No: that would train on the check.
4. Is lower training loss enough? No: check held-out prediction and intended behaviour.
5. Is adapting pretrained weights equivalent to learning from random weights? No: starting knowledge and compute requirements differ.

References: [PyTorch optimization](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/optimization_tutorial.html), [TinyStories paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07759), [TinyStories data/license](https://huggingface.co/datasets/roneneldan/TinyStories).

reading.title: The language-model training loop
reading.definition: Training changes a language model's parameters using examples. A batch supplies input tokens and known targets; the model predicts, a loss measures mistakes, backpropagation computes gradients and an optimizer updates the parameters. Validation and generation use the model differently: they do not apply these training updates.
reading.example: A sequence [3,7,2,9] supplies inputs [3,7,2] and next-token targets [7,2,9]. One supplied target probability illustrates loss, while a separate scalar gradient illustrates an update. They explain the stages but are not one fully differentiated numerical model.
reading.connection: The foundations and DL course introduced loss, gradients and updates. This lesson assembles them for token sequences, keeping the repeated training path separate from periodic validation, checkpoint selection and fixed-weight use.

steps.title: Prepare inputs, targets and masks
steps.prose: Use training-only text and a compatible tokenizer to construct a batch. Shift tokens once so each input position predicts its successor. Define visibility and target masks before the forward pass; document and conversation boundaries affect what can be learned.
steps.terms: B counts batch examples and T prediction positions. A causal mask controls access to future positions; a loss mask selects targets that contribute to the objective.
steps.next: Run the current model on these permitted inputs without changing its parameters yet.

steps.title: Calculate predictions with current parameters
steps.prose: The forward pass maps input IDs through embeddings and model layers to vocabulary logits. Softmax defines a distribution for each scored position. The supplied probability 0.5 is an illustration, not the measured output of the scalar update below.
steps.terms: A logit is an unnormalized vocabulary score. Parameters define the predictor; computing predictions is not itself an optimizer update.
steps.next: Compare the assigned target probabilities with the known labels to obtain a scalar loss.

steps.title: Calculate loss over valid targets
steps.prose: Take the negative log-probability of each included correct token, then reduce under the intended convention. Here one target with probability 0.5 gives log two. Padding and unscored prompt positions must not enter the denominator accidentally.
steps.terms: In the equation m_t selects targets, p_t(y_t) is the correct-token probability and the mask sum counts valid targets. Natural logs give nats.
steps.next: Differentiate the declared loss through the recorded computation to obtain parameter gradients.

steps.title: Compute gradients by backpropagation
steps.prose: Backpropagation follows the chain rule to measure how changing each trainable parameter would change the loss locally. It writes gradients, not new weights. The next stage's scalar gradient 2 is supplied separately to explain an optimizer.
steps.terms: Theta denotes trainable parameters; nabla L is their gradient. A gradient's sign and magnitude are not a certainty estimate about an answer.
steps.next: Pass the gradients to an optimizer under the chosen accumulation and clipping rules.

steps.title: Apply one optimizer update and repeat
steps.prose: The scalar illustration changes weight 1 using gradient 2 and the selected learning rate. A real AdamW update also uses optimizer history and decay rules. Clear gradients at the correct boundary, fetch another batch and repeat under the budget.
steps.terms: Eta is learning rate and g a gradient. An optimizer step can combine several microbatches; it is not necessarily one pass over the dataset.
steps.next: Continue with the next batch; at scheduled intervals, evaluate separate validation text without updates.

steps.title: Evaluate periodically on validation text
steps.prose: Pause updates, use the intended evaluation mode and disable derivative recording. The hypothetical losses [1.2,1.0,1.1] select checkpoint two. Validation supports selection; feeding its gradients into the optimizer would change the experiment.
steps.terms: Evaluation mode controls behaviors such as dropout. No-grad controls derivative recording. Development evidence is not the untouched final test.
steps.next: Save selected weights or complete restart state according to the checkpoint's purpose.

steps.title: Save state for selection, resumption or use
steps.prose: A weights export supports inference only with compatible configuration and tokenizer. Exact continuation additionally needs optimizer, scheduler, random and sampler state as appropriate. Generation loads fixed parameters and appends chosen tokens instead of receiving known future targets.
steps.terms: A checkpoint's contents determine its supported use. Selecting a checkpoint, resuming training and generating from it are different actions.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Language-model training repeatedly asks the network to predict known tokens, measures their probability, and changes weights to reduce an objective. The text supplies the targets. Generating a continuation is different: the target is unknown and the model's chosen token becomes part of the next input.

### Construct the prediction problem

For a token sequence `[a,b,c,d]`, a three-position input can be `[a,b,c]` with targets `[b,c,d]`. At each position, causal attention permits only the prefix ending there. The final input c has a target d, even though d is outside the input slice. Padding masks and ignored labels remove artificial or deliberately unscored targets. Attention masks separately control what each position can read.

### Predict, score, differentiate, update

Embedding lookup maps IDs to vectors. Decoder blocks transform them. A vocabulary projection produces logits at each position. Softmax describes the next-token distribution, while a stable cross-entropy implementation can consume logits directly. If probabilities assigned to three realised targets are 0.5, 0.25, and 0.8, total negative log-likelihood is about 2.303 and mean is about 0.768 nats over three targets.

Backpropagation computes gradients of that loss through trainable operations. The optimizer applies an update using those gradients and any stored history. Clear gradient buffers at the intended update boundary, not indiscriminately between microbatches that should accumulate. Repeat with training examples. Teacher-forced training scores many positions in parallel under the causal mask; it does not sample a new sequence for every ordinary next-token update.

### Check progress without fitting the answers

Periodically evaluate development loss with frozen weights and evaluation behaviour. Use it to select a checkpoint. Test evaluates the selected model, not every trial until a pleasing score appears. Save compatible tokenizer, config, weights, and the additional optimizer/sampler state needed for continuation. A best checkpoint and the latest checkpoint answer different questions.

In this lab, scratch runs use real optimizer steps. Development loss is measured at step 1, each 20 steps, and the final step. `last.pt` is overwritten; it is not a history of model states. The standard export contains selected weights and final evidence, not a replay of all earlier token probabilities. The architecture diagram's head-only derivative is an illustration; the trainer differentiates the full trainable scratch network.

Sources: [D2L: language-model training](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/rnn-scratch.html), [PyTorch: CrossEntropyLoss](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss.html), [PyTorch: checkpointing](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).
